THE COMPLETE EDITION
Corrections and edition updates
Report a correction

Send corrections to juned.alam.dev@gmail.com. Use the subject Agentic AI Engineering - correction. Include the edition/version from the copyright page, the chapter and section heading, the printed page number, and a short description of the problem. A source, calculation or small reproducible example helps distinguish a technical error from a different design choice.

For code problems, include the lab name, Python version, installed dependency versions, command, expected result and observed result. Remove credentials, customer data and private records before sharing a reproduction. The examples use fictional records and local fixtures; a report should not require access to a reader's production system.
How corrections are recorded

Reports are reviewed before they become confirmed errata. A confirmed entry records the affected edition, stable chapter/section, issue, correction and first corrected version. Page numbers can move after typesetting, so chapter and section identifiers remain the preferred reference. Unresolved questions remain distinguishable from verified errors.

When a corrected file is issued, its version and preparation date change and the companion changelog records the differences. Examples and their dependency notes are updated together when a correction changes executable behavior. This process does not imply a fixed response time or a guarantee that every future framework release will be supported.
Edition status and learning scope

Version 1.0-rc.1, prepared 17 October 2026, is a publication review candidate. Independent human technical review, professional copyediting and target-reader testing are pending. The preparation date is not a claim that the book has been publicly released.

AI tools were used to generate and revise manuscript text, assist with examples and technical checks, and create cover illustrations. Automated checks and AI-assisted review do not establish independent human approval. Technical diagrams are editable illustrations developed for the book; the case studies and named teaching systems are fictional.
Working with the companion

The attached Agentic_AI_Engineering_companion.zip contains the example guides, dependency lists, tests and the chapter sources used by snippet tests. Keep the extracted chapters/ and examples/ folders together. Read START_HERE.txt before choosing a lab and consult its guide for the boundary between executed checks, simulated services and unexecuted integration work.

The diagrams, analogy limits, exercises and self-checks are part of this complete book. Technical references remain in the chapters and appendices so readers can inspect the mechanisms and version-specific claims behind the explanation.

semantic_records.text: THE VISUAL LEARNING ROUTE
See it. Trace it. Predict it.

A diagram becomes useful when you can explain what changes inside it. Each chapter has three complete visual labs. The A lab connects an analogy to a concrete mechanism. The B lab applies it to an inspectable case. The C lab develops another mechanism using a primary source and an original worked example.

A three-pass reading habit See: Name the records, actors, permissions or quantities in the picture. Read the starting conditions before following a line. Trace: Follow the three numbered reading cues. Identify what changed and what stayed true. A green cell marks a changed field; a PASS or ALLOW label states a decision. Predict: Answer the question in the dark strip. Say which visible fact supports your answer. Then use the answer link to check your reasoning.
Read the picture accurately

Numbered routes are matched to their route log. A denied route ends at a stop mark. Lines in a time lane show event order, not elapsed duration. Numeric bars and capacity trays use proportional lengths. An interval shows uncertainty around a measured proportion in a constructed sample.

Every lab states its assumptions. A real system needs the contracts and checks discussed in the chapter; a drawn boundary cannot enforce them. Status words and symbols accompany colour, so the important decisions remain visible in monochrome.

All visual learning is integrated into this complete book. Prediction answers are in Appendix H. The new C labs link to primary references in Appendix I. The part-opening maps show the learning route; security and authority remain requirements throughout.
THE COMPLETE EDITION
Preface: build understanding before autonomy

An AI agent can look impressive after a short demonstration. Give a model a few tools and it may search a document, inspect an order and propose a refund. The difficult work begins when the order belongs to another customer, the payment service times out, the model reads a malicious instruction, or the process restarts halfway through the task.

This book explains the engineering that makes those situations manageable. Its central idea is simple: the model proposes what to do; the surrounding application decides what may happen, performs the work and checks the result. Once that distinction is clear, the rest of the architecture becomes easier to understand.
One familiar picture

ANALOGY / A capable assistant in a well-run workplace Imagine hiring an assistant who can read quickly, explain unfamiliar material and suggest a useful next step. You would still give that person a defined role, access to the right records, a spending limit and a way to ask for approval. You would record important decisions and check that promised work actually happened. The assistant's talent would not replace those arrangements. An agent system needs the same separation of responsibilities. The model supplies useful judgment-shaped proposals. Your software supplies the records, rules, tools and checks. Where it stops: a model does not become a responsible employee merely because its language sounds human. Its apparent confidence is not evidence of permission, accuracy or successful execution.

The analogy is a starting point, not a substitute for precise terms. Each chapter connects an everyday situation to a concrete mechanism, then marks the point at which the comparison stops helping. That lets you remember the idea without inheriting a misleading assumption.
Two systems we will build on

ShopAssist is a customer-support agent for a fictional retailer. It can read an order, retrieve a returns policy and help prepare a refund. A refund is a useful teaching example because it is easy to understand and expensive to repeat accidentally. We will use it to connect tool schemas, identity, approval, idempotency, evidence and recovery.

AegisOps is an incident-response system. It investigates a failing service, collects evidence, proposes a response and, when policy permits, helps execute a controlled change. It forces us to connect several disciplines: distributed systems, access control, workflow, verification, monitoring and human judgment. We will build its responsibilities in stages rather than begin with a crowd of autonomous agents.

The examples are fictional teaching systems. Their purpose is to expose decisions you will face in a real system. A number printed in an example is an assumption for that example unless a source or measurement method says otherwise.
The route through the book

Chapters 1-4 explain the model and the basic control patterns. Chapters 5-11 build the runtime around it: tools, state, context, memory and reusable skills. Chapters 12-15 connect the runtime to knowledge and other systems. Chapters 16-18 add workflows, collaboration and human approval.

Chapters 19-22 explain the boundaries that an action-taking agent must respect. Chapters 23-28 cover failure, testing, evaluation, observation, operation and cost. Chapters 29-35 map the ideas onto platforms, frameworks and specialized use cases. Chapters 36-39 assemble the pieces into capstone projects.

Figure P.1. Learn the system in layers. Each layer gives the next one something dependable to stand on. Security is required before you ship actions, even if you are reading the book in a different order. Start with one bounded task, then add only the machinery it needs. Diagram labels in reading order: Understand the model; Chapters 1-4: capability, intent and control.; Build the runtime; Chapters 5-11: tools, state and context.; Connect and coordinate; Chapters 12-18: evidence, protocols and people.; Constrain and measure; Chapters 19-28: security, quality and operations.; Assemble and verify; Chapters 29-39: platforms and working projects.

If you are building your first agent, read Chapters 1-2, 5-8 and 11 first. Then read Chapters 18-24 before enabling consequential actions. If your work is mainly retrieval, add Chapters 12-13 and 25-26. If you operate a platform, continue through Chapters 27-33. Architects can use Chapter 35 to review a proposed design, but the questions become much more useful after the underlying mechanisms are familiar.
Choose a starting point

You do not need to train a neural network to use this book. You should be comfortable reading a small Python function, a JSON record and an HTTP request. SQLite, transactions and asynchronous execution become useful as the runtime grows. When a term is unfamiliar, use the glossary and the short model bridge in Chapter 1 before continuing.

Your immediate goal | Reading route | What to build or explain
Understand models and agents | Chapter 1 model bridge, then 2-3 | Separate learned weights, supplied context and software authority.
Build retrieval | 12-13, then the evaluation and tracing parts of 25-26 | Run the same questions through a fixed and a bounded adaptive search.
Coordinate work | 16, then 17, then 15 | Learn dependencies and delegation before remote-agent protocol details.
Build the capstone | 35, then 36-38 | Choose a design, define its contract, run the small example, then extend it.

This is a spiral: first learn the decision, then the mechanism, then the failure cases. Keep Chapters 18-24 in your route before enabling consequential actions.
Get the runnable examples from this PDF

This complete PDF carries an attachment named Agentic_AI_Engineering_companion.zip. In a PDF reader that supports attachments, open its Attachments panel, save the ZIP, and extract it into a local folder. Some browser previews hide attachments; save the PDF and open it in an attachment-capable reader. Read START_HERE.txt and examples/README.md in the extracted folder. The editable source package contains the same examples.

Begin with the standard-library harness and retrieval lab. The framework capstone and telemetry regression checks use their own documented dependency environments. Each lab states which services are simulated, what was actually executed, and what its tests establish. The included chapter files let regression tests execute the same functions printed in the book. Keep chapters/ beside examples/ when extracting the companion.

The digital edition includes heading and reading-order tags, text alternatives for diagrams, and linear alternatives for compact tables. These help navigation and interpretation; they do not constitute a PDF/UA certification or a substitute for assistive-reader testing. The labels and explanations also remain visible on the page.
How a chapter should feel

Begin with the situation and the analogy. Read the explanation until you can say what the system must remember, what it may change and how it knows the task is finished. Follow the diagram with your finger, including the failure path. Then work through the example and predict what would happen if one assumption changed.

Do the self-check before looking at Appendix G. For an exercise, use the acceptance criteria to decide whether your implementation demonstrates the intended property. Appendix F gives the solution approach; it does not replace running your code and observing its behavior.

The diagrams use a small set of consistent meanings. Deep ink marks model or core-system responsibilities. Cyan-teal marks ordinary runtime work and information flow. Amber marks side effects or waits. Red marks a denial, a risk or a control boundary. Green highlights verification and outcomes. Blue highlights records or evidence; violet marks external dependencies. Every important distinction also has a word, shape or label, so it remains understandable without colour.
Code and evidence

Most snippets are deliberately small. A listing marked illustrative shows a mechanism and its stated interface; it is not a complete production service. The included mini-harness, retrieval comparison, judge-evaluation fixture and graph capstone are executable teaching programs with deterministic checks. Their documentation states exactly what is simulated, what persists, which failures each demonstrates and what remains outside the example.

Never turn a teaching simplification into a production promise. A checkpoint is not automatically a durable workflow. A successful API response is not always proof of the business outcome. A local unique key does not, on its own, make an external effect happen exactly once. The book returns to these distinctions because they change how systems behave after failure.

Framework APIs and protocols change. Use the dated primary references in the relevant chapters and check the version you install. The durable skills are learning to define a contract, identify a failure window, test an invariant and collect evidence that the invariant held.
A useful habit

Before adding a new agent or tool, write one sentence that names its job and one sentence that names its boundary. Then state what evidence would convince you that it succeeded. If those sentences are hard to write, more autonomy will make the design harder to understand. A small system with visible responsibilities is a better foundation for learning and for production.

PART I / LEARNING MAP. Foundations & Mental Models. A READING ROUTE, NOT AN EXECUTION SEQUENCE. 01. Model runtime. Separate generation from execution.. 02. Agent anatomy. Give every responsibility an owner.. 03. Control patterns. Choose how the next step is selected.. 04. Instructions. Keep policy and task context distinct.. WHAT YOU CAN EXPLAIN OR BUILD. Explain what the model proposes and what your software must control.
Chapter 1. LLM Runtime Fundamentals for Agent Engineers

A customer tells ShopAssist, "I was charged twice." A language model can interpret that sentence, propose a payment lookup and write a clear explanation. It cannot make the refund legitimate merely by describing it confidently. Someone must identify the customer, obtain records, check policy and decide whether money may move. The software performing those jobs is the runtime. Understanding this boundary is the starting point for every agent we will build.

This chapter follows one model request from preparation to response. We will connect tokens, structured output, tools, streaming, errors and cost to the responsibilities of the surrounding application. Our goal is a useful engineering model of an LLM endpoint, not a complete account of neural-network training. Once the boundary is clear, later chapters can add control loops without pretending that a prompt supplies permissions, durable memory or reliable execution.

ANALOGY / The consultant and the case folder Imagine hiring a knowledgeable consultant who receives one case folder at a time. The folder contains your brief, relevant records and forms for requesting work from other departments. The consultant returns an explanation or a completed request form. Your office checks the request and performs any authorized work. For the next consultation, you prepare another folder containing the information needed to continue. Where it stops: the consultant represents a model endpoint, not a person with intentions. A model has knowledge learned during training, and provider services may retain conversation or reasoning state. Your application must understand those services rather than assume the folder contains every kind of state.

VISUAL LAB 1A / SEE · TRACE · PREDICT. What goes into this consultation?. ShopAssist prepares a second consultation about ORD-104233. The first lookup found two captures; no refund has been approved.. Call folder. Order: ORD-104233. Captures: PAY-A and PAY-B. Policy: duplicate-v3. Retained run. Lookup result: OBS-7. Continuation: opaque REF-9. Refund status: not proposed. Action desk. Allowed: own-order lookup. Refund needs exact approval. Verify external receipt. The call folder selects retained, permitted facts.. Action checks apply to every proposed operation.. Inspect the payment identifiers supplied to this call.. The continuation reference stays in the runtime, where the adapter can preserve required provider items.. The action desk decides whether a proposal may execute.. PREDICT. If the next folder omits OBS-7, may the model assume the duplicate captures still exist?. A call receives selected evidence; authority remains outside the generated response.. Fictional records; folder contents simplify serialized context. Provider continuation requirements vary, and the consultant analogy supplies no human accountability.. Check your prediction
What the model actually does

A token is a unit used to represent content. For text it may be a word, a word fragment, punctuation or another small piece. The exact split depends on the tokenizer, so a character count is only an estimate of token count. An identifier that looks short to a person can occupy many tokens. This matters because providers commonly meter input and generated output in tokens, and because a request must fit the model's permitted context.

For a conventional autoregressive text model, generation repeatedly chooses a next token from a distribution conditioned on the available context. Each generated token becomes part of what conditions the next choice. This explains both fluent continuation and sensitivity to an early mistake: a guessed order number can influence later tool arguments. It does not explain away all useful reasoning as "just autocomplete." The engineering point is that a plausible continuation is a proposal whose factual and operational consequences still need checking.

Temperature, where supported, changes how concentrated the sampling distribution is. A lower setting generally reduces variation; it does not turn an LLM service into a deterministic business function. Backend execution, model revisions and other settings may still change output. Some reasoning endpoints do not expose the same sampling controls as ordinary chat models. Select parameters supported by the endpoint and evaluate them on the task, rather than assuming that one setting works everywhere.

The context window is a limit on the content available to one inference operation. Treat learned general knowledge separately from current evidence. The model may know what a refund is, yet have no reliable knowledge of this customer's current payments. In the case-folder analogy, general expertise belongs to the consultant; the exact payment records belong in the folder. Reserve room for the requested output and any provider-specific reasoning budget, and count the serialized request rather than only the visible user sentence.

Figure 1.1. A reply is a proposal. Prediction and execution have different owners. Fluency does not grant permission. Diagram labels in reading order: Prepare context; Runtime selects instructions, records and tool contracts.; Generate proposal; Model emits text or a structured tool request.; Proposal crosses into application authority; Validate response; Runtime checks status, shape, meaning and authority.; Use the result; Only accepted output may drive the next operation.

A provider's stop reason tells the runtime why generation ended, for example an ordinary end, a tool request, a length limit or a refusal. Normalize these outcomes without losing their operational meaning. A response cut off by its output limit is not a complete JSON decision. A refusal is not an invitation to keep repairing the same request. Inspect status before parsing or scheduling work, and preserve provider-specific distinctions needed by the controller.
Messages and roles

Chat interfaces often organize content into messages with roles such as system, developer, user, assistant and tool. Their precise hierarchy is provider-specific. The application supplies standing instructions; the user supplies a request; earlier assistant messages contain model outputs; tool messages contain observations returned by the runtime. Preserve these distinctions when adapting providers. Combining every field into one anonymous string can lose both provider-required structure and useful provenance.

A role is not a sufficient security boundary. A tool response may contain a customer email, and that email may contain instructions telling the agent to send private data elsewhere. Calling the containing message "tool" does not make its contents trustworthy. The runtime should know which fields are verified records and which are external text. The model can be told to treat external text as data, but permission checks and data-egress controls must still live outside it.
A short bridge from learning to generation

Machine learning fits parameters from examples rather than writing every decision rule by hand. Deep learning uses multiple learned transformations to build representations: numerical features that help a model perform its task. A text transformer begins with token identifiers and learned representations plus position information. Attention combines information from permitted positions, while other learned layers transform those representations. In a causal language model, a prediction position cannot attend to future answer tokens. A final projection produces scores over the vocabulary; normalization and the decoding policy turn those scores into a next-token choice.

Figure 1.2. One next-token prediction. A conceptual text-generation path; real model and serving implementations vary. The request supplies context; learned weights supply transformations. Diagram labels in reading order: Token IDs and positions; Tokenizer output enters learned representations.; Transformer layers; Causal attention and learned transformations combine context.; Vocabulary scores; One score per candidate next token.; Decode one token; Choose under the endpoint's supported policy; repeat.

Training evaluates a learning objective on examples and uses an optimizer to update weights. Inference uses the deployed weights to process a request and produce output. Adding a policy passage to a prompt changes the request context; it is not ordinarily a weight update. Fine-tuning performs additional training, whereas retrieval supplies selected external facts at inference time. An endpoint can separately store conversations or collect data under its service policy, so unchanged inference weights do not imply that no data is retained anywhere.

Think of weights as a practiced way to read the consultant's folder and context as this case's contents. Where this extension stops: weights are distributed numerical parameters, not a filing cabinet of exact propositions, and attention weights are not a reliable explanation of why a claim is true. We need neither a human intention nor an exact stored quotation to explain generation. For engineering, the distinction tells us why a newly retrieved order can guide an answer without retraining, and why a plausible answer still needs a source check.

Prerequisites: basic Python functions and HTTP request/response vocabulary are enough for this chapter. After it, you should be able to separate learned weights, request context and runtime authority. Chapter 12 develops comparable retrieval representations; Chapter 30 develops adaptation choices. The original Transformer paper explains the architecture's foundations; its encoder-decoder design is not identical to every present-day causal model.
Structured outputs: making the model speak in contracts

Programs need decisions they can inspect reliably. A refund router might return an intent, an order identifier and a short explanation. Prompting for JSON is a useful starting point, but the result may contain prose, missing fields or an unexpected value. JSON mode, where available, improves syntactic validity without necessarily enforcing the application's schema. Schema-constrained output adds another layer by restricting supported output shapes. Providers differ in the JSON Schema subset and strict-mode conventions they accept.

Shape and meaning are different checks. A field can be a valid integer and still name an order belonging to another customer. A positive refund amount can exceed the remaining captured balance. Use schema validation to eliminate malformed requests, then use domain checks against current authoritative records. A provider's decoding constraints do not replace either application validation or authorization. They reduce avoidable parsing failures and make the boundary easier to inspect.

The following working schema uses Pydantic 2. It validates the decision locally; an adapter must separately transform its JSON Schema into the provider's supported form. The after-model validator checks the complete object, including fields supplied through defaults. This avoids relying on a field validator that may not run for an omitted default-valued field.

Validation failures can sometimes be repaired by giving the model the rejected object and a concise description of the errors. Bound that process. Two repair attempts mean at most three logical generations, not necessarily three network attempts: each generation may also contain transport retries. Record usage for every completed response, including rejected ones. A cost counter that sees only the final valid object hides the most expensive part of a difficult request.

Figure 1.3. Accept shape and meaning separately. A valid form can still describe an invalid transaction. Count rejected responses as real work and real cost. Diagram labels in reading order: Generate decision; Use provider-supported output constraints.; Check shape; Parse the response using the application schema.; Check meaning; Confirm identifiers, preconditions and business rules.; Accept or stop; Repair only within a separate, recorded allowance.
Tool calling is intent, not execution

A tool call contains a capability name, arguments and usually an identifier tying the eventual result to the request. ShopAssist might propose list_payments for ORD-104233. Nothing has happened to the payments system yet. The runtime first confirms that the tool exists, validates its arguments and checks whether this principal may access that order. It then invokes the implementation and returns the observation associated with the call identifier.

On the next model request, the payment observation becomes part of the available context. The model can now distinguish two captures from one authorization and one capture. If it proposes issue_refund, the runtime applies a different gate because money may move. Authorization, approval, preconditions, idempotency and execution budgets belong here. This is why the distinction between a form and the work requested by that form is useful: the same model output can be accepted, denied, deferred or escalated.

Never send an arbitrary generated string directly to a shell, interpreter, database or unrestricted HTTP client. A typed capability should expose the narrow operation the application intends to allow. Even a read tool needs resource authorization, result minimization and a deadline. Reads can reveal private information, consume quotas or trigger billable services. Tool calling makes operations easier to structure; it does not make their consequences automatically harmless.
Streaming, latency, rate limits and provider behaviour

A streamed response delivers pieces before the full output is available. This helps a person see progress and can let the runtime detect the shape of an intended tool call earlier. It does not make partial arguments safe to execute. Assemble the complete request, check the response's completion status and validate its arguments before acting. If the stream fails halfway, distinguish an incomplete response from a successful decision rather than trying to guess the missing suffix.

Measure time to first token from the client's request start. That measurement normally includes network, provider queueing and initial processing visible to the client. After the first token, the remaining generated content adds time at a variable throughput. A useful approximation is client-measured TTFT plus remaining generated tokens divided by observed generation rate. Do not add queueing again if TTFT already includes it. Tool loops multiply these costs because each decision may require another model round trip.

Provider failures need different responses. A rate limit may justify delayed retry with jitter and Retry-After support. A transient service failure may justify a bounded retry or evaluated fallback. A malformed request or unsupported schema is usually an application error. An oversized context needs pruning, not identical repetition. A safety refusal should be surfaced or handled through an appropriate alternative, not treated as malformed JSON to repair until the model complies.

Retries need one owner and one allowance. If the SDK permits four total attempts and the application permits four total attempts, one logical operation can produce sixteen downstream attempts. Here an attempt cap includes the initial call: four extra retries at each layer would instead permit (1 + 4) x (1 + 4) = 25 attempts. Set a request deadline and a maximum attempt count across the chosen owner. Respect cancellation during backoff. A retry policy should improve availability without turning a provider incident into a quota or cost incident. Provider responses may be billable even when the application later rejects them.
Hallucination, uncertainty and grounding

Hallucination is useful shorthand for content that is unsupported or false despite sounding plausible. In ShopAssist, a fabricated policy sentence is damaging because it may become a promise or a refund proposal. Grounding supplies relevant evidence: current orders, payment records and policy passages. It does not guarantee that the model interprets them correctly. The runtime must still verify consequential facts and distinguish supported conclusions from guesses.

Use evidence identifiers that resolve to retained source records. Ask for short, checkable justifications, such as the payment identifiers and policy section supporting a refund. Include an explicit insufficient_evidence outcome so the model has a valid way to stop. A self-reported confidence score can be studied as a routing feature, but it should not be the sole basis for moving money. Calibration requires labeled examples and measurement, not merely a number between zero and one.
The stateless model and the stateful runtime

For ordinary independent requests, continuity comes from the application supplying relevant history and state. Losing that application record can lose the explanation of what happened, even if the next model is highly capable. Provider conversation storage is useful, but understand its retention, retrieval and failure semantics. The application still needs enough durable information to audit actions, recover work and move between providers when those are requirements.

Do not reduce every modern endpoint to plain text alone. Reasoning APIs may require opaque reasoning items or other provider-specific fields to be carried between tool turns. A normalized interface should preserve such required continuation information without exposing private reasoning as a user-facing transcript. Provider substitution is therefore a tested capability, not a promise that swapping a model name preserves every behavior. Context compatibility and evaluation matter alongside message serialization.

Figure 1.4. The case folder has several records. These are conceptual layers, not proportional storage sizes. Recoverable continuity needs explicit ownership. Diagram labels in reading order: Run state; Goal, verified facts, budgets and pending work.; Conversation record; Messages and tool-call/result associations.; Provider continuation; Required opaque items, retained under policy.; Model context; A selected per-call view of the retained records.
Provider abstraction and basic routing

Put provider differences behind an adapter. The rest of the application should receive its own message, tool-call, response-status and usage types rather than a scattered collection of SDK objects. Normalize refusal, truncation, rate limits and invalid requests carefully: a convenient common type must not erase a distinction the controller needs. Retain required provider extension data in a controlled field when complete normalization would lose information.

Basic routing chooses a model policy for a task class. A small model may handle a measured classification workload; a stronger one may improve diagnosis or planning. The choice depends on evaluated success, latency, token use and operational limits. Fallbacks also need evaluation. A cheaper provider that interprets the same tool contract differently can create a more expensive failure. Start with a small routing policy whose reasons can be explained and observed.

Failure modes and how to recognise them

A sudden token bill increase can mean growing history, repeated repair or duplicated retries. Diagnose those mechanisms separately before changing the model. A wrong resource identifier points toward missing semantic validation or unsupported evidence. A broken JSON fragment points toward truncation or unsafe character slicing. A behavior change after a provider upgrade points toward contract compatibility and evaluation. These symptoms are actionable because the adapter and runtime record their decisions.
Production lens

Every model call should have a correlation identifier, model/version information, completion status, elapsed time and usage records under an appropriate privacy policy. Retry and repair allowances must be visible and separate. Do not log credentials or indiscriminately retain raw customer records to achieve observability. A compact context manifest and controlled source references often explain a decision with less sensitive material. Chapters 8 and 26 develop these records in detail.
Interview drills

If asked where an LLM application's state lives, distinguish application records, provider service state and the context available to one inference. If asked why a valid tool call is insufficient, trace schema, resource authorization, preconditions and execution. If asked how to handle invalid JSON, begin with completion status and provider constraints, then describe bounded local validation and repair. Each answer should identify the owner of the guarantee rather than merely name a framework feature.
Key takeaways

The useful boundary is between a generated proposal and an authorized operation. Tokens and context limits explain important cost and latency behavior, while explicit records explain continuity. Structured output improves the shape of decisions; evidence, business rules and permissions determine whether those decisions may be used. A provider adapter makes those distinctions available to the controller. It succeeds when failures remain understandable, bounded and recoverable.

Chapter 2. What Is an AI Agent? Anatomy, Autonomy & Boundaries

ShopAssist could answer a refund question by following a fixed script: fetch the order, check a policy and draft a reply. It could also investigate a less predictable problem, choosing another payment lookup when the first result reveals something unexpected. Both systems may use the same language model. What changes is who chooses the next step and how much freedom that choice has. This chapter turns that distinction into an architecture you can inspect.

We will use a deliberately narrow working definition: an LLM agent is a goal-directed software system in which a model repeatedly chooses among bounded capabilities, observes results and continues until verified completion or an explicit stopping condition. Other fields use broader meanings of agent. Our definition is useful because every part maps to something an engineer must implement, test and operate. It also makes autonomy a design decision rather than a marketing label.

ANALOGY / A taxi with a destination and operating rules A taxi passenger chooses a destination, while the driver chooses turns using current traffic and road conditions. A fixed train route chooses the path in advance. The taxi company still sets operating rules: licensed driver, permitted area, fare limits and a way to stop the journey. An agent resembles the taxi when discoveries change its route; a workflow resembles the train when known steps determine the path. Where it stops: software authorization must be enforced before actions, and a model is not a licensed person exercising accountable professional judgment. A driver analogy does not prove that a generated decision is safe.

Chatbot, LLM app, workflow or agent?

A chatbot is an interaction pattern: the user asks, the system replies. That interface may conceal a simple model call, a fixed workflow or an agent. An LLM application is the broader category of software that uses a model; it does not imply autonomous control. A workflow defines its sequencing and available branches in application code. The model may classify a ticket into one of those branches while the workflow retains overall control.

An agent repeatedly decides what to do next from observations. The number and order of useful operations may not be fixed beforehand. ShopAssist investigating duplicate charges might first inspect payment records, then consult a refund policy, then ask for clarification if the records contradict the customer's account. The capability set and boundaries remain authored. Model-directed sequencing does not require unrestricted tools or the ability to invent new privileges.

Most useful systems mix these shapes. A fixed support workflow can contain one bounded investigation node. Conversely, an agent can call a refund skill whose eligibility checks and transaction sequence are deterministic. Ask where a decision benefits from fresh judgment and where a stable rule already describes it. Add freedom at that boundary. This is more precise than arguing whether the entire application deserves the word agent.

Choose the smallest useful architecture first

Before adding a loop, ask whether one model call with a checked output contract solves the task. Use a fixed workflow when sources and decision branches are known. Add retrieval when the answer depends on current or private facts. Add a bounded agentic investigation when observations genuinely change which authorized source or operation should come next. Multiple agents add coordination and ownership obligations; they need a concrete division of work and evidence of value. Chapter 35 returns to this design review with the full operating picture.

Model adaptation answers a related but different diagnosis. Unclear instructions or malformed output suggest improving prompting, schema and validation first. Missing or changing facts suggest retrieval and source lifecycle work. A stable recurring behavior with reviewed training examples may justify evaluating fine-tuning. Serving cost or latency may suggest routing, caching, distillation or serving changes, all under the same quality gates. These interventions can coexist and none guarantees improvement. Chapter 30 supplies the detailed adaptation discussion; start with a measured failure, not a favorite technique.
The anatomy of an agent

Start with a task specification. It describes the desired result and how the controller can verify it. "Resolve the duplicate charge" is incomplete unless resolution means something observable: the duplicate capture was identified, an allowed refund was recorded, the customer received the outcome and the support ticket contains evidence. Some tasks have softer completion criteria, such as a sufficiently supported research answer. Their verifier needs a documented rubric rather than pretending that every outcome is mechanically provable.

The controller runs the loop and decides whether work may continue. It asks a context builder for the current view, invokes a model adapter, checks proposed operations and collects results. A tool registry names available capabilities and their contracts. A policy component checks identity, resource scope and risk. State records what is true about the run; memory may contribute governed information from earlier runs. Telemetry explains which steps occurred and why the run stopped.

These components have different kinds of uncertainty. Controller logic can be deterministic while a database result changes between reads. A tool may call an unreliable network service or even another model. Therefore "outside the main model" is not the same as "always deterministic." The goal is explicit contracts and owners: deterministic checks enforce invariants, while variable external behavior is bounded, recorded and reconciled. Pretending all tools are predictable makes recovery harder to design.

The agent loop: observe, decide, act, update

Observation begins before the model speaks. The runtime assembles the user's request, current goal, relevant state, allowed tool descriptions and fresh evidence. ShopAssist handling ORD-104233 starts with customer identity and an order lookup permission. It does not start with permission to refund an arbitrary payment merely because the user mentioned money. The context records what is known and what remains to be checked so the model does not reconstruct progress from guesswork.

The model then proposes list_payments for the order. The controller validates the identifier and confirms that the authenticated customer may inspect that resource. If allowed and within budget, the executor calls the payment service. Its result contains two captures of 2499 minor units, each with a stable payment identifier and timestamp. The runtime records the observation, its source and its retrieval time. Only then can the next decision reason about a duplicate capture.

Suppose the next proposal is a refund. The same loop now encounters a financial action requiring stronger checks. The runtime confirms the captured and already-refunded amounts, derives the remaining refundable balance and creates an approval proposal bound to the exact payment, currency and amount. It checkpoints the pending work and returns a waiting outcome. The model has changed the route, but it has not bypassed the route's gates. Chapter 18 develops approval binding and review in detail.

Deterministic boundaries around probabilistic decisions

A prompt can tell ShopAssist never to refund more than the captured amount. That instruction helps the model propose sensible actions. The refund service must enforce the same invariant against current records because another input, another model version or an injection may produce a different proposal. Put checks where their protected consequence occurs. The service boundary is also valuable because the invariant still holds when a human tool or another application uses the service.

Checks before the model govern what information and capabilities it receives. They include task schema, authenticated identity, tenant isolation, data classification and allowed tools. Checks after the model govern whether a proposal may become work: argument validation, resource authorization, risk routing and available budget. Checks after execution govern what may be recorded as fact or success. This three-part structure avoids making the model the last line of defense at any important boundary.

A useful review test is to replace the model with an adversarial scripted source. Let it propose every registered capability, oversized amounts, foreign order identifiers and false completion. What remains protected? If a dangerous operation now executes, the architecture relied on cooperative generation rather than enforcement. This test does not prove the application is universally secure, but it reveals missing boundaries cheaply and without a live model.
Autonomy levels

Autonomy describes how decisions become actions. In an assisted mode, the system provides information and a human performs the operation. In a propose mode, it prepares an exact action for human approval. In a supervised mode, some bounded actions proceed automatically while riskier ones require review. In an autonomous mode, an evaluated action class proceeds within policy, with monitoring, audit and a fast way to suspend further work.

Choose these modes per action class, not once for the whole agent. ShopAssist may autonomously retrieve the customer's own order, propose a refund for review and always escalate an account-security change. Read access still requires entitlement and egress controls. A low-risk internal ticket note may have a different policy from an external message, even when both tools look like text writing. Classify consequence, reversibility and blast radius rather than treating every write alike.

Promotion needs evidence relevant to the action's harm. Approval acceptance rate is one signal, but a high rate can conceal rubber-stamping or rare severe errors. Combine representative evaluation, rejection detection, incident history, review quality and governance requirements. Define how promotion is reversed. A configuration change should stop scheduling the action class promptly; active operations still require their own cancellation or reconciliation. More autonomy is useful only when it creates value at an acceptable operational cost.

Termination: budgets, loop limits and completion criteria

Success is an outcome supported by acceptance evidence. A model saying "done" is a claim to inspect. For a refund task, ask the payment service whether the intended refund exists and record its status. For a coding task, run the agreed checks and inspect the resulting artifact. For research, verify coverage and support according to the stated rubric. Different task types require different verifiers; the controller must not hide those differences behind one universal completion string.

Limits are another kind of termination. Bound model turns, executed tool calls, tokens, financial cost and elapsed time. Check remaining allowance before each operation, not only at the top of the loop. A model can return several tools in one response, and one slow tool can consume the whole deadline. An observed-cost counter can exceed a monetary limit by the cost of its last call; a hard cap requires conservative reservation or provider-side enforcement. Name the actual contract honestly.

Progress detection catches pathological work before a hard limit arrives. Repeated canonical tool arguments may indicate a stall, but repeated reads can also be legitimate polling. Define progress in the domain: new relevant evidence, a completed plan step or a changed external status. Store enough history to explain the decision. If the same payment lookup is returning unchanged data, schedule bounded waiting or escalate instead of charging for an endless model loop around it.

Every exit needs a reason and an appropriate next action. Completed, incomplete, waiting_for_approval, denied, cancelled, deadline, no_progress and outcome_unknown describe different realities. A safe stop does not undo effects already completed, nor does it guarantee that an in-flight external transaction never happened. Preserve partial results and uncertain intents so another worker or a human can reconcile them. Clear terminal states are as important to users as to incident investigators.

Build it: a mocked decision/action loop

Before adding a live model, exercise the control boundaries with a script. The following complete function uses explicit interfaces supplied as arguments. decide returns either a finish claim or a tool request; checked_execute performs argument validation, authority checks and bounded invocation. The verifier independently assesses a finish claim. The sample is intentionally synchronous and has a turn limit; it is not yet the durable multi-budget harness built in Chapter 11.

First script a valid lookup followed by a false finish claim. The verifier should return no acceptance evidence and the run should end incomplete. Then script a forbidden resource and assert that the tool counter remains zero. Finally script a mutation requiring approval and confirm that the run returns waiting without blocking for a person. These checks establish the owners of completion, authority and waiting before model variability makes failures more difficult to reproduce.
Failure modes

An unbounded agent consumes resources without reaching a useful outcome. An overpowered agent reaches capabilities its task did not need. A premature-completion agent gives the user a confident message while the external record remains unchanged. A prompt-only policy works in happy-path demos and fails under manipulation. Each failure suggests a different repair: operational budgets, filtered capabilities, independent acceptance verification or enforcement at the action boundary. Changing the model cannot substitute for these missing mechanisms.

Another failure is choosing an agent for a stable process. If all refund steps are known and eligibility is deterministic, a workflow with classification and drafting may be simpler to operate. Conversely, a brittle workflow can fail an investigation whose next useful source depends on new evidence. Compare the smallest designs that meet the goal. The right question is where judgment improves the path, followed immediately by how that judgment is contained.
Interview drills

When asked what makes a system agentic, identify the model's control over the next step rather than listing features such as memory or multiple tools. When asked where autonomy lives, point to concrete action classes and their gates. When asked how to prevent infinite loops, describe both hard resource allowances and domain-aware progress, then explain what record survives the stop. A good design answer connects each control to the failure it prevents.

For a support-agent design exercise, state the task and acceptance criteria first. Then name its permitted reads, proposed writes, external authorities and failure outcomes. Explain why a workflow suffices or why discovery requires a bounded agentic loop. Only after that choose a framework. This ordering makes the design review useful even when the model vendor or orchestration library changes, because reviewers can inspect the operating contract directly.
Key takeaways

An agent is a controlled system, not merely a model with tools attached. The model may choose the route while the controller owns permission, budgets, state and stopping. Autonomy belongs to evaluated action classes. Success needs acceptance evidence, and unsuccessful runs need explicit outcomes that preserve partial work and uncertainty. These principles give the next chapter a foundation for comparing reasoning patterns without confusing flexibility with reliability.

Chapter 3. Reasoning & Control Patterns

A tool-using model can be arranged in several ways. It can choose one route, choose every next operation, make a plan for an executor or review an answer before release. These arrangements determine where judgment enters the process and how often the application pays for it. The names are useful only when they make those decisions clearer. This chapter compares patterns as control flow, using the same ShopAssist task so differences remain concrete.

Consider a customer asking whether two captured payments represent a duplicate charge. Some work is predictable: the order and payments must be read, eligibility must be checked and any refund must pass policy. Other work may depend on discovery: a payment record could be missing, a policy may contain an exception or the customer's explanation may be ambiguous. We want judgment at those uncertain points without making the entire process an open-ended investigation.

ANALOGY / The editor organizing a reporting desk An editor can assign a reporter to one specialist desk, approve an outline before research, let the reporter follow each new lead or ask another editor to verify the final story. Several reporters can cover independent parts and return notes. These are different ways of organizing the same work, not a ladder from weak journalism to strong journalism. Where it stops: a software critic may share the generator's errors, and an agent's evidence and permissions require explicit machine-enforced contracts. A second opinion is not independent merely because it comes from another model call.

The pattern landscape

A deterministic workflow fixes sequencing and known branches. A router chooses among predefined handlers. A plan-and-execute design makes a reviewable outline before execution. A ReAct-style loop chooses the next action using the latest observation. Reflection adds critique and revision. Parallel workers divide independent work; a hierarchy introduces delegation and coordination. These mechanisms can be combined, and their presence does not identify one universally superior architecture.

Separate two questions: how often does the model choose the next step, and how is work organized or checked? A router makes one sequencing choice, while a ReAct loop makes many. Reflection may operate inside a fully fixed workflow. A supervisor may delegate deterministic jobs rather than autonomous subagents. Drawing all these patterns on one autonomy scale obscures those distinctions. Describe the actual model calls and their authority instead of assuming the pattern name answers both questions.

Figure 3.1. Sequencing and review are separate choices. Patterns combine rather than occupy one autonomy ladder. Count decisions and identify their owners before choosing a framework. Diagram labels in reading order: Who selects the path?; Workflow: application code; Router: one bounded classification; Plan: outline then execution; ReAct: choice after each observation; How is work organized?; Reflection: verify and revise; Parallel work: divide independent parts; Hierarchy: delegate and coordinate; Any shape still needs policy gates
ReAct: the tool-use loop

ReAct is commonly used to describe alternating reasoning, action and observation. The original research expressed thoughts and actions explicitly. A modern tool loop can use native tool requests and short checkable justifications instead of printing private internal reasoning. What matters for control flow is feedback: the model chooses an operation, the runtime executes an accepted request and the returned observation changes the next decision.

ShopAssist first searches the duplicate-charge policy. The policy says captured duplicates are eligible within a stated window. The model then asks for the order's payment records and learns that two captures occurred two seconds apart. It can now explain eligibility, or propose another lookup if one capture has already been refunded. A fixed plan need not guess those facts, but it must include branches for them. ReAct makes discovering such branches part of the ongoing decision process.

Its strength is adaptation; its cost is repeated calls and less predictable trajectories. A model may search several nearly identical phrasings or alternate between tools without improving the evidence. Place a step allowance, a total cost contract and progress detection around the loop. When progress stops, do not force a confident answer merely to terminate. Check whether existing evidence meets the acceptance criteria; otherwise return incomplete or insufficient_evidence with the useful records collected so far.

The following complete teaching function receives a checked executor and a verifier. These interfaces are intentional: policy and completion are not hidden inside model behavior. The result envelope stays valid JSON because bounding happens inside the executor's fields before serialization. A production loop additionally needs durable state, cancellation, provider status handling and per-operation deadlines; Chapter 11 provides a working small version of those boundaries.

Figure 3.2. A lead becomes an observation. An unchanged observation need not justify another paid decision. Feedback earns its cost only when it changes what the system can know or do. Diagram labels in reading order: Bounded ReAct; Read current evidence; Goal, accepted facts and unresolved questions.; Propose next operation; Model chooses an allowed capability.; Check and execute; Runtime enforces authority and resource limits.; Record the observation; Valid result envelope with source and call ID.; Assess progress; Continue, verify completion or stop explicitly.
Routers: cheap, reliable specialisation

A router makes a structured classification: order_status, refund, product_question or escalate. Each route leads to a handler with an appropriate capability set and policy. An order-status workflow can be inexpensive and deterministic after routing. A refund handler can require approval, and a product handler can retrieve catalog passages. Separating them reduces tool ambiguity and prevents unrelated capabilities from appearing in every request.

Include an escape path for unsupported or ambiguous inputs. If a customer reports both an account takeover and a refund, the router should not confidently place the entire request into an ordinary refund workflow. Evaluate per-route precision and recall on representative labeled requests, including mixed intents and unfamiliar language. A small model is a candidate, not a guarantee of lower total cost: misrouting can consume downstream work and create harmful promises.

A generated confidence score may help define a routing feature, but an arbitrary threshold such as 0.6 is not calibrated reliability. Study confidence against actual errors and compare it with deterministic signals, disagreement or missing required information. The escape path contains uncertainty; it does not excuse careless classification. Measure how often it is used and whether its handler can safely resolve the request, rather than declaring every escalation a successful route.
Plan-and-execute

A plan makes intended work visible before actions begin. Use short steps with stable identifiers, allowed actions, dependencies and reasons. A plan for ShopAssist might fetch the order, inspect captures, evaluate refund eligibility, propose review and notify the customer after verified execution. The deterministic executor checks that identifiers are unique, dependencies exist, the graph is acyclic and every action fits the task's capabilities. A fluent plan is still untrusted proposed control flow.

References between steps need typed resolution. If step 3 needs the payment identifier returned by step 2, do not let a generated string silently become an arbitrary lookup into runtime objects. Define permitted references and validate their types before execution. Resolve them only after the dependency produced an accepted result. Missing or failed dependencies should trigger an explicit branch rather than allowing later work to continue with empty or guessed values.

Planning is useful when reviewability and progress tracking outweigh the larger initial call. Its weakness is staleness. An order may already have a refund, a tool can fail or a new policy passage may invalidate the amount calculation. Replan remaining work using the original goal, completed effects and the surprise. Preserve completed action identities; replanning does not make earlier work disappear. Bound the number of replans and require renewed approval if the proposed financial effect changes.

A useful hybrid has a short outer plan with a small ReAct loop inside each uncertain step. The plan supplies a reviewable direction, while each local loop can search or diagnose within its own allowance. Avoid writing an eight-step outline merely to wrap eight unrestricted agents. Nested budgets must compose into a run-level budget, and the supervisor must know whether a local step completed, exhausted its allowance or returned uncertainty.
Reflection, critics and evaluator-optimizer loops

Reflection asks for critique followed by revision. An evaluator-optimizer makes the loop explicit: generate, evaluate against a rubric and revise until accepted or the allowance ends. The evaluator is most useful when it brings a check the generator did not already perform. For a refund explanation, that could mean opening the cited policy version or comparing amounts with the payment record. For a code change, it could mean executing the relevant tests.

A critic reading only the same draft with the same unsupported assumptions can rubber-stamp an error or invent objections. Explicit criteria improve consistency, but model scoring remains an estimate. Define the output as accepted, rejected or unverified and retain the reasons. If the final revision has not been evaluated, do not return it in the same shape as an accepted draft. Return a result containing the text and its verification status so downstream code cannot accidentally promote it.

Deterministic checks should come first where they are sufficient. A parser can check a schema, and a business service can verify a refund cap more directly than a second model. Model critique may still help with coverage, relevance and clarity. Measure its incremental benefit on the same cases with and without reflection. Extra calls are justified by observable improvement or reduced harm, not by the reassuring appearance of a second pass.

Parallel workers, map-reduce and hierarchy

Parallelism helps when subtasks are independent. Several workers can extract relevant facts from separate documents and a reducer can synthesize their attributed results. It reduces wall-clock delay when capacity is available; it does not inherently reduce total token cost. Each worker may repeat instructions and request overhead, and the reducer adds another operation. Limit concurrency and aggregate the same run-level resource accounting across all workers.

Partial failure must survive reduction. If one of four sources could not be processed, the reducer needs both the missing source's identity and the resulting coverage gap. Do not simply drop exceptions and produce a confident complete answer from the remaining notes. Each partial result should retain source references and verification status. If the missing document could alter the answer, return partial or request another retrieval rather than claiming complete coverage.

Hierarchy adds a supervisor that assigns subgoals and combines outcomes. It is useful for meaningful specialization, such as an AegisOps metrics investigator and a change-history investigator. It also adds coordination, duplicated context and potential ownership conflicts. Keep writes under one owner, define handoff contracts and decide whether a worker is allowed to delegate further. Chapter 17 explores those boundaries; here, treat hierarchy as a decomposition choice rather than automatic sophistication.

Comparing the patterns quantitatively

Run candidate patterns on the same task set and compare accepted outcomes, failure types, model calls, input/output tokens, cost and latency distributions. Include straightforward requests, ambiguous cases, tool failures and insufficient evidence. A pattern that wins on easy examples but fails expensive edge cases is not necessarily preferable. Synthetic diagrams can explain shape, but they are not performance evidence. If you draw example call counts, label them as assumptions and explain which operations were counted. For a measured comparison, publish the model versions, prompts, tool behavior, dataset and scoring procedure. That makes the tradeoff inspectable and repeatable. Model choice, retrieval quality and runtime limits can change the result, so keep the conclusions scoped to the evaluated workload.

When a deterministic workflow beats an agent

Use a workflow when the route is known, the rules are stable or every branch must be inspectable before execution. ShopAssist can deterministically calculate refundable balance after the necessary facts arrive. It need not ask a model how to subtract already-refunded amounts. Classification or drafting may still use models while orchestration stays fixed. This concentrates probabilistic judgment where it contributes value and gives ordinary code responsibility for invariant calculation.

Use model-directed exploration when the next useful step depends on discoveries too varied to enumerate economically. An incident investigation often fits because new symptoms point to different sources. Even then, keep resource access, mutation policy, approval and verified outcomes deterministic around the investigation. The simplest sufficient pattern is a design result, not an ideological preference. A workflow and a bounded agent should be compared against the same goal and operating constraints.
Failure modes

ReAct can wander; routers can misclassify; plans can become stale; critics can accept unsupported claims; parallel reduction can conceal missing sources; hierarchies can duplicate work or overwrite shared changes. Diagnose the pattern's actual failure before adding another layer. For example, reflection does not fix an unauthorized tool boundary, and more workers do not repair a missing source. Add a control that addresses the mechanism and verify its effect on representative cases.
Interview drills

To compare ReAct with planning, explain the timing of sequencing decisions, the role of observations and the resulting cost and reviewability. To explain reflection, identify the evaluator's new evidence or rubric and its acceptance contract. To justify parallelism, show task independence, the concurrency cap and partial-result handling. A useful answer follows one concrete request through the chosen shape and names what happens when its strongest assumption fails.
Key takeaways

Control patterns organize judgment. They do not replace the runtime's authority or guarantee a particular quality level. Choose decision frequency, planning, verification and decomposition separately, then combine only what the task needs. Preserve evidence and explicit statuses through every branch. Evaluate the smallest plausible candidates on the same workload, and let observed outcomes justify additional calls rather than treating complexity as progress.

Chapter 4. Prompt & Instruction Architecture

ShopAssist's refund behavior changes when its instructions change. A sentence that once said "propose a refund" may become "issue a refund," altering tool selection and user promises even when application code is unchanged. That makes instructions an operational artifact: they need ownership, tests, versions and a way back. Their importance does not make them a substitute for policy enforcement. They tell the model how to work within a contract whose hard boundaries remain in software.

This chapter organizes instructions into a maintainable structure, then follows them from authoring to release and runtime composition. We will separate trusted configuration from customer text, use examples deliberately and test behavior against meaningful cases. The resulting system should explain both what the agent was instructed to do and what the runtime actually allowed. Those are related records, and they should never be confused.

ANALOGY / The operations handbook A support company gives staff a handbook. Different owners maintain its chapters: payments owns refund rules, privacy owns disclosure rules and customer experience owns reply style. A shift lead assembles the approved edition for the job. Letters from customers and documents found during investigation go into the case file, not into the handbook as new management orders. Where it stops: a model can misinterpret or follow hostile text despite this organization. Handbook structure guides behavior; authorization, data access and financial invariants still require checks outside the model.

The instruction hierarchy

An application trust hierarchy describes which sources may define behavior. Reviewed standing policy and trusted task configuration can supply instructions. A user's request describes desired work within that policy. Retrieved documents, tool results, emails and web pages provide information whose authority must be assessed. A document containing "ignore the refund rules" is a statement found in a document, not permission to override the application. This is an architecture rule, not a claim that formatting makes every model follow it.

Map the application's policy to the actual provider's message hierarchy. Providers differ in system/developer roles, supported fields and precedence. Do not assume that combining the roles makes them interchangeable. Keep business policy ownership independent of the wire format, then let the adapter put reviewed instructions into supported fields. Trusted task-specific guidance should come from validated runtime configuration; user-supplied strings must not become high-authority instructions simply because a template inserted them there.

Anatomy of a production system prompt

Begin with role and purpose. ShopAssist helps authenticated customers with their orders, returns and eligible refunds. State scope and an escape path: it does not handle account-security changes or legal advice, and those requests go to escalation. Define what successful work looks like, such as an evidence-backed answer or a reviewed financial proposal. This gives the model a useful destination without asking it to invent the operating rules along the way.

Next explain policies and tool guidance. Describe when to read the order, when to search the current policy and what must be verified before proposing a refund. Make reasons concrete: order identifiers must not be guessed because doing so can expose another customer's records. Explain uncertainty behavior and distinguish drafting from execution. The runtime must still enforce these rules, but clear instructions reduce invalid proposals and make the agent's normal trajectory easier to understand.

Finally specify evidence and output requirements. The model should cite retained evidence identifiers, admit missing information and produce the format the next consumer expects. A customer reply might have a short length limit and a chosen language; a routing decision needs a machine-readable schema. Avoid asking one giant output to serve incompatible consumers. The operations handbook can contain common principles, while the particular task adds the appropriate report form.

A useful starter instruction is: "Look up an identified order using the permitted order tool. Use current payment and policy evidence for refund decisions. Propose financial actions with the exact effect and evidence required by the runtime. Do not claim a refund succeeded until the payment system confirms it. If evidence is missing or conflicting, state the gap and use escalation." This is a behavioral brief, not the financial authorization mechanism itself.
Templates, variables and task policies

Separate reviewed wording from runtime values. Tenant brand, locale, current date and configured refund-policy version can vary without copying the entire prompt. Define required variables and validate their types and permitted values before rendering. The current date should have an explicit time zone appropriate to the decision. A missing policy version is a configuration error to surface, not an invitation for the model to guess a default rule.

User-controlled content may be useful, but belongs in the request or data portion. A customer name or subject line is not trusted merely because it is a normal business field. If an instruction template says "Follow the policy supplied in $subject," an attacker can supply instructions through that variable. Keep trusted parameters narrow and place free text in a lower-authority message with attribution. The composition manifest should record which reviewed template and validated configuration were used.

This complete renderer checks variable names, not whether values are trustworthy. Its caller must validate the source and content of values. That distinction is intentional: a generic template cannot know which tenant settings are authorized. Keep source validation in a configuration boundary and use render tests to cover absent, extra and unsupported parameters. This allows the template to stay simple without hiding the trust decision.
Few-shot examples and behavioural constraints

A few-shot example demonstrates the response pattern or trajectory the model should imitate. Show a normal case, a decision boundary and an uncertainty or refusal case rather than several nearly identical easy answers. For ShopAssist, useful examples distinguish duplicate captured payments from a pending authorization, and a refund proposal from a confirmed completed refund. If the output includes tools, show tool order and evidence use as well as the final customer message.

Examples can also teach mistakes. A fictional identifier may be copied into a real response; an obsolete tool name may keep appearing after deprecation. Review examples with the same owners as the policy they express and test for unwanted verbatim copying. Keep them short enough that their purpose is clear. The goal is to demonstrate a reusable behavior, not to fill context with a parallel library of cases that silently becomes another policy source.

Prefer testable constraints. "Use no more than 120 words" can be measured, while "be concise" needs interpretation. Even measurable constraints should have a reason and a failure response. If a required disclosure cannot fit the length limit, define which rule has precedence rather than letting the model decide randomly. Separate style checks from factual and permission checks: a beautifully formatted reply may still contain an unsupported promise.
Prompt decomposition and role-specific packs

Instruction packs make ownership visible. A pack might define identity, refund guidance, privacy, order-tool use or customer-reply format. Each has an identifier, version, owner, applicability and reviewed text. A composer selects the packs for the role and records their exact versions in a manifest. This lets a privacy change be reviewed once and deployed to applicable agents without rewriting every prompt. Shared ownership does not eliminate the need to test the composed result.

Reject ambiguous compositions. Two versions of the same pack should not both enter the body while the manifest records only the last one. Define a stable order, reject duplicate identifiers and detect conflicting output contracts. Automated lint can catch obvious duplicates or forbidden variables, but semantic contradictions often need human review and behavioral cases. The manifest is an audit artifact: it must faithfully describe the text the model actually received.

Versioning, provenance and change control

Store reviewed instructions in version control or another controlled source with equivalent traceability. A runtime registry can serve immutable releases, but production should reference an exact approved version or content hash. A version range is useful during dependency resolution; it is not an immutable record of what a run used. Record the resolved pack manifest, model identifier, tool-schema versions and relevant configuration hash with the run.

Treat the release as a behavior change. Review the wording, run render/contract tests, evaluate on a fixed case set, stage it and canary it within a controlled traffic slice. Compare business outcomes as well as parser success: refund proposals, escalation, unsupported promises and user-language handling. A wording fix can alter behavior as much as a policy addition, so a semantic-version label is organizational shorthand rather than proof that a patch is harmless.

Rollback selects a previously approved composition. It should not require discovering an old string in logs or editing the current prompt by hand. Runs already in progress need a defined pinning rule: continue under their original version or explicitly migrate with a recorded reason. A rollback changes future instructions, not completed effects. Use provenance to identify affected runs and inspect their actual operations before deciding whether further reconciliation is necessary.

Trusted and untrusted content

Delimit external material clearly and keep its provenance. A wrapper can mark a passage as a document with a source identifier, escape delimiter characters and bound its text. It helps the model recognize where case material begins and ends. It does not authenticate the passage or guarantee resistance to prompt injection. Least-privilege capabilities, authorization and external-action gates remain necessary when the model reads untrusted content.

This function protects its own tag structure by restricting the tag name and escaping the source/body. It does not remove hostile semantics. A passage can politely request a data leak without any malformed tag. Make the provenance visible, avoid promoting its statements to policy and constrain what actions can follow. Sanitization is a formatting and minimization tool within a broader boundary; confusing those roles creates a false sense of security.
Writing instructions for today's models

Use clear goals, applicable constraints and concrete reasons. Specify when a tool is required rather than emphasizing "always" without context. ShopAssist should search refund policy before deciding refund eligibility, not before answering "hello." Ask for a short justification tied to evidence instead of a private reasoning transcript. Reasoning effort controls, when supported, belong in the adapter's evaluated model policy rather than in a universal incantation to think harder.

Prompt behavior is model-specific. Advice about calm wording, examples, document ordering or reasoning controls should be validated against the actual model and version. Put stable content first where provider prefix caching benefits from it, and volatile case material later when the contract permits. Attention needs and cache efficiency can conflict; measure both. A source's recommendation about one provider is a useful starting hypothesis, not a law that every frontier model follows.
