Chapter 15. A2A & Remote-Agent Interoperability

AegisOps can investigate application latency itself, but the database team owns the PostgreSQL diagnostic service. That team uses different models, tools and deployment rules. Giving the incident commander access to every database tool would erase an important ownership boundary. A better arrangement lets the commander request a diagnosis, track the work and inspect the result while the database team retains control of its implementation.

This chapter explains that arrangement. You will describe a remote capability, establish who may use it, submit a bounded task, handle questions and failures, and bring the result back into your own evidence ledger. The central problem is not transporting a prompt. It is maintaining a reliable relationship between two independently operated systems, neither of which should gain authority merely because the other produced convincing text.

ANALOGY / Commissioning an outside contractor A project manager commissions a specialist report. The contractor advertises services, receives a written brief, asks questions, submits deliverables and may miss a deadline. The manager keeps responsibility for the overall project and checks the report before relying on it. An Agent Card resembles the contractor's profile; a remote task resembles the work order. Where it stops: a profile and signature establish claims and origin, not competence, correctness or automatic deduplication. Those require explicit contracts and checks.

Why a remote agent is more than a simple tool call

A simple tool interface describes an operation and its arguments. A remote agent can accept a goal, choose its own intermediate operations and return a deliverable after several interactions. Its caller may not know the implementation or be allowed to inspect it. That makes task identity, progress, questions, cancellation and acceptance criteria part of the contract. A function-shaped interface can still expose this behaviour, but the caller must understand what happens behind that interface.

Do not define the distinction by speed or determinism. A tool can run for hours, call a model, ask for further input or cross an organisation boundary. A remote agent can finish immediately. The useful distinction is the responsibility exposed to the caller: requesting a capability through its operation contract, or commissioning independently managed work through a collaboration contract. A2A and MCP overlap in transport patterns while addressing different integration concerns.

The open Agent2Agent protocol supplies a vocabulary for agent discovery and collaboration. In this edition, protocol examples refer to A2A 1.0; production adapters should pin the specification and SDK versions they actually support. Protocol interoperability does not make policies interchangeable. Two teams can agree on a task message format and still disagree about data access, deadlines or what constitutes a satisfactory answer. Integration tests need to cover those decisions as well as wire-format parsing.

Identity, discovery and capability cards

Discovery answers where a suitable agent can be found. An Agent Card describes the advertised agent version, supported interfaces, skills, content modes and authentication requirements. An interface combines an endpoint with a protocol binding and protocol version. An advertised skill narrows the broad agent description into a task the caller can reasonably request. This helps the commander choose database diagnosis instead of sending an unrestricted instruction to an unknown service.

An enterprise agent registry, governed alongside the MCP registry from Chapter 14, can add information the public card does not establish: the owning team, approved environments, allowed tenants, data classifications, support contact and integration test results. Static configuration is also reasonable for a small deployment. A well-known discovery address is convenient, but discovery itself is not authorisation. The caller must verify that the endpoint belongs to the approved service and that its configuration has not drifted since the integration was reviewed.

Signed cards protect authenticity and integrity when the signature is verified against a trusted key. They do not prove that a skill works, that an endpoint is currently healthy or that its outputs are true. Signed cards were supported before version 1.0, so avoid treating their presence as a newly introduced correctness guarantee. Pin an accepted card or its relevant contract fields and decide which changes require re-review: a new endpoint, broader data modes or changed security requirements usually do.

For AegisOps, the approved registry entry might describe a database reliability agent with two skills: query-performance diagnosis and replication-health inspection. The registry permits read-only diagnosis for tenant Northwind's clusters and disallows customer record exports. The Agent Card advertises how to connect; the registry and policy engine decide whether this caller may connect for this task. Keeping those decisions separate prevents an attractive skill description from becoming an entitlement.

Task delegation, status, messages and artifacts

A task is a stateful unit of remote work. Its identifier connects the original submission, later messages, progress updates and outputs. Messages carry interaction between caller and worker. Artifacts are deliverables, such as a diagnosis JSON file or a report. Status describes whether the work is pending, progressing, waiting for input or finished. These objects serve different purposes; a friendly progress message should not be mistaken for a validated result.

In the database example, the commander sends incident INC-77, the approved cluster identifier, a time window and references to relevant metrics. The worker may reply that the cluster identifier is ambiguous. An input-required state therefore pauses the investigation rather than proving that it failed. The commander obtains the missing identifier from trusted run state or asks an authorised human. It then continues the existing task instead of starting a second investigation with a longer prompt.

An authentication-required interruption is different. A model should not paste credentials into a conversation to satisfy it. The application must route that requirement through the approved identity flow and determine whether continued access remains within the task's authority. A rejection is also different from a technical failure: the remote agent may decline a task it does not support. Completed, failed, rejected and canceled outcomes should remain distinct in local state and user-facing explanations.

Artifacts need acceptance rules agreed before submission. A diagnosis might require the affected cluster, observation window, findings linked to evidence, uncertainty and proposed next checks. Parse its shape, verify the referenced resources belong to the expected tenant, and label its provenance. Schema validity establishes that required fields exist; it does not establish that the diagnosis is correct. The commander should compare the report with independently obtained evidence before proposing a consequential action.

Synchronous, streaming and asynchronous interaction

Synchronous interaction holds a request open until a result arrives. It suits short work with a bounded duration and a simple caller. Streaming keeps the caller informed through progress and partial results. Asynchronous interaction returns a task handle so the caller can disconnect and retrieve progress later through polling or a callback. A system may combine these modes: stream while a user is present, then continue asynchronously if the work outlasts the interactive window.

For a long investigation, correctness should survive loss of the stream. Store the remote task identifier and a local status checkpoint before entering a durable wait. On reconnection, query the task rather than assuming the missing connection means failure. A callback is a notification to examine authoritative state, not an instruction to execute whatever its payload suggests. Authenticate its source, match it to an expected task and process duplicate notifications without repeating the local transition.

Choose polling frequency from the operational need rather than from the model's eagerness. Polling every second for a day-long task creates unnecessary traffic; polling every minute for a ten-second user interaction feels unresponsive. Enforce an individual RPC timeout, a task deadline and an overall run budget. The first bounds one network call, the second bounds the delegated job, and the third protects the caller's whole workflow. One timer cannot reliably serve all three purposes.
Handoffs versus remote-agent calls

A handoff changes which component controls the next stage of a conversation. ShopAssist might route a billing question to a refunds specialist, which now selects the next response. Delegation keeps the caller in control: AegisOps commissions a database diagnosis, receives findings and decides what to do with them. Either pattern can cross a runtime boundary, so physical location is not the definition. Ownership of the current goal and continuation is the clearer distinction.

Write that ownership into state. During delegation, the commander owns the incident, budget and stopping decision; the remote worker owns only its bounded task. During a handoff, record the receiving owner, relevant context, pending obligations and an escape path if the recipient cannot continue. A transfer of software control does not erase organisational accountability. The human team operating the overall service remains responsible for defining the authorised behaviour and handling failures.
Authentication, authorisation and tenant boundaries

Every call needs a verified caller identity and an explicit permission decision. A workload identity identifies the software making the request. Where the agent acts for a user, preserve that user relationship through the approved delegated-access mechanism described in Chapter 20. Request a scope for database diagnosis rather than a broad administrative token. The remote system must enforce its own resource and tenant checks; trusting a tenant field supplied by the caller is insufficient.

Send the smallest useful brief. Resource identifiers, time windows and permitted evidence references often suffice. Do not send the entire incident transcript, unrelated customer records or credentials merely because the remote context window is large. Reference-based sharing still requires authorisation: the worker must not gain access to a document simply because a URL appears in the message. Expire shared references where appropriate and record which data was released to which remote service.

On the return path, remote output is external data. A report can contain attacker-controlled log text or instructions embedded in a retrieved document. The caller must not treat such text as policy, permission or a new user request. Keep provenance and trust labels when reports pass into another agent. An instruction to restart a database in a diagnosis artifact remains a recommendation to evaluate; it is not an approved action or a reason to expand credentials.

Timeouts, partial failure and idempotent delegation

An unanswered submission has an uncertain outcome. The remote service may have created the task even though the response never reached the caller. Repeating the request can create duplicate work unless the service has an agreed deduplication contract. A2A assigns task identifiers on the server. The caller can send a stable message identifier, but A2A 1.0 permits rather than requires idempotent Send Message behaviour. Verify support instead of assuming that identifier reuse is enough.

A robust adapter persists a logical delegation key before submission and maps it to the returned remote task identifier. The remote service or gateway must atomically recognise repeated submissions for that key within a documented retention window. If the create response is lost, the caller needs a supported lookup or reconciliation path. When no such mechanism exists, record outcome-unknown and escalate or reconcile before creating replacement work. Avoid a helper named get-or-create unless its contract actually establishes these semantics.

A timeout after task creation is easier to recover: query the saved task ID, continue waiting within the deadline or request cancellation. Cancellation is best effort for work already underway; it may not undo effects the remote service performed. A diagnostic worker should be read-only, but even reads can incur cost or reveal data. Accept partial artifacts only if they pass validation, label their limitations and make missing evidence visible in the final conclusion.

The following pseudocode assumes a durable store, a deduplicating remote adapter and bounded RPCs. Its purpose is to show ordering, not supply those services. The adapter must document key retention, task lookup and what happens when creation has an uncertain outcome. A production implementation also authenticates calls, handles version negotiation and records trace context. Keeping these interfaces explicit makes the example honest without hiding the critical idempotence requirement in an unexplained utility.

async def start_delegation(store, remote, key, brief):
    op = await store.reserve_delegation(key, brief)
    if op.task_id is not None:
        return await remote.get_task(op.task_id)
    # Required adapter contract: atomic dedupe by key.
    task = await remote.submit_once(key, brief)
    await store.bind_remote_task(key, task.id)
    return task

Gateways, versions and cross-platform interoperability

A gateway can centralise authentication, token exchange, rate limits, contract validation and audit for remote calls. It can also translate transport bindings or maintain an organisation's deduplication extension. That translation is a responsibility, not magic compatibility: preserve task identity, terminal states, content modes and error meanings. If one backend cannot support a required lifecycle feature, reject the integration clearly rather than flattening a long task into a misleading immediate success.

Version the Agent Card, skill expectations and local adapter together. Run contract tests in staging for normal completion, input-required, rejection, duplicate submissions, callback duplication and lost responses. Trace a delegation as a child of the caller's run while retaining both the local operation key and remote task ID. Use a circuit breaker for persistent dependency failure and a documented fallback such as reduced local diagnosis or escalation to the database team's humans.
MCP versus A2A, and the final design choice

MCP connects applications with exposed capabilities such as tools and resources. A2A supplies an agent-collaboration contract with discovery, messages, tasks and artifacts. A remote database agent may use MCP internally, and the commander may expose an A2A delegation through its own tool registry. MCP also has task-oriented extensions for long-running work, so “long task means A2A” is not a sufficient architecture rule. Select the contract whose ownership and lifecycle semantics match the integration.

Before integrating a remote worker, answer a design question: what does the worker own that the caller should not absorb? Then answer the recovery question: how will the caller find the same job after a lost response or restart? If either answer is vague, the attractive multi-agent diagram is premature. A small, explicit remote contract usually produces a more dependable system than sharing broad prompts, context and authority between teams.

Chapter 16. Workflow & Graph Orchestration

An incident investigation needs room to explore. The commander may inspect metrics, compare logs and reject several hypotheses before finding a useful explanation. A production rollback needs a different kind of freedom: the system must not omit authorisation, execute an expired proposal or declare success without verification. A single unrestricted loop makes these two kinds of work look alike. Graph orchestration separates the exploratory work from the required route around it.

A graph represents execution as named steps connected by allowed transitions. Each step reads state and returns an update. A transition determines which step follows. The model can still decide within a step or select among permitted branches, but the runtime owns the graph and its constraints. You will build that structure, decide how parallel results merge, pause for external decisions and understand what persistence must provide before a graph becomes durable.

ANALOGY / The railway and its stations A railway map defines stations, connecting tracks and signals that choose a route. A train cannot invent a new track simply because a passenger asks. A platform can hold it while other trains continue. Nodes, edges, routers and durable waits serve similar purposes in a workflow. Where it stops: a permitted station can still perform the wrong work. Safe routing does not constrain the tools a node holds, prove an approval is valid or make a checkpoint durable by itself.

Graph shapes and the work they fit

A linear graph has a fixed sequence, such as extract an order identifier, validate it and store a result. A conditional graph selects one of several routes, such as refund investigation or shipping investigation. A cyclic graph revisits a step, such as revising a hypothesis after a failed test. These are control-flow shapes, not promises about quality. A well-formed sequence can still extract the wrong identifier; a declared loop can still waste resources without a stopping rule.

Most agent workflows combine these shapes. AegisOps uses a fixed incident skeleton with an exploratory investigation node inside it. The investigation can make several read-only observations, but a proposed mutation must leave that node and pass through policy and approval. After execution, verification determines whether the incident is resolved or needs further investigation. This structure gives the model useful choice while preserving the transitions the service owner requires.

Think first about invariants, then about boxes. An invariant might say that no production mutation occurs without a valid approval for its exact proposal, or that no terminal success is reported before an outcome check. Draw the graph so its routes respect the invariant, then restrict capabilities so nodes cannot bypass it internally. An investigation node that already holds an unrestricted rollback tool can violate the invariant without crossing an illegal graph edge.

Nodes, edges, routers and loop guards

A node should have one clear responsibility and an explicit input/output contract. “Investigate” is too vague unless its tool set, evidence output and budget are specified. A useful investigation node reads a goal and known evidence, uses read-only tools, and returns findings with provenance plus a proposal or escalation reason. It does not edit the whole global state arbitrarily. The runtime applies its partial update through the state rules.

An unconditional edge always selects the same next node. A conditional edge evaluates a router against the updated state. A deterministic router can inspect risk or task status. A model-driven router must return a value from a declared set, and the runtime must validate that value before dispatch. An unknown destination should produce a controlled error or escalation, not a dynamic node that a model invents through text.

Every cycle needs a guard that applies to every entrance. In an investigation graph, both a request for more evidence and a failed post-action verification can return to investigation. Limiting only the evaluator's retry branch leaves the verification branch unbounded. Count total investigation attempts or allocate a separate budget to each loop, and test the worst route. Also enforce a whole-run visit, time and cost limit so combinations of individually bounded loops remain bounded.

The guard's exit is part of the design. Throwing a generic exception at the visit limit may stop computation, but it does not automatically produce a useful or safe outcome. Record why the budget ended, checkpoint the known effects and choose a terminal status such as incomplete, escalation-required or compensation-pending. Reserve enough headroom to perform that transition. Stopping a train in the middle of an unsafe section is not the same as routing it to a safe platform.
A minimal graph engine and its exact limits

The following teaching dispatcher owns a declared transition table and validates each result. Its state type represents the narrow information needed for this example. Nodes may return an update, but this snippet does not supply database persistence, parallel scheduling or side-effect deduplication. Those are separate contracts. Naming the limits avoids teaching that a compact dictionary loop has already solved the distributed problems addressed in later chapters.

from typing import Literal, TypedDict

class RunState(TypedDict):
    next_node: str
    visits: int
    attempts: int
    outcome: str | None

ALLOWED = {
    "plan": {"investigate"},
    "investigate": {"evaluate"},
    "evaluate": {"investigate", "approve", "end"},
    "approve": {"act", "end"},
    "act": {"verify"},
    "verify": {"investigate", "end"},
}

def checked_next(node: str, proposed: str) -> str:
    if proposed not in ALLOWED[node]:
        raise ValueError("undeclared transition")
    return proposed

In this sketch, every entry into investigation increments attempts before the work starts. The same counter therefore covers both return paths. A real scheduler should persist that increment and the next transition with optimistic concurrency or workflow-engine ownership. The functions also need a typed proposal and evidence contract when they become an application. The small example makes one mechanism visible: legal routes and bounded re-entry, rather than claiming an entire production harness.
Build it: plan, investigate, evaluate, act and verify

Start with an incident goal that can be tested, such as restoring checkout latency below an agreed threshold. Planning records the relevant service, investigation scope and initial questions. Investigation gathers evidence, and evaluation chooses among answering, requesting more evidence, proposing an action or escalating. A proposed action includes exact arguments, anticipated impact and preconditions. It is a record to review, not a command that executes when the evaluator writes it.

Approval is an interrupt before the protected action. A rejected or expired decision ends that proposal safely; a modification creates a new proposal that needs its own binding. An approved decision resumes only after the application verifies identity, entitlement, proposal digest and current resource version. Execution uses the stable logical operation identifier described in Chapter 6. Verification then reads the resulting system state and checks success against the original goal.

If verification fails, the graph records the actual effect before returning to investigation. It must not pretend that no action happened. The next proposal may need compensation, an alternate action or escalation, and it receives a new identity and approval when its arguments differ. A retry of the same uncertain action reuses the original operation identity. Keeping these two cases separate prevents a retry loop from becoming a sequence of newly authorised-looking duplicate mutations.

State passing, reducers and joins

State is the shared contract between nodes. Keep it smaller than the entire conversation: the goal, selected plan, evidence references, attempts, pending proposal, effect ledger and current status are often enough. A reducer defines how an update combines with the existing value. Scalars may replace a previous value; evidence may merge by a stable evidence identifier. The merge rule must be explicit because parallel updates otherwise lose or inconsistently overwrite information.

Suppose the metrics branch returns evidence E1 and E2 while the logs branch returns E2 and E3. A union by evidence ID avoids duplicating E2, but that raises another question: what if two records with ID E2 contain different payloads? Silently retaining whichever arrived last is unsafe. Reject the conflict, require immutable evidence identifiers or keep separate versions with provenance. Deduplication should not hide disagreement that the evaluator needs to inspect.

A join decides when the combined state is ready. It may wait for all required branches, a defined quorum or a deadline. A deadline join must record which branch results are absent and why. A result assembled from metrics and changes but missing logs is partial, even if it looks persuasive. Reducers combine values; they do not decide whether missing evidence is acceptable. That decision belongs to the join contract and the downstream policy.

For a scheduler with nondeterministic completion order, prefer reducers whose result does not change with ordering, or define a deterministic merge order explicitly. Associativity helps when partial updates are grouped differently; commutativity helps when branch order changes; idempotence helps when the same update is delivered twice. Not every state field needs all three properties. What matters is matching the reducer to the delivery and replay semantics the scheduler actually provides.
Fan-out, fan-in and parallel branches

AegisOps can inspect metrics, logs and recent changes concurrently because these investigations have independent read inputs. Give each branch only its required state slice and its own timeout and tool budget. Sharing a mutable dictionary between branches invites accidental coordination through undocumented writes. It also defeats the least-privilege intention of scoped inputs. Each worker should return an update or a labelled failure, while the owner performs the merge.

Cancel work that is no longer needed, but await cancellation and account for external calls already started. In Python, cancelling an asyncio task requests cancellation; it does not make remote computation or effects disappear. A branch may complete while cancellation is being requested. The collector needs a clear treatment for completed, failed and cancelled tasks, and it must drain pending tasks so exceptions and resource cleanup are not left behind.

Parallelism shortens wall-clock time only when there is capacity. Three branches can contend for the same provider quota or database connection pool and become slower than serial work. Apply a semaphore or scheduler limit, include branch cost in the parent's budget and reserve capacity for safe termination. Choose independent investigations rather than parallelising steps where the second requires the first one's evidence. The dependency graph should determine concurrency, not the desire for a more impressive diagram.

Interrupts, checkpoints and resume

An interrupt records that the next step needs input from outside the current worker. Persist the continuation, proposal and pending request, then release the worker. When the input arrives, an authorised resume operation loads the checkpoint, validates the decision and advances the run. A boolean stored in a process variable is not a durable approval. The checkpoint and decision service must survive a restart and prevent conflicting resumes from advancing the same proposal twice.

Checkpoints also support crash recovery. Saving after a node limits repeated computation, but a node that performs an external effect can crash after the effect and before the save. Its re-execution therefore needs downstream idempotency or an uncertain-outcome reconciliation path. Persisting the intention before the effect and its observed result afterward helps recovery understand the gap. A graph checkpoint alone does not give an external API exactly-once behaviour.

Use versioned state updates or workflow-engine ownership to protect a resume from a competing worker. Expiring leases need fencing and owner-checked renewal, as Chapter 29 explains. Resume may occur hours later, so re-read facts that authorise the action rather than trusting the old checkpoint blindly. A deployment version, order status or policy can change while approval is waiting. Retaining the old state supports audit; it does not make those old facts current.

Long-running timers and durable execution

An in-process sleep disappears when the process dies. A durable workflow engine records timers, activity results and external signals so it can reconstruct progress after a restart. Temporal is one example. Its deterministic replay reruns workflow code against recorded history to reconstruct the same orchestration decisions. Model calls and ordinary network I/O belong in activities, whose recorded outcomes can be reused during replay rather than being generated again in workflow code. Workflow code must follow the selected SDK's determinism rules.

An activity can still execute more than once when an attempt fails or its completion is not recorded. The activity's external effects therefore need the same operation identity and downstream contract as any other retryable mutation. Durable execution improves orchestration recovery; it does not remove distributed uncertainty. Configure activity timeouts, retry classifications and cancellation behaviour explicitly, and keep an approval signal tied to the exact proposal rather than treating any late signal as permission for the current action.

For AegisOps, the workflow can request diagnosis, wait up to a policy-defined approval deadline, execute one approved operation and schedule verification checks. During the wait no dedicated worker needs to remain blocked. The engine still consumes durable storage and scheduling resources; “no worker waiting” is a useful architectural statement, not a claim of zero resource use. Long histories may also require supported history-management patterns rather than keeping one workflow alive indefinitely without limits.

Choosing a graph or a free-form loop

A graph is valuable when required phases, long waits, permission changes or parallel joins must be visible and testable. A free-form loop can fit short research or debugging where the next useful read is genuinely unknown. Often the right answer combines them: the graph owns required transitions while a bounded agent chooses investigative reads inside a node. Avoid expressing every small action as a graph node if doing so obscures rather than clarifies the invariant.

Review failure modes through the route and the effect boundary together. An undeclared transition is a routing defect. Lost evidence is a merge defect. A restarted wait without a decision record is a persistence defect. Duplicate mutation is an effect-contract defect. A loop that ends without a useful escalation is a termination-design defect. Naming the failure layer makes the correction clearer than simply increasing prompts, adding nodes or selecting a stronger model.

Chapter 17. Multi-Agent Architectures

ShopAssist must answer a customer's question about a delayed refund. The answer needs payment records, policy evidence and a customer-facing explanation. It is tempting to create three agents because there are three nouns in that description. That is not yet a reason to use a team. One agent with well-designed read tools may complete the work more cheaply and with fewer opportunities to lose context. The architecture needs a measurable benefit, not an appealing organisation chart.

A multi-agent system divides work between independently instructed components. The division can create specialisation, parallelism or a useful permission boundary. It also adds delegation decisions, copied context, latency and failure paths. This chapter shows how to choose that division, keep one owner of the overall outcome, exchange scoped information and measure whether the team improves on a simpler baseline. Multiple agents are an engineering option rather than an automatic level of sophistication.

ANALOGY / A project team with one accountable manager A manager assigns a policy researcher and a payment analyst different tasks, gives each the relevant documents and combines their reports. The manager owns the deadline and decides what is ready to deliver. Specialists help when their separate skills or access matter; meetings and repeated explanations can otherwise consume the benefit. Where it stops: agents do not have human professional judgement or independent expertise merely because they have job titles. Their errors may be correlated, and software must enforce ownership and permissions.

When multiple agents are justified

Start by identifying the obstacle a single agent cannot handle well. A narrow refund specialist may need different policy and tools from a shipping specialist. Separate workers can each read a large corpus slice that would not fit in one context. Independent investigations can run in parallel. Another team may own a remote capability that the caller should not absorb. A read-only investigator and an approved action executor can also have intentionally different authority.

Those benefits differ. Specialisation improves the match between instruction, tools and task. Context partitioning limits what each worker sees. Parallelism changes elapsed time. Isolation changes worst-case harm. An ownership boundary preserves another team's operational responsibilities. Do not bundle them into an unmeasured claim that “a team is smarter.” Identify which benefit you expect, how you will measure it and what coordination cost is acceptable for that benefit.

For a straightforward refund-status question, ShopAssist can call an order tool and a payment tool in one controlled run. A team becomes more plausible when the case involves a disputed policy exception, several payment systems or separate data owners. Even then, compare the team with a single agent and a deterministic workflow on the same representative cases. Measure correct outcomes, forbidden actions, elapsed time and cost. A longer answer or a larger number of agents is not evidence of improvement.

Least privilege means restricting each worker to the capabilities and information required for its task. That permission argument also requires care. Giving a research worker only read tools reduces its authority, but a supervisor with unrestricted write tools can still act on a manipulated research report. The boundary is useful when reports are treated as untrusted evidence and the sensitive executor applies independent policy. Workers should not manufacture an approval or convert their confidence into authorisation. Separation is valuable because it makes enforced responsibility clearer, not because crossing an agent boundary cleanses data.

Core patterns and their ownership rules

In supervisor-worker coordination, the supervisor owns the goal, plan and final stopping decision. It assigns bounded tasks and integrates worker results. This fits AegisOps investigations where metrics, logs and changes require different evidence collection. The supervisor can become a bottleneck, so delegation must earn its cost. It need not use a model for every assignment: deterministic dispatch can handle known stages, while a model helps with genuinely uncertain choices.

A router-specialist design selects one destination and hands the request to that specialist. There is little ongoing coordination. ShopAssist can route an order-status question to a status workflow and a refund dispute to a refunds agent. The router needs a clear fallback when intent is ambiguous, and the receiving specialist must be able to reject a misrouted request. An initial classification is not a permanent entitlement to every tool in the selected domain.

A handoff chain changes the owner of the next conversational phase. Triage may transfer to refunds, then to a human. Record who owns the continuation and what unresolved obligations are transferred. Handoffs become unstable when overlapping criteria allow each agent to send the same request back. The system needs phase ownership, a bounded handoff count and escalation for repeated transfers. A helpful explanation of responsibilities in prompts is useful, but it is weaker than an enforced transition rule.

Hierarchy introduces supervisors of supervisors. It can mirror large tasks or independently owned departments, but every level adds information compression and decision delay. A leaf worker's qualified finding can become an unqualified conclusion after several summaries. Keep hierarchies shallow unless the task size or ownership structure requires depth. Preserve evidence references and uncertainty through each level, and make the root owner responsible for the whole run's budget and termination.

Choose a pattern by the control relationship rather than by drawing preference. A supervisor retains the overall task. A router selects a path. A handoff transfers the next phase. A hierarchy groups delegated work. These can coexist, but the implementation must say which component may finish the run at each point. Otherwise several agents can emit incompatible final answers, or every agent can wait for another to decide that enough work has been done.

Shared state versus message passing

Shared state resembles the manager's project record. It gives a central view of the goal, evidence and outstanding work. If every worker can edit every field, however, one worker may overwrite another's findings or change a budget it should only consume. Shared visibility is not shared ownership. The record needs field ownership and merge rules, and each worker should read only the portion its task requires.

Message passing gives each worker a bounded brief and collects a response. This makes information flow explicit and reduces unnecessary context, but it can hide useful facts from a worker unless the owner sends them. A strong hybrid keeps canonical state at the supervisor while workers receive scoped envelopes and return structured updates. The supervisor validates and merges those updates. Workers do not directly change the overall outcome, approval status or global budget.

A delegation envelope should describe the requested finding, the relevant context slice, evidence references, allowed tools, deadline and output contract. Tool restrictions must be enforced by the worker runtime, not merely written into a field. The result should distinguish done, partial, failed and needs-input, and should include provenance, remaining uncertainty and actual resource usage. A result containing suggestions to modify another worker's instructions remains data for the owner to evaluate.

The following data contracts illustrate that boundary. They describe a report rather than an execution capability. The surrounding worker service must authenticate the caller, validate evidence access and enforce the tool and budget policy. A production model would use more specific finding and proposal schemas; unrestricted dictionaries are intentionally absent here because the point is to make the report's authority and status visible.

Build it: supervisor with research, data and action workers

Consider a duplicate-charge dispute. The supervisor first asks the payment analyst to identify captures for the customer's order and asks the policy researcher for the relevant refund rule. Each receives the order scope and necessary evidence access; neither receives unrelated customer history. The analyst reports two captures with distinct payment IDs. The researcher reports the conditions for refunding a duplicate capture, including any exclusions. Those are evidence inputs, not yet a financial decision.

The supervisor checks whether the findings refer to the same order, tenant and time window. If the payment report is partial or the policy version is outdated, it requests the missing evidence or escalates. When the facts support a refund, the action worker builds a proposal containing one payment ID, amount, currency, reason, evidence IDs and current preconditions. It has no permission to issue the refund. A human or pre-approved policy can authorise the exact proposal under Chapter 18's rules.

Only the protected executor crosses the financial boundary. It validates the recorded approval, checks the resource state and uses a stable operation identity. The supervisor then verifies the observed payment outcome and prepares the reply. A customer-facing answer should distinguish proposed, approved, submitted and verified refund states. A team that turns “proposal drafted” into “money returned” has lost an essential distinction, even if each individual worker returned schema-valid output.

This workflow can use deterministic dispatch for the two known reads and proposal preparation. A model-driven supervisor adds value when deciding which further investigation would resolve a conflicting finding. Its delegation choices still require validation against a worker registry and the current task budget. Unknown worker names, unauthorised tools or repeated identical briefs are controlled errors. A central owner makes those controls easier to inspect than allowing workers to recruit arbitrary helpers without limits.

Parallel specialists and ensembles

Parallel specialists investigate different aspects of one problem. AegisOps can gather metrics, logs and recent changes concurrently, then compare whether the observations support the same timeline. This saves elapsed time when branches are independent and capacity is available. Their outputs should meet through a deadline-aware join, which records missing branches and conflicts. More concurrent workers do not help if all of them contend for one rate-limited search endpoint.

An ensemble asks several workers to solve the same problem. It can reveal disagreement, but agreement is not a proof of correctness. Workers using the same model, prompt and evidence can share a false premise. For a high-impact decision, independent evidence collection or an external outcome check is often more valuable than another opinion based on the same context. Measure error correlation and the reliability of the combination rule rather than assuming several votes multiply confidence.

The combining rule must match the task. Majority vote may fit a well-defined classification, while a judge can compare open-ended proposals against a rubric. Both can fail when all candidates are wrong or the judge lacks the evidence needed to identify the error. An escalation-on-disagreement policy may be appropriate when the cost of a wrong action is high. Define the operational cost of that policy too: excessive disagreement can overwhelm the human queue.

Use ensembles selectively. A routine order-status query rarely justifies several independent model answers. An ambiguous incident hypothesis may justify a second investigation with a different evidence source. Compare quality improvement with calls, tokens, latency and human review demand. A worker's role name, model family or different random seed does not by itself establish meaningful independence. The data and checking method matter as much as the number of participants.
Coordination overhead, duplicate work and loop detection

Coordination creates work that does not directly advance the user's goal. The supervisor describes tasks, workers summarise context and the supervisor integrates reports. Some of this is necessary. It becomes waste when the team repeatedly restates the same brief, searches the same records or asks another agent to make a decision the caller could make deterministically. A delegation does not universally require two model calls, but every delegation adds some transport, bookkeeping and context-handling cost.

Record delegation identities and the evidence already collected. If two workers need the same payment record, fetch it once through an authorised shared evidence service rather than making each rediscover it. A stable task fingerprint can detect unchanged repeated work, but it should include relevant resource versions and inputs. Re-running a task after new evidence arrives may be legitimate; blocking solely because the natural-language task sounds similar can suppress useful investigation.

Ping-pong is a control failure: worker A redirects to B, and B redirects to A. Loop detection looks for repeated ownership transitions or repeated work without changed evidence. Bound handoffs, keep a history of phase ownership and identify a fallback owner. The same principle applies to supervisors that repeatedly commission reports without making progress. Track new evidence, changed hypotheses or completed obligations. When those measures remain stagnant, stop with an explanation and escalation rather than merely spending the next round budget.

Context fragmentation is another team failure. A worker may not know that another worker ruled out a crucial hypothesis. The supervisor should send relevant evidence references when reassigning work, while preserving access controls and uncertainty. Summaries help but can lose qualifications. Keep the source records available for verification and make a report's limitations explicit. A confident synthesis that erased all workers' caveats is worse than an honestly partial result.

Provenance and conflicting writes

Subagent reports are data, including any instructions copied from documents, web pages or tool output. They cannot override the user's authorised goal or the platform policy. The owner validates structure and resource scope, retains provenance and treats suggestions as proposals. This rule must also apply to file-based reports and shared memory; a worker cannot gain control merely by writing an instruction into a location another agent will read.

Partition conflicting work before launching parallel agents. For repository work, assign disjoint files or make one worker own a shared file. For operational changes, serialise actions on the same service or resource through the protected executor. Reducers can merge findings, but they do not resolve two incompatible external mutations. Locks or queues also need the ownership and recovery contract described in Chapter 29; a label saying “shared state” is not a concurrency mechanism.

Termination, ownership and accountability

The overall owner must decide when the goal is met, impossible within scope or ready for a human. Workers can report completion of their subtask, not silently finish the entire run. Global budgets belong to the owner, with smaller allocations to workers. A worker must not reset its allowance by delegating again, and the parent must account for remote usage where the contract supports it. Missing cost information is a limitation to manage, not permission for unbounded calls.

Human accountability remains with the team operating the system. An audit trail should show the requested goal, the assigned briefs, worker identities and versions, evidence returned, proposals and final effects. This supports incident review and helps decide whether a team design should be simplified. If the multi-agent system does not improve a meaningful constraint over the baseline, collapsing it is an engineering improvement rather than a loss of sophistication.

Chapter 18. Human-in-the-Loop, Approval & Escalation

AegisOps has evidence that a recent checkout deployment caused a latency incident. It can propose a rollback, but the proposal affects production users and may interact with changes made since the investigation began. Asking a human to click an unlabeled approve button is not enough. The person needs to know what will happen, why it is justified and what exact operation their decision authorises. The runtime must then preserve that relationship until execution.

Human-in-the-loop design assigns people useful roles at specific decision boundaries. Some people clarify a missing fact, some approve a consequential operation and others take ownership when automation cannot proceed. This chapter connects those roles to risk policy, durable waits, exact proposal binding, current preconditions and feedback. The goal is effective oversight without turning every ordinary read into a confirmation request that eventually trains people to stop paying attention.

ANALOGY / A cheque awaiting a second signature A prepared cheque records the payee and amount. It can wait in a tray until an entitled signer decides, without an employee standing beside it all afternoon. If someone changes the payee or amount, the old signature does not authorise the new cheque. An agent proposal, durable approval request and validated resume follow that pattern. Where it stops: a signature does not prove the payment is sensible or that its preconditions still hold. Software must check decision identity, current authority and resource state before executing.

Where humans belong

An approver decides whether a proposed action may happen. A clarifier supplies a missing fact, such as which of two orders the customer means. An escalation owner takes over a task that the agent cannot or must not continue. A reviewer examines sampled completed runs, while a corrector edits a draft. A policy owner changes future rules through a governed process. These roles have different interfaces, response times and authority; sending all of them to one vague human queue hides those differences.

Place human decisions where judgement changes the outcome. High-impact, irreversible, unusual or ambiguous operations may need an approval or escalation. Routine low-impact work can proceed under explicit policy, with sampling for later review. The decision should follow action class and context rather than the model's confidence alone. A model can sound certain about an unsafe action and uncertain about a harmless read. Confidence may be one signal, but it cannot determine the final permission boundary.

Oversight also costs attention. If every order lookup requests approval, reviewers may learn to click quickly without examining evidence. Conversely, allowing every financial operation automatically can expose customers to a mistake or manipulated request. Define which classes need fresh approval, which are covered by tested pre-approved rules and which are blocked outright. Measure whether the resulting queue lets approvers make informed decisions within the task's useful time window.

Approval interrupts and resumable waits

An approval request is a durable record, not a temporary yes/no variable. It contains the run and proposal identifiers, exact action and arguments, evidence, expected impact, preconditions, required approvers and expiry. Persist the request and the run's continuation before releasing the worker. A notification points a person to that record; it is not the record itself. If chat delivery fails, the pending request should remain visible in the approval service.

A decision records who acted, which proposal they reviewed, the outcome, time and any explanation. Rejection, expiry and approval-with-modification are separate outcomes. A modification creates a new proposal with a new digest; it should not silently reuse the original approval. When the decision arrives, the resume service checks the record through an authenticated channel, validates the current approver entitlement and signals the waiting run. A worker on another host can then continue from durable state.

Replacement also retires the old proposal. In one owned transaction, mark the predecessor superseded, persist the new immutable proposal and advance the run's active proposal/version. Its historical approval remains an audit fact, but no longer authorises fresh dispatch. A delayed worker must compare its proposal ID and expected version with authoritative live state at the protected execution boundary, using a compare-and-set or an equivalently fenced gate. The binding helper below cannot enforce this lifecycle rule from immutable snapshots alone; a valid old digest is not proof that a proposal remains active.

For example, P-208 is approved, then P-209 replaces it. A delayed P-208 worker must be rejected even if its old approval has not expired. Replacement and dispatch must contend on the same authoritative state so only the current version can win. A local version check followed by an unfenced remote request leaves a race; downstream acceptance needs a compatible fence or an explicit dispatch/reconciliation protocol. If P-208 has already been accepted downstream, replacing local state does not cancel it. Reconcile that operation before treating P-209 as a substitute, or use a separately authorised compensation.

The exact proposal needs a canonical digest. Include the action, normalised arguments and relevant resource/version context. Hashing two stored hash fields against one another does not prove the current arguments are unchanged. Recompute the digest from the immutable proposal snapshot at validation time. Treat external identifiers and canonicalisation rules carefully: different dictionary key order should not create a new operation, while a different amount, recipient or environment must create one.

The following compact example illustrates binding and decision checks. Proposal and decision records are trusted immutable objects loaded from the service. The policy interface must verify approver roles, separation of duties and the required count of distinct approvers for this action. It is explicitly called rather than hidden in a comment. This function prepares an authorised operation; a downstream conditional executor still protects the resource-state check.

Precondition re-validation checks that the facts authorising the action remain current. After validation, execute against the approved resource version or equivalent atomic precondition. A read of current state followed by an unconditional write has a race window: another actor can change the order or deployment between the two calls. An API that supports a version check, conditional update or transactional constraint can close that window. If the downstream system cannot enforce the required condition, choose a safer operation or reconciliation process rather than claiming that the local check guarantees freshness.

Idempotency addresses a different problem. The approved logical operation has one stable identity, reused after an uncertain response or worker restart. A downstream deduplication contract prevents repeating that same operation. It does not make a stale proposal appropriate, authorise a changed action or substitute for checking the decision outcome. Freshness, permission and duplicate prevention are separate conditions. Keeping them separate helps both the implementation and its tests identify which condition failed.

Risk-based approval policies

A risk policy maps a proposed action and its context to a required decision. Useful inputs include side-effect class, amount, environment, affected resources, reversibility and anomaly signals. Define the policy in deterministic code or a policy engine, version it and test both allowed and denied cases. A model can extract facts or suggest that a request is unusual, but the final mapping must remain outside the model's authority.

For ShopAssist, ordinary order-status reads might proceed automatically. A low-value refund could proceed under a reviewed rule that checks eligibility, amount and aggregate refunded total. Larger or exceptional refunds might require one or two entitled approvers. Destructive production changes can be blocked or escalated when no approved recovery path exists. These are examples of policy structure, not universal financial thresholds. The service owner must define the actual limits and regulatory obligations.

Pre-approved runbooks are standing authorisations under explicit conditions. AegisOps might restart one stateless pod only when enough healthy replicas remain, the operation targets an approved service and no conflicting change is underway. The runtime evaluates those conditions at execution time. A runbook title or a model's claim that the action is routine is insufficient. If any required condition fails, the system returns to an approval or escalation path rather than weakening the check to finish the task.

A risk score is a compact value computed from the action's risk features and used to select an approval rule. It can help organise policy, but a single number loses detail: two proposals can receive the same score for different reasons and need different approvers. Retain the contributing features, policy version and resulting requirement in the request. Deterministic does not mean correct. Test the rule, review autonomy increases and never lower a safety requirement merely because budget or reviewer time is scarce.

Escalation, override, rejection and correction

Escalation is a designed outcome. The receiving human needs the goal, known facts, evidence, attempted steps, blocked proposal and reason the agent stopped. Without that package, the person repeats the investigation and the automation saves little effort. Record the new owner and what the agent may still do. An agent that has escalated a financial dispute should not continue issuing alternative mutations while a human handles the case.

Rejection can lead to a revised proposal, a factual explanation or closure, depending on the reason. Feed the reason back as an observation, not as an instruction to evade the policy. Approval-with-change creates a new reviewed proposal. A manual override is an external action the agent must observe and reconcile with its state. If an operator already rolled back the deployment, the pending rollback should become stale rather than executing simply because its original decision later arrives.

Corrections to drafts have less authority than policy changes. A reviewer may rewrite a customer reply without changing which refunds are eligible. Preserve that distinction in event types and interfaces. Otherwise a sentence such as “next time refund immediately” can become an accidental permanent rule when the intent was only to repair one response. The system should route feedback through the reviewed improvement process instead of treating every human utterance as a global permission update.

Approval UX: evidence for an informed decision

An approval card should lead with the concrete change. “Roll back checkout-api from release 5.14 to 5.13 in production” is clearer than “call rollback tool.” Show the exact parameters or configuration diff beside the plain-language explanation. The approver should be able to identify the service, environment and target without interpreting a long transcript or reconstructing tool arguments. Short does not mean vague; precise information prevents accidental approval of a different action.

Explain why the action is proposed through links to relevant evidence. AegisOps might show when latency rose, which release preceded it and which alternative causes were checked. Separate observations from hypotheses. A temporal association is evidence to investigate, not proof of causation. Include missing evidence and counterarguments so the card does not persuade by omitting uncertainty. The person needs a decision aid, not a sales pitch written to maximise approval rate.

Describe expected impact, affected users, reversibility and the verification plan. If rollback can itself fail, say so. “Undo” may mean a compensating operation rather than restoration of the exact prior world. Show alternatives considered and why they were rejected, along with the deadline and what happens if no one decides. When the proposal changes, the interface must make the change visible and obtain the required new decision rather than preserving an old approve button.

Track approval quality, not merely speed. Useful measurements include decision time by action class, rejection reasons, subsequent incidents and sampled review of whether the decision matched the evidence. A high approval rate can reflect good proposals or fatigue. A comment count is a signal, not a universal quality metric; some correct routine approvals need no prose. Investigate patterns using actual outcomes rather than inventing a benchmark curve for how quickly approvers ought to respond.

Human feedback for evaluation and improvement

Every approval, rejection, edit and escalation can teach the team something about system quality. Capture the signal with its context: which proposal, evidence, policy and model version produced it. Rejection with a structured reason can reveal weak proposal quality or an overly broad tool. Draft edits can become style or factuality evaluation cases. Escalation patterns may expose missing knowledge or an interface that repeatedly asks people to supply the same facts.

Feedback is not automatically ground truth. Reviewers can disagree, misunderstand evidence or express preferences that apply only to one customer. Evaluate the quality of labels and protect sensitive data before placing production examples in a dataset. Changes to prompts, knowledge, risk policy or tool scope should pass through their ordinary review and release process. Writing a correction directly into long-term memory can overgeneralise a local decision and make a new injection channel.

SLAs, expiry and reassignment

An approval service needs an owner and a time policy. Use group queues rather than a single person's availability where appropriate. Define reminders, reassignment and escalation before expiry, and choose a safe default when the request expires. Silent execution after a deadline defeats the purpose of the gate. Time policy should reflect the action's urgency: a proposed incident rollback may have a shorter useful lifetime than a customer draft awaiting review.

Separation of duties depends on verified identities, not name strings copied into model context. The requester or the user whose action needs independent review must not supply the required second approval. A two-person rule needs two distinct entitled principals; two clicks from one person are not two reviewers. Re-check role membership if the policy requires current entitlement. A person may leave a privileged group while a request remains pending, and old queue assignment should not grant continuing authority.
Audit trails, accountability and failure modes

Record the proposal, decision and observed execution as separate events. Link them by run ID, proposal ID, operation ID and trace context, and retain exact hashes and policy versions. The audit should answer who requested the action, what evidence supported it, which entitled people decided, what arguments actually executed and what happened afterward. Store it under appropriate access control and tamper-evident protection rather than mixing sensitive decision records into unrestricted operational logs.

Test failure paths as deliberately as approval success. Reject a matching proposal, expire it during a wait, change the resource version before execution, alter arguments after approval and restart the worker after the downstream effect. The expected result differs for each fault. Rejection and expiry produce no mutation; stale facts require reconciliation; an uncertain response requires same-operation recovery. A final answer saying “handled safely” is not a substitute for proving the executor count and external state.

Chapter 19. Agent Security Fundamentals

A user asks an assistant to summarise unread messages. One message contains a hidden instruction to forward invoices to an outside address. The user did not request that action, but the model may read the instruction alongside legitimate email content. If the same run can read private invoices and send external mail without a policy check, ordinary summarisation has become a data-theft opportunity. The vulnerability lies in the combination of content exposure and authority.

Agent security therefore begins with a question about power: if the model were manipulated during this run, what could it cause? Strong instructions and detection can reduce the chance of manipulation, but the architecture must bound the consequences. This chapter follows untrusted content from its entry points to possible harm, then places identity, permissions, isolation and output checks at the boundaries where they can actually prevent an effect.

ANALOGY / A bank clerk with limited keys A clerk reads letters from customers and can be deceived by a convincing request. The bank does not give every clerk a vault key and rely only on training. It restricts accounts, amounts and recipients, and requires independent checks for consequential transfers. An agent should likewise have only the tools and authority needed for the task. Where it stops: software permissions can be misconfigured, and permitted actions can still be harmful. Each rule needs enforcement, testing and monitoring rather than a reassuring name.

The agent attack surface

An attack surface is the set of paths through which an attacker can influence the system or obtain an effect. For an agent, entry paths include user messages, retrieved documents, emails, web pages, tool outputs, memory records and tool descriptions. Some contain legitimate data mixed with attacker-controlled text. The model may not reliably separate that text from instructions. Treating every retrieved paragraph as a trusted instruction erases the boundary the application is supposed to maintain.

Harm can leave through mutating tools, external messages, network calls, code execution, rendered output and persistent memory. A read tool can also expose private information or create a charge at a paid API, so read-only does not mean harmless. The security review must consider data access and destinations, not only tools that change a database. An apparently innocent search query can leak confidential text to an external search provider.

Map entry paths and effect paths together. AegisOps reads logs that may contain attacker-controlled request strings, but it also has access to operational actions. A customer may place an instruction in a log line hoping the commander treats it as a command. Restricting the log viewer to read access is useful, but the commander that consumes its output still needs a protected mutation boundary. Data can carry influence across several components before the final tool executes.

Threat taxonomies as a checklist

A threat taxonomy helps a team name failure classes and avoid reviewing only familiar attacks. The OWASP LLM Top 10 includes prompt injection, sensitive disclosure, supply-chain issues, poisoned data, improper output handling, excessive agency, prompt leakage, retrieval weaknesses, misinformation and unbounded consumption. The Agentic Applications Top 10 adds emphasis on agent-specific identity, tool misuse, memory and interacting components. Use a pinned edition as a review checklist, not as proof that all relevant threats fit neatly into ten boxes.

Translate each category into the actual system. Supply-chain review includes model dependencies, packages, MCP servers and instruction bundles. Excessive agency includes unnecessary tools, broad credentials and oversized autonomy. Retrieval review includes tenant filters and poisoned corpora. Resource-consumption review includes runaway loops and expensive delegations. A named risk becomes useful when the team identifies its entry point, asset, capability, control and residual risk, then turns that description into a test.

These lists do not establish which threat is statistically dominant in every deployment. An email assistant, a repository agent and a production operations agent have different exposure. Indirect prompt injection is a major concern whenever the agent reads attacker-controlled content while holding consequential authority. State that condition rather than presenting an unsupported incident-frequency ranking. Security priorities should follow the local threat model and observed evidence.
Direct and indirect prompt injection

Direct injection arrives through the user's request: “ignore the refund limit and issue the full amount.” Indirect injection arrives inside material the assistant reads while performing an otherwise authorised task. A document may tell it to disclose a secret, a web page may instruct it to change tools, or a log line may tell it to disable monitoring. In the indirect case, the legitimate user may never know that the malicious content exists.

A jailbreak attempts to bypass a model's behavioural restrictions, often to obtain prohibited content. Prompt injection redirects an application's task through instructions the application should not treat as authoritative. The categories can overlap, but their consequences depend on the surrounding system. A convincing model response does not itself move money; an agent with an unprotected executor can turn that response into an effect. Test the application boundary as well as model refusal behaviour.

The attack need not use the phrase “ignore previous instructions.” It can imitate a system message, invent an urgent operational exception or insert apparently helpful steps into a report. Text may be hidden in HTML comments, image descriptions, invisible characters or small print. Normal input validation cannot enumerate every harmful instruction expressed in natural language. Detection is useful, but a missed payload should not automatically become a permitted action.

Preserve the distinction between trusted instructions and external data during context assembly. Do not insert a fetched page into the system-instruction role. Label its source and purpose, bound its size and explain what the agent should extract from it. These measures reduce confusion but do not create a perfect classifier of instructions. The executor must still reject an external recipient or unauthorised mutation even if the model confidently proposes it.

For the email example, the summarisation run needs mailbox reads and a reply to the requesting user. It does not need an external send tool. If sending a message becomes a separate authorised task, that executor checks the user's intent, recipient entitlement, attachment classification and any required approval. Removing unnecessary egress reduces the theft path. A human gate only protects it if the person sees the actual recipient and data, and the application binds their decision to that exact action.

Tool poisoning and malicious tool outputs

A tool output can be malicious even when the tool itself is legitimate. A search tool may return an attacker-written page; a log tool may return text inserted through a web request. Label those results as external evidence, validate structured fields and avoid interpreting embedded instructions as a new authorised request. Trusting a transport channel does not establish trust in every item transported through it.

Tool poisoning affects the advertised contract itself. A malicious description may tell the model to call another tool first or send extra data. A name may imitate a trusted tool. Dynamic discovery therefore requires approved registries, namespacing, reviewed schemas and descriptions, and change detection. Pin the relevant contract or version and require re-review when its authority or behaviour changes. A previously approved endpoint can also change after approval, which makes monitoring important.

Schema drift means the discovered tool contract changed from the reviewed version; detect it before accepting new requests. Version pinning is not a complete supply-chain defence. Review how the tool is deployed, which credentials it holds and how to disable it quickly. Give each tool narrow downstream scopes and enforce its data destinations. If a database tool is compromised, limiting it to one tenant's read operations reduces the possible damage compared with a shared administrative credential. Its output still needs validation because a narrow credential does not prevent misleading results.
Data exfiltration and secret leakage

Exfiltration means moving data to a destination that is not entitled to receive it. Email and uploads are obvious channels. Less obvious channels include search queries, translation requests, public tickets, webhook parameters and rendered image URLs. A generated Markdown image can trigger a browser fetch when rendered; if its URL contains a confidential value, the value can leave through the renderer rather than through the tool registry.

Treat rendering as an effect boundary. Sensitive applications should not automatically fetch arbitrary model-generated URLs or active content. Use approved destinations and controlled rendering, and ensure a proxy does not merely forward confidential query strings to the same untrusted destination. Output encoding prevents code interpretation in a particular destination; it does not decide whether the text is allowed to be disclosed. That needs a data-flow and recipient policy.

Keep credentials outside model context, memory and ordinary tool results. The executor obtains narrow credentials from the identity system and uses them without exposing the token to the model. System prompts should not contain secrets because their wording may be disclosed. Secret scanners in outputs and telemetry are a second layer, not permission to place credentials in context first. A scanner can miss a reformatted or indirectly encoded secret.

An important risk combination is private data, untrusted content and an outbound channel in one run. Removing a leg or placing a correctly enforced control on it blocks that particular route. Do not treat the combination as a universal proof: other harms and covert channels may remain. Scope the conclusion to the architecture reviewed, and test the actual destinations and outputs through which data could leave.

SSRF, path traversal and unsafe access

Server-side request forgery occurs when a tool uses its privileged network position to fetch a destination chosen by an attacker. Internal services and cloud metadata endpoints are common targets. Parse URLs, restrict schemes and destinations, reject unexpected ports and resolve addresses against the required network policy. An allowlisted hostname can still redirect to an internal destination or change its DNS answer, so enforce destination rules at the egress proxy and network layer as well.

Path traversal similarly uses a requested filename to escape the permitted workspace. Resolve paths against a fixed base and reject paths outside it, but consider symlink changes and races between validation and opening a file. The sandbox's filesystem view should expose only permitted files rather than giving the harness broad host access and relying on a string check. Reserved filenames, input size limits and output validation also protect the file boundary.

The following pure teaching function validates a resolved candidate path against a fixed workspace. It does not claim to prevent every filesystem race or substitute for OS isolation. Its usefulness is narrower: it rejects obvious escapes before the request reaches a constrained file service. A production file-opening contract must handle symlinks, concurrent changes and permissions in the environment where the actual open occurs.

from pathlib import Path

def checked_workspace_path(base: Path, requested: str) -> Path:
    root = base.resolve()
    candidate = (root / requested).resolve()
    if not candidate.is_relative_to(root):
        raise PermissionError("outside workspace")
    return candidate
Code, shell and browser execution risks

Generated code is untrusted computation. Blocking a few imports or shell words cannot cover alternate expressions, native extensions or vulnerabilities in allowed libraries. Run it inside an environment with explicit filesystem, network, resource and lifecycle limits. The harness should retain credentials and provide authorised input data through a narrow interface. Chapter 21 examines the isolation choices and the output release path in detail.

A browser agent also ingests hostile pages and can perform real actions. Isolate its profile and credentials, restrict destinations where the task allows, scan downloads and mediate irreversible submissions. A screenshot or DOM snapshot is evidence, not trusted instruction. When a page says that the assistant should upload a private file to continue, the executor must verify whether the user authorised that exact upload and whether the destination may receive it.
Capability isolation, allowlists and least privilege

Least privilege means granting only the capability required for the current task and principal. Filter tools offered to the model, but also re-check execution because a model can request a tool that was not advertised. Use resource and argument restrictions, rate and amount limits, short-lived credentials and destination allowlists. These controls reduce the worst case even when the model is fully persuaded by malicious content.

A reader-actor split separates processing untrusted material from consequential action. The reader returns typed findings; the actor receives those findings through a controlled interface. This reduces exposure only when the actor verifies provenance and applies independent entitlement and destination rules. A schema-valid recipient can still name the attacker, and a free-text string can still carry a hidden instruction. Typed does not mean trusted or authorised.

For ShopAssist, a reader can extract payment evidence and policy clauses. The actor then determines whether a particular refund proposal is permitted using trusted resource state and policy. The reader cannot mark its own proposal approved. For AegisOps, an investigation worker gathers log evidence while the action executor uses current deployment state and verified approval. The boundary deliberately prevents an external log line from becoming a production-operation permission.
