Durable workflows for long-running tasks

Use a durable execution mechanism for waits, timers, external callbacks and long obligations that must survive worker changes. A workflow encodes the skeleton and decisions; activities perform model, tool and harness I/O under recorded results and retry policy. Keep workflow code within the selected engine's determinism rules. A sleeping process is not a durable timer, and a checkpoint callback is durable only if its storage and transactional contract actually provide that property.

Activities can be attempted again, so external effects still need stable operation identity and downstream deduplication or authoritative reconciliation. A workflow engine's recorded result prevents reissuing completed recorded work during replay; it cannot erase the gap after an external commit whose activity completion was not recorded. Preserve that uncertainty and make the activity contract clear. Durable orchestration and one external effect are distinct claims.

Choose one clear source of orchestration truth. If both a workflow engine and an application database store state, define which facts each owns and how references connect them. Duplicated unsynchronised status can make one system say waiting while another schedules execution. Use transactional outbox/inbox or the engine's supported durable scheduling boundary where coordination requires it. The platform must not lose a continuation because state was saved but the next queue message was never published.
State, checkpoints and object stores

Current run state fits a durable database with versioned updates. An append-only event log supports history, while audit may need separate integrity/retention protection. Large transcripts and artifacts belong in object storage referenced by ID rather than bloating every checkpoint. Cache and lease stores can improve coordination but should not become the sole record of critical obligations. Workflow history has its engine's own persistence and retention contract.

State writes need optimistic concurrency or an equivalent owned transaction. The simplified SQL below shows a version and fencing epoch checked together. Taking over ownership must advance the epoch through an atomic trusted service; workers cannot invent an epoch. Zero updated rows means the writer is stale and must stop/reload, not overwrite the latest state. This statement demonstrates a state boundary; the external executor also needs an ownership/effect contract.

UPDATE agent_runs
SET state = :new_state,
    version = version + 1,
    updated_at = now()
WHERE run_id = :run_id
  AND tenant_id = :trusted_tenant
  AND version = :expected_version
  AND lease_epoch = :fencing_epoch;

Store events with stable sequence or event identities so duplicate delivery does not create inconsistent history. Save related intent, checkpoint and scheduling information atomically when the design requires them to agree. Large artifact references should point to authorised immutable/versioned objects or include a clear update contract. A database backup is useful only when the referenced object versions and event history needed for recovery remain available too.
Vector/search architecture and multi-tenancy

A shared retrieval index can serve many small tenants efficiently if tenant and entitlement filters are enforced inside every query. An index or collection per tenant provides stronger logical separation and easier independent tuning/deletion, with more operational overhead. A cluster per tenant can provide a physical boundary for selected high-scale or regulated deployments. Choose from isolation, capacity, residency and operating requirements rather than declaring one layout mandatory for all customers.

The query layer must derive tenant and entitlements from trusted context, not a model's arguments. Retrieval of another tenant's passage followed by a final-answer refusal is already an exposure if the passage entered context or telemetry. Keep source freshness, policy versioning and deletion coverage observable. Indexes may be restored from backups or rebuilt from authoritative sources, but document the recovery time and version consistency. A rebuilt index can differ if source content changed after the backed-up run.
Kubernetes/OpenShift, autoscaling and isolation

Container orchestration can separate gateway, API, workers, sandbox pools and model-serving resources. Scale workers using queue depth/age and observed progress when they mostly wait on I/O, rather than relying only on CPU. KEDA is one possible event-driven autoscaling integration. Concurrency and provider quota remain independent limits: forty pods each launching twenty requests can overwhelm a service even when the autoscaler correctly followed its queue target.

Define resource requests/limits, readiness, liveness and graceful shutdown. On termination, complete or checkpoint the current bounded step under its ownership contract and avoid accepting new work. Pod disruption budgets can reduce planned simultaneous disruption but do not prevent every node or region failure. Put untrusted sandbox workloads on appropriately separated execution resources with the reviewed runtime class and network policy. GPU inference has different capacity and cold-start behaviour, developed in Chapter 30.

OpenShift or another Kubernetes distribution adds platform-specific security and operational policies. Use supported identity, admission and runtime configuration rather than assuming a portable YAML fragment supplies the whole deployment. The same applies to event scalers: connection authentication, queue mode and provider-specific metadata are required alongside the scaling target. Keep examples compact and refer to the pinned platform documentation for deployable configuration instead of presenting omitted authentication as working infrastructure.
CI/CD, infrastructure as code and GitOps

Version infrastructure, deployment configuration, agent definitions, prompts, policy, tool schemas and evaluation gates. Promote a reviewed release bundle through development, staging and production with the tests and rollout evidence from Chapters 24-27. GitOps reconciliation can provide an auditable desired-state history, but reconciliation does not prove the behaviour is correct. Keep observed running versions and outcome monitoring connected to the desired-state manifest.

State and dependency compatibility matter during promotion. A new schema must support planned resume and rollback, or the release needs an explicit migration strategy. Pin supported tool/model interfaces and keep approved rollback dependencies available. Secrets should be referenced through the platform's secret/identity mechanism, not committed into infrastructure code. Record current emergency execution controls separately from a run's reproducible behaviour bundle so rollback does not accidentally remove a containment restriction.
Secrets, network policy and service identity

Give each component a verified workload identity and minimal service access. The worker needs model/tool gateways and relevant state stores, not unrestricted internet and cluster administration. The tool executor holds narrow downstream credentials; generated code does not. Use secrets management for unavoidable static secrets and supported rotation. Service-to-service encryption and identity, such as mTLS where appropriate, protect transport but do not replace per-action policy.

Network policy should make permitted paths explicit. Sandboxes start with denied egress; workers use approved gateways; data services restrict clients. Verify the network implementation actually enforces the selected rules. Egress proxies need destination and payload policy, not just logging. Apply tenant and purpose checks at the application boundary too, because an allowed connection to the payments API can still carry an unauthorised refund request.
HA, disaster recovery and regional design

High availability handles component failure through replication and controlled takeover. Disaster recovery restores service after larger loss, with a stated recovery point objective for tolerable data loss and recovery time objective for restoration. Define them separately for run state, audit, operation/dedupe records, artifacts and retrieval. Replicated current state is not a backup against every erroneous change, while an occasional backup may not meet the recovery point needed for financial operations.

Regional failover must preserve the identity and outcome of in-flight effects. Reusing a key is safe only when its downstream deduplication record still exists and remains reachable for the retry horizon. Restoring run state but losing effect records can make a previously executed operation appear new. Reconcile uncertain operations before resuming mutations. Keep approved provider/region and tenant residency requirements during failover; availability does not authorise moving restricted data to an unapproved region.

Test recovery as a procedure. Restore stores and referenced objects, verify sequence/version consistency, inspect pending approvals and reconcile external effects. A healthy database endpoint does not prove all runs recovered correctly. Preserve audit integrity across the restore and document legal/retention implications of reintroducing old data. A warm standby reduces setup time but still requires tested routing, ownership and capacity at the recovery location.

Scaling a stateful agent horizontally

Workers can be interchangeable when durable state owns the continuation and the ownership protocol prevents stale advancement. A lease has a limited validity window. A paused worker can outlive it and resume after another worker takes over. Renewal alone is not a proof of exclusive authority. Downstream idempotency protects repeating the same logical operation; it does not authorise two conflicting new proposals. These mechanisms cooperate. Do not reduce the contract to “a Redis TTL ensures one worker.”

Chapter 30. LLM Gateway, Provider Abstraction & Self-Hosted Inference

Several teams use models for routing, extraction, tool decisions and evaluation. If each team independently manages keys, quotas, fallbacks and data policy, the organisation has no consistent view of model traffic. A request can change provider during an outage without preserving the tenant's region rule, or several agents can exhaust one shared quota. An LLM gateway creates a common boundary for model access while leaving the agent's task logic outside it.

The gateway can connect managed APIs and models served by the organisation itself. Self-hosting changes the operating responsibility, not only the endpoint URL. The team now owns capacity, model loading, serving software, licensing and lifecycle. This chapter explains those trade-offs and the mechanisms behind efficient inference, so a platform decision follows workload evidence rather than the assumption that open weights are always cheaper or that compatible APIs make providers interchangeable.

A purchased catering service is simpler to operate; an owned kitchen gives more control but requires equipment, staffing and maintenance. During service, staff reuse preparation where appropriate and keep many tables progressing. Where it stops: models differ in competence and protocol features, and a kitchen's menu does not prove quality. Placement, privacy and measured task performance still constrain every route.

Why an LLM gateway

A gateway centralises caller authentication, task-aware routing, quota allocation, approved fallback, usage accounting and data-placement checks. Agents call a stable internal interface using verified workload identity rather than carrying provider keys. The gateway can enforce which providers and regions a tenant may use, record actual model identity and apply shared observability. This reduces repeated cross-cutting implementations, but it also creates an important service whose availability and fail-closed policies need design.

Keep its responsibility narrow. It mediates model requests; it does not replace the business executor's approval or resource policy. A gateway that filters generated text cannot guarantee that a later tool call is authorised. The agent harness still validates decisions and the protected tool gateway still enforces effects. Likewise the gateway should derive trusted tenant/agent context from authentication rather than granting privileges because a request body says risk=low or tenant=Northwind.

Define a request contract with task type, required capabilities, output constraints, bounded generation settings and trusted data classification. Responses normalise content, tool intents, stop reasons, usage and errors. Record routing reason and release/model identity so evaluation can compare the actual configurations used. The gateway should not silently substitute an unsupported output feature or reduce a high-risk quality floor to make a request succeed.

Provider adapters and compatible interfaces

Many serving systems expose an interface compatible with familiar chat-completion APIs. That can simplify transport, but features differ: tool-call representations, structured output, streaming, token usage, context limits, caching and reasoning controls may not match. An adapter should translate into the application's own types and state what it supports. Compatibility at an endpoint path is not proof that a task's output contract or quality remains equivalent.

Test the adapter with recorded success, truncation, refusal, tool-call and error fixtures. Reject unsupported required capabilities before spending quota. Normalise billing categories without guessing that every provider's input count includes cached tokens or that every failed response consumed nothing. Preserve the actual resolved model version and relevant server settings. A provider migration is an evaluated configuration change, not only replacing an API base URL in a file.

Own the state and tool schemas the agent depends on. Translate schema details at the adapter boundary rather than letting vendor objects spread through the whole harness. Some useful provider features remain specialised; hide them behind an explicit supported capability instead of pretending they are universally portable. Soft dependence can be worthwhile when measured benefits justify it, but document the fallback limitation and the cost of migration.
Routing, quotas, fallback, caching and policy

Routing first filters by tenant/data placement, task quality and required features, then considers health, capacity, cost and latency. Quotas can include concurrency permits, requests, tokens and tenant spend. These are different resources with different accounting rules. Reserve estimated usage atomically and release concurrency when the attempt ends. Settle financial/token allowance against observed usage or a defined uncertain-use record rather than applying one refund rule to every exception.

If a provider explicitly rejects a request before processing under its documented contract, the gateway can release the unconsumed local reservation. A timeout or broken stream does not prove that processing never occurred. It may have produced tokens or incurred cost without a complete returned result. Record the uncertain usage and reconcile where possible. Provider rate limits are also not identical to the platform's financial budget; refunding local capacity does not reset the provider's own rolling limit.

The following pseudocode demonstrates that distinction for one attempt. confirmed_unprocessed must come from a verified adapter error classification, not a model assertion. Reservation and ledger services are durable/concurrency-safe application interfaces. The finally block releases only the concurrency permit. The caller chooses a qualified fallback within a total deadline; unrelated unexpected errors should not be hidden as routine provider failover.

Cache policy also belongs at this boundary where model identity and data placement are known. Prefix-friendly request shaping can reuse approved processing. Exact/semantic response caches need the entitlement, correctness and freshness safeguards from Chapter 28. A gateway that serves a cached answer must still validate current scope. Redaction should occur before content reaches provider and telemetry destinations, with trusted classification and purpose checks rather than a generic regex claimed to remove all sensitive data.
Managed APIs versus self-hosted serving

A managed API transfers much of serving operation to the provider. The organisation still owns identity integration, data contracts, quota planning, task evaluation and fallback policy. It gains access to the provider's supported models and operations without running those GPUs itself. Latency includes network, provider queueing and generation. Pricing and retention follow the actual contract, so do not infer data handling from an API-compatible interface or a general marketing label.

Self-hosting gives control over the environment, model artifact, serving configuration and data placement. It also requires GPUs or other supported accelerators, drivers, runtime security, scaling, model loading and on-call. Capacity costs continue while idle, and utilisation matters to economic comparison. Include staff, reliability headroom, energy/hosting and lifecycle costs where relevant rather than comparing only one GPU's raw hourly rate with a provider's output price.

Quality depends on the chosen model and task. Managed services can expose both proprietary and open-weight models; self-hosted models can be strong at specialised tasks and differ on complex reasoning. Do not present model size or ownership as a universal quality ordering. Evaluate routing, extraction, tool selection and high-risk slices separately. A common design uses qualified self-hosted models for narrow high-volume work while retaining other approved routes for tasks those models do not meet.

How high-throughput serving works

Autoregressive generation commonly has a prefill phase and a decode phase. Prefill processes the prompt and prepares reusable intermediate state. Decode produces tokens incrementally using that state. Long prompts can make first-token latency large, while long outputs consume many decode steps. A single tokens-per-second number cannot describe both user experiences. Measure time to first token, inter-token latency and queueing under the prompt/output distributions the service actually expects.

The key/value cache, or KV cache, stores attention key/value tensors for tokens so each new token does not recompute all earlier work. For a simple dense cache, a rough storage estimate is two times layers times KV heads times head dimension times bytes per value times stored tokens, before other overhead and parallelism details. Model architecture and serving choices change the estimate. Weights, temporary buffers and other allocations also consume memory, so KV storage is not the only capacity constraint.

For a constructed model with 16 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 64 and two bytes per value, the estimate is 32 KiB per stored token. At 4,096 tokens that is 128 MiB of key/value storage for one request, excluding other allocations. This arithmetic illustrates why long contexts and many concurrent requests affect capacity; it is not a benchmark or specification of a named model. Use the actual architecture and engine measurements for planning.

PagedAttention, associated with vLLM, organises KV storage in fixed-size blocks and maps logical tokens to blocks instead of requiring one large contiguous allocation per request. This can reduce fragmentation and support useful sharing. Page/block metadata and eviction policy still matter. Prefix caching reuses eligible KV state for shared prefixes under the engine's supported hashing and isolation rules. SGLang is another serving system with prefix-reuse mechanisms; implementation details need version-specific review.

Continuous batching admits new requests and removes completed requests as generation progresses instead of holding a fixed batch until its longest member finishes. It improves utilisation for mixed lengths when capacity and scheduling allow. The scheduler must balance prefill, decode and fairness; a large arriving prompt can compete with interactive generation. Throughput improvement is workload-dependent, and keeping every seat occupied is not the same as meeting each user's latency objective.

Quantisation reduces the precision used for weights or caches, often reducing memory requirements. Throughput can improve, worsen or remain similar depending on kernels, hardware, batch sizes and other bottlenecks. Evaluate quality and latency on the target workload; lower-bit storage does not itself prove a faster service. Speculative decoding uses a draft process whose proposed tokens a target model verifies under a supported algorithm. Its benefit depends on acceptance and implementation overhead, so benchmark rather than assuming universal speedup.

Tensor parallelism divides model computations across devices, while pipeline parallelism divides stages. These techniques can fit larger models and change throughput, memory and communication cost. More devices introduce coordination and network constraints; they are not free capacity. Serving engines and platforms expose different supported combinations, so pin their configuration and test the actual deployment. A compatibility table or a model-fit calculation is the beginning of planning, not a substitute for load measurement.

Scalable serving on Kubernetes

Serving platforms such as KServe and Ray Serve can coordinate deployment, routing and autoscaling around engines such as vLLM. Their supported versions and integration details evolve, so consult the pinned platform documentation. GPU requests, node pools, model storage and network paths need explicit configuration. Distinguish scaling the HTTP frontend from scaling loaded model replicas; the frontend may become ready quickly while the weights are still unavailable.

Autoscaling should consider queue/concurrency and the task's latency/capacity measurements. Loading weights can create a long cold start, so scale-to-zero is suitable only where that delay is acceptable. Warm capacity costs money but may protect interactive objectives. Reserve different priorities or pools for bulk evaluations and interactive generation if they compete. A queue of large batch jobs should not silently consume all decode capacity intended for incident response.

Load-test realistic distributions, not only identical short prompts. Vary prompt lengths, output bounds, arrival bursts and model routes, and record queue time, first-token latency, generation pace and failures. Locate the operating region that meets objectives with headroom. A rising latency curve may reflect memory pressure, compute saturation or queueing; label a hypothetical chart's assumptions rather than attributing every knee solely to KV exhaustion.
Observability, cost and model lifecycle

Track model/server release, quantisation, request routing, time to first token, inter-token latency, tokens per second, queueing, batch size, cache use and device memory. Record autoscaler events and loading delay so latency incidents can be separated from generation bottlenecks. Cost comparisons should use utilisation-adjusted compute and total workload outcomes, including idle reliability headroom and unsuccessful work. An impressive peak throughput number says little about the cost of a sporadic interactive service.

Register model artifacts with source, licence, version, allowed use, integrity information and evaluation results. Open weights do not automatically mean unrestricted commercial terms or no attribution duty. Review fine-tuned and quantised derivatives under the relevant licence and governance process. Deploy model changes through canary/rollback, monitor them and retire obsolete artifacts. Security patching of serving software and dependencies remains an operating obligation even when model weights themselves do not change.

Shared prefix caching needs a privacy boundary. vLLM documents cache salting to isolate reuse across trust groups and reduce timing-based inference of cached content. Choose a scope appropriate to the tenant and data policy, and review other selected engines' mechanisms. A cached prefix can improve performance while exposing information about prior requests if sharing is uncontrolled. Restrict telemetry and provider access too; self-hosting alone does not solve every shared-service side channel.
When to fine-tune or distil small models

Fine-tuning can improve a narrow, stable task such as classification, extraction format or a fixed tool-call contract when the team has enough reviewed training data and a strong evaluation set. It is rarely the first correction for missing tools, stale knowledge or broken approval logic. Requirements that change weekly may be easier to handle through instructions and retrieval. A specialised model can retain other abilities, so do not claim it becomes useless outside one form; measure any loss or transfer explicitly.

Distillation trains a smaller model using a larger model's outputs or other supervised signals under a defined task/data process. It can reduce serving cost or latency if quality remains adequate. The teacher's output is not automatically true, so review labels and keep held-out evaluation independent of training. Production data needs its purpose and privacy governance, and model/provider terms may constrain the use. Compare with prompt improvements, routing and retrieval before taking on training and retraining operations.

The workflow includes dataset versioning, training configuration, artifact registration, task-slice evaluation, deployment and monitoring. Retrain when the task or tool contract changes, and keep an approved previous artifact for rollback if compatible. A stable high-volume classifier can justify that investment; an open-ended research workflow with changing evidence may not. The economic decision includes the training/data pipeline and operations, not only the new model's per-token runtime cost.
Avoiding provider lock-in

Own the internal model interface, tool schemas, state, memory and evaluation data. Keep vendor SDKs and response translation inside adapters. Test important prompts and contracts across qualified alternatives rather than waiting for an outage to discover incompatibility. Preserve supported snapshots and feature flags in the release manifest. A unique provider feature can be worthwhile, but record the soft dependency and what degraded behaviour is possible if the feature disappears.

Portability is a measured option, not a promise that every provider produces the same answer. Migrating changes quality, latency, usage and sometimes data placement. Run the evaluation and rollout process before switching, and preserve the ability to explain which service processed each run. The gateway makes that change more controllable; it does not remove the need for evidence or let a compatibility layer override a tenant's contract.

Chapter 31. Framework Mapping: LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Spring AI & Others

ShopAssist has a small job with serious consequences: explain an order, decide whether a refund is eligible, and move money only after the required checks. The earlier chapters separated those responsibilities. We can now ask a more useful framework question than which library has the most features: which responsibilities will this library implement, and which responsibilities must our application still enforce?

This chapter maps the same refund flow onto several ecosystems. The examples are implementation sketches with explicitly described domain services. They are not complete payment applications. Framework statements are checked for the October 2026 edition; pin exact package versions, preserve your lockfile, and rerun the approval and restart tests whenever you upgrade. An unchanged method name does not prove unchanged behavior.

ANALOGY / Buying vehicles for a delivery business A delivery business already knows its routes, parcel limits and driver rules before choosing vans. A manufacturer supplies an engine, transmission and dashboard. The business still decides who can drive, which parcels a driver may carry, and how a delivery is confirmed. Agent frameworks supply different engines and controls for a job whose rules should already be understood. Where it stops: software frameworks can change persistence and execution semantics between releases; knowing the controls is not enough to establish safety or portability.

The concept map

An agent definition describes instructions, a model and available capabilities. A controller repeatedly asks for a decision, checks it, and runs permitted tools. State records progress; a checkpoint supports continuation; an approval records authority for one proposed action. A framework might provide these as objects, graph nodes, decorators or services. Start with those meanings, then map them to names in the chosen SDK.

In LangGraph, the principal execution object is a compiled graph, with subgraph composition available for reusable capabilities. In the OpenAI Agents SDK, it is an agent run managed by a Runner. In Spring AI, a ChatClient call passes through advisors, including the tool-calling loop. These are different programming surfaces. None of them defines your organization's refund limit, proves that the customer owns the payment, or makes an arbitrary payments API idempotent.

Keep a framework-neutral tool contract with a typed request, bounded response, error classes, authorization rule and side-effect class. Keep an application run record containing the tenant, principal, remaining budgets, proposal and effect identifiers. Framework messages can be adapted at the edge. This takes some effort initially, but it keeps the rules reviewable and prevents a library upgrade from silently becoming a business-policy change.

The same distinction applies to memory and observability. Conversation history is not necessarily a complete interrupted execution. An OpenTelemetry trace is not necessarily a durable audit record. A namespaced store is not automatically tenant-isolated. Write down what each feature actually guarantees. In our delivery analogy, a dashboard recording speed does not replace the delivery ledger, and a glove compartment does not become secure parcel storage merely because it has a label.
LangGraph: state graphs, checkpoints, interrupts, durable orchestration

LangGraph represents work as nodes that read state and return updates. Edges schedule the next work. Reducers specify how updates combine, while checkpointers persist graph progress. This fits ShopAssist when the application must visibly pass through gather, assess, approve, execute and finish. Chapter 32 develops the details; here the key choice is whether an explicit graph helps reviewers see the mandatory boundaries.

Place the approval in a node that constructs a proposal card and calls interrupt(). Resume that thread using Command(resume=...). The interrupted node restarts from its beginning, so anything before the interrupt must tolerate repetition. Put the financial effect in a separate node, with its stable effect identifier and downstream idempotency contract. Separating nodes avoids approval-related repetition; it does not close the crash window around an external payment.

The approval service must check the proposed action ID, argument hash, authorized approvers, expiry and consumption status. The payments service must check current captured and refunded amounts atomically. The graph should call these services rather than reproduce their rules inside prompts. A rejected approval terminates or escalates; an expired approval requests a new decision; an unknown payment outcome enters reconciliation. These outcomes deserve distinct recorded reasons.

For production, choose durable checkpoint storage and define who may read or resume each thread. An in-memory saver is useful in tests but disappears with its process. A thread ID identifies stored execution; it is not authentication. If a user can name another tenant's thread and your API resumes it without an ownership check, the persistence feature has become an access-control defect.
OpenAI Agents SDK: agents, tools, handoffs, sessions, guardrails, tracing

The OpenAI Agents SDK organizes a run around agents with instructions and tools. A Runner manages model calls and tool execution. A handoff transfers conversational control to another agent; an agent exposed as a tool can return work without transferring ownership. ShopAssist can use triage to hand a refund request to a specialized refund agent, while keeping a single application record for the conversation and its budgets.

Sessions preserve conversation history. They are useful for follow-up questions, but do not substitute for the application's approval record or financial ledger. Input and output guardrails validate at defined points in a run. Tracing records execution detail. The application must still decide which checks need to run before every effect, how sensitive fields are redacted, and which events must survive trace sampling or retention.

There are two legitimate approval designs. A propose_refund tool can create a durable approval request while an external workflow handles execution. Alternatively, a function tool marked needs_approval=True can pause the SDK run. Choose one explicit design for the refund path; do not allow both to create independent authorities for the same effect. The SDK's pause records pending calls, while your service decides who may approve them.

Store serialized RunState on the server under the run's tenant and owner. Do not accept a client-edited snapshot as authority. An approval request may identify the run and pending call, but the server loads the trusted snapshot and applies the verified decision. After resume, the model can request another tool, including another approval. Therefore the response handler must check for interruptions after every run, not only the first invocation.

The following sketch deliberately omits SDK setup and payment integration. Its service contracts are the important part: storage loads an owned snapshot; approvals returns only individually authorized call decisions; the runner can pause again. effect_id belongs to the persisted business proposal, not to a newly generated retry timestamp. Currency is represented separately from an integer amount in minor units, so retries cannot depend on floating-point rounding.

async def continue_refund(run_id, principal, runtime, store):
    saved = store.load_owned(run_id, principal.tenant_id)
    state = await runtime.restore(saved.snapshot)
    for pending in state.pending_calls():
        decision = store.validated_decision(
            run_id, pending.call_id, principal
        )
        if decision is None:
            continue
        state.apply_decision(pending.call_id, decision)
    result = await runtime.run(state, saved.budgets)
    store.save_owned(run_id, result.snapshot, principal)
    return {
        "status": result.status,
        "pending": result.pending_calls,
        "answer": result.final_output,
    }

This is pseudocode for an adapter interface, not an SDK API listing. A complete adapter also persists remaining cost and time budgets across continuation. Resetting a Runner's invocation limit does not reset the organization's financial allowance. The official human-in-the-loop documentation and RunState reference describe the supported serialization and approval surfaces.
Spring AI: the Java enterprise path

Spring AI fits model calls and tools into Spring applications. A ChatClient is configured with instructions, tools and advisors. Annotated @Tool methods expose application capabilities; advisors supply concerns such as conversation memory and retrieval. VectorStore and ingestion components support knowledge access. Micrometer observations connect the interaction to established telemetry. This is especially useful when order ownership, payment accounting and transaction boundaries already live in Java services.

In Spring AI 2.0, the tool-calling loop is an auto-registered ToolCallingAdvisor in the ChatClient chain. That allows application-controlled interception around tool calling, rather than relying on a private loop inside each model integration. Structured-output validation can retry formatting failures, but it does not establish eligibility. MCP client/server support and annotated capabilities provide interoperability. Consult the Spring AI 2.0 release explanation when migrating older configurations.

A refund tool should call an authenticated domain service, not a repository directly with whatever order ID the model supplied. Use BigDecimal or integer minor units with explicit currency rules. A proposal method can return an approval ticket containing evidence and binding fields. A separate executor consumes that ticket and invokes the payments service. A database transaction protects local accounting, while downstream idempotency protects the remote operation; neither substitutes for the other.

Claude Agent SDK: a production agent loop with built-in tools

The Claude Agent SDK includes an agent loop with built-in file, shell, search and other capabilities. It supports sessions, subagents, hooks and permission controls. That broad tool surface can reduce implementation work for coding or research systems. It also makes capability restriction an early design task. A customer-facing refund agent does not need the same workshop as an agent repairing a repository.

Permission rules and tool visibility are related but different. allowed_tools supplies preapproval. It should not be read as proof that every other capability is inaccessible. The Microsoft, Google and AWS agent stacks

Microsoft Agent Framework combines ideas from Semantic Kernel and AutoGen with agent abstractions and explicit workflows, including MCP and A2A interoperability. Microsoft Foundry supplies managed services, while Entra ID and Azure data services provide the surrounding enterprise identity and knowledge components. The April 2026 version 1.0 announcement establishes the edition's terminology. Treat framework support and managed-service availability as separate facts when planning a deployment.

Google's Agent Development Kit supplies agent and workflow building blocks. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides managed runtime, session, memory and related platform capabilities. The names describe a development-to-deployment path, not a guarantee that every component meets your retention or approval policy. AWS offers Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock paths, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supplying runtime and gateway services. Its policy integration can enforce Cedar rules outside the model at tool access.

For all three, inspect the same contract: inbound identity, outgoing delegation, state ownership, regional availability, exportable telemetry, data retention and supported resume behavior. A managed gateway may remove credential plumbing while leaving business eligibility entirely yours. A managed memory service may store records while your application still owns write consent and deletion. Chapter 33 turns these questions into deployment tracks; do not choose a cloud by counting differently named boxes.
LlamaIndex and LangChain components

LlamaIndex is useful for connecting, parsing, indexing and querying knowledge. LangChain supplies model, tool, retrieval and document-processing integrations commonly used beneath LangGraph. Use these components behind a retrieval interface that accepts a scoped question and returns evidence with source locators. The interface should preserve document version, entitlement filters and freshness. Returning a fluent answer without those fields discards the properties the application needs to verify it.

These libraries can reduce mechanical work, but the organization still owns relevance evaluation, document updates, sensitive-data boundaries and citation checks. Run a fixed retrieval test set when changing a splitter or reranker. The delivery business may buy a better navigation system, but it still needs the correct destination and parcel permissions. An answer generated from the wrong policy version remains wrong even if every individual integration call succeeds.
CrewAI and AutoGen as multi-agent pattern exposure

CrewAI exposes role-based agents, tasks and processes, with flows for explicit orchestration. AutoGen helped popularize conversational collaboration between agents; Microsoft Agent Framework is the successor path described above. These systems are useful places to observe delegation patterns quickly. Their convenience should not decide the number of agents in your production design. Add a specialist for measurable isolation, expertise, context or parallelism benefits, then measure the coordination overhead.

Keep one owner for the task, an explicit handoff envelope, scoped capabilities and shared limits. Test what happens when a specialist returns an unsupported claim or cannot finish. A missing result should become partial evidence or escalation, not an invented success. A supervisor's decision must pass the same effect checks as a single agent's decision. Multi-agent conversation does not multiply the authority granted to the underlying user.
A tested adapter rather than a compatibility claim

The companion examples/capstone_lab.py executes one actual LangGraph path against SQLite. Its model, GitOps change service and telemetry are deterministic fakes. It pauses for an external approval record, survives a process dying after a simulated effect commits, and resumes without another logical effect. This provides a concrete starting point for the framework comparison exercise. It does not implement the other SDK adapters or establish parity between their persistence and cancellation contracts.

The executed baseline is Python 3.12.14, LangGraph 1.2.16, langgraph-checkpoint 4.3.0, langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite 3.1.2, langgraph-prebuilt 1.1.1 and langchain-core 1.6.12. Temporal SDK 1.34.0 is imported and its activity boundary is exercised locally; no Temporal server was run. There is no provider SDK, model deployment, MCP transport or negotiated protocol in this slice. examples/requirements-capstone.txt pins the complete resolved environment; examples/CAPSTONE_LAB.md records commands and scope. A version absent from that tested matrix remains an integration task.
Selection criteria

Compare control flow, persistence, human approval, tracing, policy hooks, interoperability, operations, language fit and licensing. For each criterion, write a question whose answer can be demonstrated. “Supports persistence” is too vague; “resume a pending approval in a new process using durable storage without repeating a payment” is testable. “Supports tracing” should include export and redaction, not merely a vendor dashboard screenshot.

The operational burden belongs in the comparison. Count databases, queues, migration procedures and services your team must maintain. Ask how paused runs survive code changes and how a compromised worker is contained. Check whether framework state can be inspected without vendor-specific tooling. An attractive prototype may still be a poor fit for a team that cannot support its runtime during an incident.

Build it: the same agent in two frameworks, and an ADR

Implement ShopAssist in two chosen runtimes with shared policy, tool and evaluation packages. Use the same model configuration and the same scripted fake outcomes first. Cover approval, rejection, expiry, malformed output, a provider timeout after processing and a process restart. Then run live-model evaluations on the same labeled conversations. Repeated trials reveal variability; deterministic failures should be fixed before attributing differences to model behavior.

Record success by case, forbidden actions, cost per successful conversation, latency and operational effort. Specify the confidence interval and which cases must pass regardless of the aggregate score. An architecture decision record states the problem, options, evidence, decision, consequences and revisit condition. Do not invent attractive percentages to make the record look complete. A small honest comparison is more useful than a polished but unsupported result.

For example, choose LangGraph if explicit routing and long pauses are decisive in the measured refund cases. Choose a Spring service boundary for Java domain logic already owned by that team. Keep framework message types inside adapters and document how stored runs would migrate. The exit strategy should name real work: state conversion, checkpoint handling, trace parity and approval continuity. Replaceability is a maintained property, not a promise made once.
Interview drills

When asked how to avoid lock-in, name the application contracts and the alternative-runtime test that keeps them honest. When asked what the framework handles, trace one request through model output, policy, approval, effect dispatch and reconciliation. Explain who owns each record. This makes the answer concrete and prevents a feature list from concealing the hardest boundary: authority over a real external effect.

When asked which framework is best, state the workload first. A coding agent needing controlled filesystem tools differs from a narrow refund service waiting hours for approval. Explain one decisive test and one operational cost. Mention the conditions under which you would revisit the decision. The goal is a defendable choice with observable consequences, not a claim that one engine wins every route.
Key takeaways

A framework earns its place by implementing understood responsibilities. Its convenience is real, but application eligibility, authorization, approval binding, external-effect safety and evaluation remain explicit contracts. Compare runtimes under the same tasks, preserve remaining budgets across pauses, and deny unfamiliar capabilities. The delivery business can change its vehicles while keeping its delivery rules; software achieves that freedom through adapters, owned records and repeated tests.

Chapter 32. LangGraph in Depth: Building Durable Agent Graphs

ShopAssist needs a refund path that a reviewer can follow without guessing what the model might do next. Gather the payment facts, assess eligibility, ask for approval when policy requires it, execute with an effect identifier, and verify the result. LangGraph makes that path explicit while still allowing model-directed investigation inside selected nodes. The important question is how the graph executes and resumes, not how attractive its drawing looks.

This chapter uses the LangGraph 1.2 release family as checked for the October 2026 edition. Exact patches and supporting packages must be pinned in your project. Code listings are compact teaching units, with domain-service contracts stated beside them. They do not constitute a complete payments or incident-response application. The Graph API and persistence documentation are the primary references for upgrades.

ANALOGY / The railway dispatch office A dispatch office schedules stations to report, combines their reports under agreed rules, records the journey and authorizes the next movement. Some reports arrive together; a train can wait for clearance without occupying the office staff. A graph has the same separation between scheduled work, merged state, recorded progress and the next decision. Where it stops: software nodes are not literal trains, and restoring an old journey record cannot undo a payment, rollback or message already sent outside the graph.

How LangGraph thinks: nodes, channels and super-steps

A StateGraph builder describes nodes and edges over a state schema. A node reads state and returns the fields it changes rather than rewriting the entire record. Each field behaves like a channel carrying a value through execution. An edge schedules work after the current node completes. Compile the builder to obtain the executable graph; compilation is where persistence and other runtime dependencies are attached.

Execution advances in super-steps. Nodes scheduled together can run in parallel. Their updates merge according to the state fields' rules, then the graph schedules the next work. Sequential nodes occupy different super-steps. This is a synchronization model, not a wall-clock timetable: one node may take seconds, another may stream tokens, and neither must finish on a literal clock tick. Checkpoint persistence depends on the configured saver and durability mode.

Figure 32.1. One graph super-step. Several nodes can belong to one super-step; not every node runs in every step. Shared state needs an agreed merge rule before parallel work begins. Diagram labels in reading order: Scheduled work; Run only the nodes activated for this step; Partial updates; Each node returns changed fields; Reducer merge; Combine updates by field semantics; Record progress; Persist according to durability mode; Schedule next work; Use validated routing decisions
State and reducers

The state schema gives names and types to the record moving through the graph. A field without a reducer normally receives the new value in a sequential update. If parallel nodes write the same such field in one step, the graph cannot resolve that conflict automatically and raises an update error. Do not confuse sequential replacement with parallel last-writer-wins behavior. Evidence disappearing after an update and a concurrency error have different causes.

A reducer is a function that combines the current value with an update. List addition appends, but it also preserves duplicate entries. For evidence, use a reducer keyed by stable evidence IDs and decide what conflicting versions mean. For severity, define an explicit ordering rather than lexicographic string comparison. Pure reducers are easy to test: feed the same current state and update, then verify the same merged result without invoking a model.

This reducer treats one evidence identity as immutable and gives deterministic ordering. A system allowing corrections should create a new version with a supersession link instead of silently changing the old entry. For chat histories, add_messages supports appending messages and updating matching message IDs. That is different from blindly concatenating a list. Choose the merge behavior because of the information's meaning, not because a convenient annotation appears in an example.
Nodes, edges and routing

Use a static edge when the next step is fixed. Use a conditional edge when a separate function chooses the destination. Use a Command when a node both updates state and chooses where to go. ShopAssist's assessment can set the eligible amount and select approval or finish. Keep money in integer minor units with explicit currency; a graph field should not introduce ambiguous floating-point accounting.

Type annotations such as Command[Literal[...]] help static tooling and graph rendering. They do not implement a business authorization rule. Validate model-generated routes against a finite destination set before constructing a Command. Also avoid mixing a static outgoing edge with Command routing from the same node: both routes can run. An approval drawing is only meaningful when actual scheduling cannot activate an execution path around the policy check.

The routing helper is a pure teaching example. The approval record it reads must have been produced by a service that validates authority and binding, not copied from an arbitrary model response. Test each destination, an unknown destination, rejection and expiry. In the dispatch office, a station's suggested next platform is information; clearance to move still belongs to the office's rules.
Checkpointers, threads and state history

A checkpointer saves graph state under a thread ID, allowing a later invocation to continue that thread. InMemorySaver is useful for deterministic tests. SQLite can support local persistent demonstrations; a shared durable implementation such as PostgresSaver is more appropriate for independently restarting workers. Operate the database, schema setup, encryption and retention as part of the application. A saver object does not maintain those operational properties for you.

Inspect the current state to find its pending nodes and values. State history supports debugging from an earlier checkpoint, often called time travel. Replaying a checkpoint branches graph execution; it does not restore the external world to its old state. A replayed investigation may call changed data sources, and a replayed mutation must still use an authorized effect contract. Audit state edits because they change the evidence on which subsequent decisions rely.

Store immutable version information with the run: graph behavior version, tool contract versions, prompt packs and model configuration. When deploying a changed graph, decide whether paused threads continue with the old behavior or migrate under a tested procedure. Renaming a pending node can strand a run. A compatibility test should include a checkpoint produced by the prior release, not only a new invocation created after the upgrade.
Human-in-the-loop with interrupt

interrupt(payload) pauses inside a node and exposes the payload to the caller. Resume using Command(resume=value) on the same authorized thread. The interrupted node begins again from its first line; at the relevant interrupt, the supplied value becomes the return value. It may restart more than twice when there are additional pauses or retries. Write repeatable code before the interrupt rather than relying on an exact counter of two executions.

The payload should identify the proposal, action, canonical argument hash, evidence, impact, rollback plan and expiry. An approval API checks the human's identity, role, tenant and decision. The resume value carries a reference to the resulting approval record. The node loads and validates that server-owned record. A button click or a matching hash alone cannot establish that the approver was entitled to authorize the action.

Keep ticket creation, email and payment effects out of the interrupted node unless they are explicitly idempotent. Even a separate execution node can be retried after an external effect completed but before its completion was recorded. Persist an intent and stable idempotency key first; use the downstream deduplication contract or reconcile an unknown outcome. Approval expiry needs an external timer or workflow service because a paused graph does not wake itself after thirty minutes.
Fan-out and fan-in with Send

Send creates runtime-dependent work, such as one investigation per selected source. Each worker receives a bounded input: service, tenant scope, source and deadline. Their outputs combine through reducers. A planner can select metrics, logs and recent changes without always invoking every possible specialist. Cap the number of tasks before scheduling them, and enforce concurrency limits appropriate to the deployment and downstream quotas.

A joined result must describe failed or missing branches as well as successes. If logs time out while metrics return, the hypothesis node needs to know that it is reasoning from partial evidence. Do not turn three responses into an arbitrary completion-order list and then infer priority from that order. Record source IDs and sort for presentation separately. The analogy's railway carriages reconnect, but their arrival order does not determine which report is most trustworthy.
Subgraphs: composing graphs

A compiled subgraph can become a parent node. Shared state fields pass information across the boundary; an adapter function can translate incompatible parent and child schemas. This gives investigations or verification procedures their own tests and versioned interface. The interface should state which evidence enters, what additions return, and how an interrupted child participates in the parent's checkpoint ownership.

Be careful with append reducers on both sides. A child may return its received list plus additions; the parent can append the received items again. Return a delta or use a reducer whose semantics safely deduplicate stable IDs. Test a nonempty input, not just the convenient empty list. A modular graph is useful when it reduces reasoning about a capability; it is not useful if its hidden state causes facts to duplicate or disappear.
Tools and the ReAct loop

A basic tool loop has a model node and a tool node. The model returns a request; the tool node returns observations; routing either continues the loop or finishes. ToolNode provides dispatch plumbing for supported tool contracts. It does not decide business authorization, risk, approval, idempotency or audit retention. Those checks belong in the tool executor or in an explicit path before a mutating tool becomes callable.

Offer only capabilities permitted for the principal, and enforce permissions again at execution. Filtering reduces model mistakes but does not secure an alternate invocation path. Bound results before storing them in messages, preserve tool-call IDs, and return a result for every requested call. Use typed error outcomes that distinguish invalid arguments, denial, dependency failure and outcome unknown. The model can reconsider a plan without being allowed to reinterpret a denial as permission.
Multi-agent graphs: supervisors and handoffs

The supervisor pattern uses a node that selects scoped specialists and receives their results. A handoff transfers control; returning a subtask result preserves the original owner. In a subgraph, Command can target the parent graph when that interface is deliberately supported. These choices affect accountability. Do not use a handoff merely because an agent object is available: first decide who owns the remaining budget and completion decision.

Record handoff counts, deadlines, evidence references and expected output schemas. A specialist cannot change the global incident plan simply by returning authoritative prose. The supervisor validates the structured result and applies it through the state rules. Add a repeated-handoff detector and a global step cap. If two specialists keep sending the same unresolved task back, escalate with the known evidence instead of financing an endless conversation.
Long-term memory with stores

Checkpoints concern a thread's execution; a store holds application data across threads. User preferences, reviewed incident summaries and approved procedural knowledge can live in namespaced store records. Namespaces should include tenant and subject scope, with access checked independently of model-supplied identifiers. A key-value path is useful organization, but it is not a substitute for authorization.

The memory write gate validates source, purpose, sensitivity, retention and supersession rules. A record that looks like a preference but instructs the agent to skip approvals is rejected. Deletion must cover served records and derived indexes, with backup expiry and restore suppression handled under the documented retention policy. Memory can improve investigation, but current system-of-record facts and policy still govern an action. The permanent railway archive advises dispatch; it does not issue clearance.

Reliability: retries, recursion limits and durability

A node retry policy handles selected failures with bounded attempts and backoff. Use it only when repetition is safe. For a mutation, the same logical effect key must reach the service on every attempt; a new key creates a new operation. Classify outcome unknown separately from a definite refusal. Never compensate an effect merely because its response was lost; first establish whether it occurred.

The recursion limit caps graph super-steps in an invocation. It is a coarse brake, not a cost or wall-clock budget, and it can restart across repeated invocations. Maintain cumulative application budgets in persisted state, and evaluate model routing by task rather than treating step counts as money limits. When a limit is reached, record a terminal or waiting reason and preserve any uncertain effect for reconciliation. A failed-safe run must not lose information needed by the human who takes over.

Durability modes include synchronous, asynchronous and exit persistence. Synchronous recording reduces the window before the next step but adds latency; exit-only persistence offers less protection during execution. Choose deliberately around effects and measure the overhead. Durable timers, reminders and escalation are a separate concern; combine the graph with an approval service or workflow engine when waits need scheduled actions. See the durability reference.
Streaming

Streaming can expose full values, partial node updates, model messages or custom progress events. Use updates for statements such as “metrics collected,” and model message chunks for user-facing text. Do not expose raw state merely because it is easy to stream. Private application fields, tool observations and intermediate approval metadata can contain information the user is not entitled to see.

The persisted run and application event log remain the source of truth. A disconnected client should reconnect by run identity and obtain current status rather than infer completion from its last token. Progress messages should distinguish proposing, waiting, executing and verifying. “Rollback requested” is not “rollback applied,” and neither is “service recovered.” Those labels help operators make decisions while the underlying graph continues asynchronously.
Testing LangGraph graphs

Test reducers and routers as plain functions. Then use a scripted model to exercise tool requests and final answers through the compiled graph. GenericFakeChatModel supplies scripted messages; an adapter or small subclass is needed when the loop expects tool binding. Keep fake model behavior explicit so a test failure identifies application logic rather than a changing hosted model response.

A persistence test should launch a start process and a resume process with shared definitions and durable instrumentation. In-memory counters reset on restart, so they cannot prove combined execution counts. Use a fresh database and thread ID per test. Kill after intent persistence, while waiting, after downstream effect success and before local completion. Assert the provider's effect ledger, approval consumption and final state, not only the graph's final sentence.
Observability and deployment

Instrument node scheduling, model calls, tools, policy decisions, interrupts and state updates with one correlation identity. LangSmith can provide graph-native inspection; OpenTelemetry can connect to the enterprise tracing system. Record versions and evidence locators, redact before export, and retain an independent audit log for approvals and effects. Sampled traces cannot be the only proof that a payment was authorized.

Deploy compiled graphs inside your services or evaluate managed/self-hosted platform offerings. In either case, define queue ownership, worker concurrency, restart behavior, checkpoint access and migration. Operators need to locate a waiting run, inspect a denial, reconcile an unknown effect and disable mutations without stopping investigation. A production deployment is the graph plus these operating contracts, not merely a web endpoint calling invoke().

Failure modes

Duplicate effects usually point to a repeatable-execution problem, not an unusually creative model. Lost waiting runs point to persistence or thread ownership. Duplicate evidence points to parent/child merge semantics. Expensive runs within a recursion limit point to missing cumulative budgets. Unapproved actions point to routing and authorization boundaries. Investigate the violated contract before adding another prompt warning; a warning cannot repair an incorrectly scheduled node.

Keep these diagnoses visible in tests. Unknown route, new tool, stale approval, missing telemetry and changed graph version should each produce a specific outcome. The operator can then distinguish a legitimate escalation from a framework exception. Clear terminal reasons also improve evaluation: a safely escalated dependency outage is not the same failure as a run that claims completion without verifying the service.
Interview drills

Explain one super-step using a state field and its reducer, then explain why parallel writes need a merge rule. For interruption, say that the node restarts and describe the effect-safe placement. For persistence, distinguish checkpoint, governed store and application audit. For deployment, describe how a paused run survives both a process restart and a code upgrade. These concrete transitions demonstrate understanding better than memorizing API names.
Key takeaways

LangGraph supplies explicit scheduling, state merging and persistence interfaces. The application supplies valid routes, governed memory, authorization, effect identity and outcome verification. Checkpoints preserve a record; they do not rewind the world. An approval pause is useful only when the human decision is bound and validated. Design the graph as the railway office's schedule, then prove that real-world movement still obeys the clearance rules.

Chapter 33. Cloud & Enterprise Integration Tracks

An agent platform becomes useful when it fits the systems the organization already operates. ShopAssist needs an identity provider, order and payment services, durable storage and an approval channel. AegisOps needs alert streams, telemetry, change systems and incident records. A cloud offers components for these jobs, but choosing components is not the same as designing their contracts. Begin with the responsibilities, then map them to the services available in your account.

Cloud product names and availability in this chapter are orientation for the October 2026 edition. Check the provider's current documentation, supported regions and account quotas before committing to a design. A managed agent service can shorten deployment work without meeting every approval, retention or isolation requirement automatically. We will build one reference deployment deeply, then document how the important contracts would survive a move.

ANALOGY / Connecting a new building to a city A new clinic needs rooms, water, electricity, roads and emergency access. The architect defines what each connection must supply; local utilities determine how it is installed. Moving the same clinic design to another city changes suppliers, permits and maintenance arrangements. An agent platform similarly joins an existing cloud and enterprise fabric. Where it stops: cloud services with similar purposes can have different delivery, identity and recovery semantics. A matching label in a catalogue does not make them interchangeable.
