Building blocks across clouds

Separate the public entry point from background execution. The entry point authenticates the caller, validates a request, assigns an owned run identity and returns progress or an asynchronous receipt. Workers perform bounded model and tool work. A durable workflow coordinates waits, retries and completion. An LLM gateway, the owned model-access service, applies provider routing and accounting. These roles stay useful across vendors because they describe behavior rather than a specific deployment product.

The data layer holds different kinds of records. Run state and event history describe execution; an approval service records authority; an effect ledger supports dispatch and reconciliation; search indexes retrieve evidence; object storage holds large raw payloads. A cache can accelerate access but should not become the only copy of a pending approval. Identity, secrets and telemetry surround the whole system. Assign an owner and failure behavior to each building block before naming its provider service.

Figure 33.1. The connections a platform needs. These are dependency relationships, not a sequential request path. Map a service to a required contract before evaluating its name. Diagram labels in reading order: Agent platform; Identity; User, workload and delegated authority; Models; Provider access through an owned gateway; Tools and knowledge; Scoped APIs and evidence retrieval; Durable work; State, waits and reconciliation; Operations; Telemetry, budgets and emergency controls

All three clouds offer container execution, serverless computation, queues, relational databases, object storage and observability. They also offer model access and increasingly managed agent capabilities. That breadth makes many architectures possible, but it does not remove trade-offs. For a long approval wait, inspect timeout and continuation behavior. For messages, inspect delivery and ordering. For state, inspect transaction and restore guarantees. These are the equivalents of checking water pressure rather than merely finding a water supplier.
Track 1 - AWS

One self-managed AWS arrangement uses API Gateway for entry, EKS or ECS for services and workers, SQS or managed Kafka for buffered work, and Aurora or RDS PostgreSQL for durable application records. S3 holds raw evidence; ElastiCache supports coordination or caches. OpenSearch or PostgreSQL with pgvector provides search, depending on workload. Bedrock access sits behind the application's model gateway so quotas, cost and provider behavior remain centralized.

Step Functions can coordinate AWS-native workflows; Temporal can provide code-driven durable workflow semantics when that is the chosen application contract. Do not choose from their diagrams alone. Run a pending approval through a worker restart, timeout, late decision and downstream unknown outcome. Confirm where retry behavior is configured and which identifier reaches the effect service. An event's redelivery must recover or find existing work rather than create another refund.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore offers managed runtime and surrounding capabilities, including gateways and policy integration. A gateway can turn supported APIs into tools; Cedar policy evaluates permission outside model reasoning. The official policy concepts describe the relevant boundary. Business eligibility and exact approval binding still belong to your application. A tool permitted by a gateway may still be invalid for the particular payment or live revision.

Use workload identity for pods or tasks rather than distributing static keys. Give the observation worker read access to its service's telemetry and the remediation executor narrowly scoped change authority. Route telemetry to CloudWatch or your chosen enterprise system, with redaction before export. Test that disabling the mutation path leaves alert ingestion and read-only investigation functioning. The deployment should keep helping responders even when authority to change production is withdrawn.
Track 2 - Microsoft Azure

An Azure reference can use API Management at the edge, AKS or Container Apps for execution, Service Bus or Event Hubs for work and events, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL for durable state. Blob Storage holds large payloads; managed Redis provides caches. Azure AI Search can combine keyword, vector and ranking capabilities for governed retrieval. Microsoft Foundry model access passes through the owned model gateway, preserving consistent application accounting.

Entra ID often supplies the enterprise user's identity already. Managed identities supply workload authentication, but they do not mean that every operation should use the workload's broad rights. A refund or rollback should preserve the user or approved system principal, the agent actor and the targeted resource. Confirm how delegated credentials reach downstream services, how audience checks are performed and how the audit records both identities.

Durable Functions can express durable orchestration in an Azure-native serverless model. Temporal is another option when the application has chosen its workflow semantics. Foundry Agent Service supplies managed agent execution capabilities. Evaluate the exact workload model, not a generic assertion that managed services cannot support approvals. Some managed paths fit the requirement well; others need an external approval coordinator or an application-owned run store.

For knowledge retrieval, apply tenant and entitlement filters inside the retrieval request, not after the model sees the results. Use Key Vault or the organization's secret platform for credentials. Export operational evidence through Azure Monitor, Application Insights or enterprise collectors. Simulate a secret-access failure and a model quota failure: each should produce a bounded degraded response, not a silent fallthrough to an ungoverned public endpoint.
Track 3 - Google Cloud

A Google Cloud reference can use Apigee or API Gateway for entry, Cloud Run for stateless services, GKE where scheduling and infrastructure control are required, Pub/Sub for buffered events, and Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for relational records. Cloud Storage holds raw evidence and Memorystore supports caches. Vector Search or PostgreSQL-compatible vector capabilities can serve retrieval. Choose the smallest arrangement that satisfies your evidence and operating requirements.

Google's Agent Development Kit supplies agent and workflow abstractions. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform includes managed runtime, session, memory and related services; names evolved from earlier Vertex AI offerings. The official platform overview describes these responsibilities. Session and memory APIs still need application rules for subject scope, provenance and deletion. A managed store cannot decide which incident conclusion should become reusable knowledge.

Use workload identity rather than service-account keys in prompts or containers. Configure model access with regional availability and data policy in mind. Workflows or a chosen durable engine coordinates long-running lifecycle operations. For a Cloud Run worker, assume the instance can disappear; persist the work before acknowledging ownership and reconcile uncertain effects after continuation. A stateless service can run a stateful task only because its state is owned elsewhere.

Search and relational storage need not share a product. Keeping vectors beside application records may simplify operations, while a dedicated search service may better fit ranking and throughput. Measure with the organization's actual document types, filters and query mix. Run restore and index-rebuild drills separately. A recoverable database does not prove the searchable evidence is fresh, and a rebuilt index does not prove its entitlement metadata is correct.
Track 4 - enterprise integration fabric

The enterprise fabric is the set of shared systems that connect applications: event streams, gateways, identity, secrets, observability and service management. An agent should join those systems through owned interfaces. Kafka alerts can start AegisOps; the API gateway authenticates operators; service identity protects tool requests; an ITSM system carries approved change records. Replacing all of that with a new agent-specific stack creates more boundaries to operate and audit.

Message consumption has two distinct deduplication jobs. A transport event ID stops the same delivery from creating duplicate work. Incident correlation groups different alerts describing the same service and symptom. Keep the first key stable across redelivery, even when a correlation time window changes. Otherwise yesterday's delayed message can be treated as a new incident simply because today's window differs. Record the original event and the correlation decision for later investigation.

Figure 33.2. An alert becomes owned work. A durable dispatch record supports recovery if the consumer dies between insert and start. Deduplicating an insert is not enough if workflow dispatch can be lost. Diagram labels in reading order: Event bus; Consumer; Run store; Workflow; 1. Deliver source event ID; 2. Insert stable ingestion intent; 3. Existing or newly owned run; 4. Start with deterministic workflow ID; 5. Record accepted start; 6. Acknowledge recorded ownership

A practical consumer needs a recoverable bridge between the database insert and workflow start. Store a dispatch intent or use the engine's idempotent start contract, then retry missing starts safely. Acknowledge the message only after its ownership is durably recorded. Define a dead-letter path for malformed or unauthorized events, and preserve enough redacted detail to repair them. Do not ask a model to infer whether the message bus delivered the same event twice.

Gateways and service meshes can provide authentication, transport protection, timeouts and egress restrictions. Inspect automatic retries: replaying a non-idempotent tool through a mesh can duplicate its effect before the harness notices. Secrets management should issue credentials to the executor under its workload identity, not pasted into context. OpenTelemetry correlation should continue across the queue, workflow, model gateway, MCP and downstream service so the operator can reconstruct one complete run.
Managed agent runtime versus self-managed

A managed runtime supplies some operating responsibilities, such as scaling, session execution and service integration. The exact bundle differs by provider. A self-managed runtime gives the team control over deployment, state and extension points, with corresponding maintenance. Neither is inherently the more responsible choice. Select the arrangement whose supported lifecycle and boundaries fit the task and the team's ability to operate it.

Figure 33.3. Who maintains the execution layer?. Both arrangements keep business authority and evidence requirements in the application. Operational convenience changes ownership, not the required outcome. Diagram labels in reading order: Managed runtime; Provider operates supported execution; Application verifies feature fit; Owned approvals and business policy; Export and migration tests; Self-managed runtime; Team operates workers and storage; Full extension responsibility; Owned approvals and business policy; Restore and upgrade rehearsals

Ask whether long waits, external signals, cancellation, retries and versioned continuation fit the runtime's model. Check isolation, regions, private connectivity, telemetry export, encryption and retention. Try the difficult workflow before the happy-path demo. A managed session that works well for chat may require additional services for a payment approval spanning a deployment. Conversely, operating a large workflow platform for a short read-only task may add little value.

Hybrid deployment can make sense when one common policy and identity system governs both paths. For example, core refund execution can remain in an owned domain service while an approved managed runtime handles answer generation. Document where state crosses the boundary and what happens if either side is unavailable. Without this ownership description, hybrid often means duplicate histories, inconsistent approvals and two teams assuming the other recorded the effect.
What is portable, and what is cloud-specific

Agent definitions, tools, prompt packs, evidence schemas, business policies and evaluation cases are good portable assets when their interfaces avoid vendor types. Containers and OpenTelemetry instrumentation can move too, although deployment and collector settings change. Portable does not mean no work: the model behavior, network latency and entitlement implementation may differ. Run the same contract and evaluation cases after a move, and record the differences rather than assuming parity.

Cloud-specific assets include identity bindings, managed-runtime APIs, queue delivery semantics, workflow definitions, secret access and private endpoint configuration. Put these behind adapters with behavioral tests. A queue adapter should specify acknowledgement, redelivery and cancellation, not merely send and receive. A model adapter should normalize stop reasons, usage and errors. That detail lets the new supplier meet the clinic's requirements instead of only matching its connector shape.

Maintain a migration inventory with asset owner, export format, retention constraint and test. Move read-only work first, compare evidence and outcomes, then migrate approved effects with a reconciliation plan. Keep historical approval and audit records available under their original identities. A database export is not a complete migration if paused threads cannot interpret their old tool versions or locate the evidence that justified a pending action.

Identity and networking differences to plan for

Workload identity mechanisms differ across EKS, AKS, GKE and serverless services. Their shared purpose is authenticated workload access without static secrets. Verify which principal is presented at every boundary, and apply resource scope downstream. A network connection from an approved pod does not prove that the current user owns the order it requests. Transport identity, user delegation and record authorization are separate checks.

Private connectivity can reduce exposure and meet data-routing requirements, but its availability and cost vary. Test model endpoints, tool services, secret issuance, flags and telemetry collectors against the real egress policy. A mutation kill switch hosted outside the namespace needs an authorized access path too. If the flag service fails, the mutation policy should fail closed while diagnosis continues. Document sidecar and control-plane accesses instead of leaving them outside the diagram.

Quotas are capacity constraints, often specific to account, region and model. Allocate them across tenants and task classes before load arrives. Track admission queues, provider throttling and cost reservations. A sudden incident storm should not let low-priority postmortem drafts consume the quota needed for urgent triage. Residency-driven designs must also confirm that the selected model and its fallback are available within the allowed region.

Build it: one reference deployment

Choose the primary cloud that fits your team's existing operating environment. Write infrastructure as code for networking, workloads, durable storage, event ingestion, secrets and observability. Deploy the agent API, workers and chosen workflow service independently. Keep effect execution in a narrow service with its own permissions and ledger. A single local container can teach the flow, but the reference deployment must show what survives process and node loss.

Use GitOps or the organization's deployment process to pin code, models, tools, policies and prompts as one release record. A rollout keeps each active run on a compatible behavior version. Prove that an approval created before deployment can be resumed after it without changing the approved arguments. If migration is necessary, make it an explicit tested operation. Do not let a new image reinterpret an old approval under new policy silently.

Interview drills

For a managed-versus-self-managed question, begin with the task's lifecycle and the team's operating capacity. Describe one pause, one crash and one authority boundary. Explain what the provider operates and what the application owns. For portability, name a queue or identity semantic that needs retesting. An answer that says “same architecture, different names” is a useful beginning, but the behavioral differences are where integration work becomes real.

For an event-driven design, trace an alert through durable ownership, workflow dispatch and acknowledgement. Explain how duplicate delivery finds existing work, how a lost start is repaired and where an unauthorized event goes. Then show how correlation groups related alerts without changing transport identity. This end-to-end account connects cloud services to failure handling and demonstrates why a unique database key is necessary but not sufficient.
Key takeaways

Map the platform's required contracts to cloud services, verify their semantics, and build one deployment your team can operate. Managed execution changes who maintains infrastructure; business authority, effect safety and evidence still need owners. Treat identity, regional capacity, egress and recovery as design inputs. Like a clinic joining a city, the platform succeeds when every connection supplies what the work requires and its failures have a known response.

Chapter 34. Specialized Agent Systems

A research agent, a coding agent and an incident commander can share a controlled loop while requiring very different evidence of success. A cited answer is not a tested patch. A passing test is not proof that a production service recovered. Specialization changes the environment, tools, timing and failure consequences. It should also change the acceptance checks, while preserving ownership, authority, budgets and recovery in the harness.

We will follow a service organization that assigns specialists to different jobs. Each specialist receives a task, the permitted workspace, a budget and an acceptance test. The supervisor does not judge every result by how confident the report sounds. It uses evidence suited to the work. This chapter develops that distinction so a team can reuse its platform without pretending every agent is the same product.

ANALOGY / A specialist field-service team A service company sends an investigator to understand a fault, a technician to repair equipment and an analyst to reconcile records. They share dispatch, identity and reporting rules, but carry different tools and demonstrate completion differently. The investigator supplies supported findings; the technician supplies measured operation after repair. Where it stops: software agents can be manipulated by text, images or tool results, and their tools can expose sensitive data at machine speed. Human job titles are not access controls.

Research agents and evidence synthesis

A research agent plans subquestions, searches approved sources, reads relevant material, extracts evidence and writes a supported synthesis. Its result must show what was checked and what remains unknown. Source quality includes authority, relevance, publication time and applicable version. A primary source can still be incomplete or outdated; a recent secondary source can help locate the right record. Do not replace source analysis with a fixed score that makes every official-looking page trustworthy.

Use an evidence ledger containing stable IDs, source locators, observed time, document version and the exact supporting passage or query result. Draft claims reference those entries. A citation verifier checks both existence and support: a real citation beside an unsupported sentence is still a defect. Conflicting sources should remain visible until a stated precedence rule settles them or the answer presents the unresolved disagreement.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class LedgerEntry(BaseModel):
    evidence_id: str
    source_ref: str
    version: str | None
    supporting_text: str = Field(max_length=500)

class SupportedClaim(BaseModel):
    sentence: str
    evidence_ids: list[str] = Field(min_length=1)

class ResearchAnswer(BaseModel):
    claims: list[SupportedClaim]
    gaps: list[str]

This schema supports sentence-level mapping but cannot establish entailment alone. The validator must load the named ledger entries, verify allowed provenance and check support. The writer should label interpretation separately from observed fact. For numerical questions, preserve units and denominator definitions. “Refund rate rose” needs a time interval, population and query, not merely a passage about a new returns policy.

Research is often read-only, but it is not harmless. Searches can reveal private questions, and fetched material can contain prompt injection. Give the researcher scoped source access, controlled outbound requests and no unnecessary mutation channel. Stop when subquestions are covered, new retrieval produces no useful evidence, or a budget is reached. An honest partial answer names the searched sources and gap; a failed search does not prove that no answer exists anywhere.

Coding and repository agents

A coding agent works in a repository through search, file reading, patch application and executable checks. Begin by reproducing the problem and identifying the relevant conventions. Then make a small change, run the acceptance checks and review the diff with the results. A second model can critique a patch, but tests, type checks and real state provide information that rereading the same explanation does not.

The execution environment must be disposable and isolated. Avoid production credentials, restrict network access to approved package mirrors, cap time and output, and give the process only required files. A read-only root prevents writes; it does not prevent reading everything visible in that filesystem. Isolation needs an explicit mount and access policy. Candidate code and repository test scripts remain untrusted executable content even when the goal is legitimate.

Repository instructions can help the agent orient itself. An approved AGENTS.md-style entry point describes build commands and constraints; architecture notes explain deliberate design decisions; a check script defines repeatable verification. Load these as trusted instructions only from a reviewed owner and ref. A user-supplied repository or a dependency README can contain hostile guidance. Provenance decides instruction authority; a familiar filename does not.

Across sessions, keep a progress record with the task, completed checks, attempts, current branch, uncertain effects and next step. On resume, reconcile that record with actual files and external systems. It may be stale because the prior worker crashed before writing it. A pull request created without a recorded response should be found by its logical identity, not recreated blindly. Progress prose supports orientation, while durable effect records support safe recovery.

Protect tests and CI configuration through a harness-owned guard when the task's policy forbids changing them. Compare the final diff to a trusted base, including renames, links and generated files. Hidden tests should run in an equally isolated environment: executing a patch outside the sandbox simply because it is being judged defeats the boundary. A dependency-upgrade task needs an explicit reviewed mode that permits the corresponding manifest and lockfile changes.

Data and SQL agents

A data agent needs agreed metric definitions before it needs clever SQL. Expose governed views or a semantic layer that defines revenue, returns, units, time zones and join relationships. A question about refund rate should specify eligible orders and counted refunds. Without those definitions, a syntactically correct query can produce an authoritative-looking number answering a different question.

Schema-discovery tools expose only authorized objects and useful descriptions. Compile semantic requests to SQL or validate the full parsed query tree. Reject writes, forbidden functions, unapproved relations and excessive work. Row limits control returned data, but do not necessarily limit scan cost. Use read-only database roles, row-level security, statement timeouts and query-cost controls as the actual enforcement layers. Parsing is defense in depth, not a replacement for database permissions.

Show the query, definitions, time range and evidence reference with the answer. Cross-check totals, units, nulls and unexpected population changes. Execution-based evaluations compare result sets with reference queries, not just generated SQL strings. Include questions whose requested dimension is missing, periods outside retention and ambiguous business terms. Refusal should describe the specific limitation. A missing seller-type column cannot establish that marketplace orders were excluded from the view.

Write access is a separate product mode. Preview affected rows, bind approval to the exact intended change, run transactional validation and support recovery. Do not expand a read-only analyst's permissions merely because the model proposes an UPDATE. In the service-team analogy, reconciling a stock report and authorizing a stock adjustment are different jobs. They may share data but have different authority and evidence requirements.
Browser and computer-use agents

A browser agent observes pages or screenshots and acts through clicks, typing and navigation. The UI is an unstable surface: controls move, state changes and on-screen text can be adversarial. Prefer a scoped API when it exists and meets the task. UI automation is useful when no suitable API is available, but its success must be checked by reading resulting state, not inferred from the input event.

Use isolated profiles or disposable desktops with only approved accounts and applications. Restrict domains, downloads and file access. Untrusted content on a page remains data even if it claims to be a system instruction. For a consequential submission, the harness applies the user's authorization and action policy; the agent presents the concrete values being submitted when confirmation is required. A screenshot can show the intended operation but does not authorize an unrelated action.

After submitting, inspect the resulting record, receipt or account state. A click on “save” can fail silently, create a duplicate or navigate away. Store the receipt and correlate it to the logical effect. If the result is unknown, stop repeated submissions and reconcile. Recording screenshots can aid audit, but redact personal information and apply retention. Do not let diagnostic convenience turn every UI step into indefinite storage of sensitive screen content.
Voice and real-time agents

A voice agent adds turn-taking and perceived delay to the same authority problem. A user speaking an order number expects acknowledgment quickly, but a payment still needs verified identity, clear values and an authorized decision. Stream recognition, model output and audio where supported. Use a fast path for known structured tasks, and explain when a slower lookup is underway. Fillers should reflect actual progress rather than conceal a stuck run.

An illustrative latency budget for first audible response is one second. One possible allocation is 250 milliseconds for end-of-speech detection, 150 for a final transcript, 350 for first model tokens, 150 for first audio and 100 for network transit. These are planning numbers, not universal measurements. Some stages overlap in streaming systems. Measure actual end-to-end percentiles with accents, background noise and realistic tool delays before choosing the product's target.

Handle interruptions explicitly. Cancel speech generation and read work where safe, but do not assume cancellation can undo a submitted refund or change. An in-flight mutation may finish after the caller interrupts. Reconcile it and tell the user its actual outcome before taking another action. Read back critical amounts, dates and recipients. Event-driven, scheduled and long-running agents

An event-driven agent begins from an alert or business event rather than a fresh conversational request. Assign an owning team and policy before enabling the trigger. Transport event identity prevents repeated delivery from creating new work; correlation groups related events into one incident. A scheduled run also needs a stable occurrence identity. “Every night” is insufficient if two schedulers can start the same job or a retry recreates its effects.

Use durable execution for waits, timers and continuation. An event storm needs admission control, priority and backpressure before model calls multiply. Define which work can be delayed or summarized and which alerts must still reach humans when the agent platform is unavailable. Every autonomous run needs a reportable status and a way to stop it. Absence of a human at the beginning is a reason to make the authority boundary clearer, not broader.

Keep notifications factual and scoped. An alert can create a draft incident update; publishing externally may require a different policy. Long-running work should carry remaining budgets and version information across sessions. A delayed approval is validated against the current world, including resource preconditions. Scheduled reminders should not silently renew an expired approval. Time extends the number of things that can change, so continuation must refresh volatile facts before effects.
IoT and operations agents

Operations agents consume telemetry and propose changes to physical or production systems. Summarization tools should return bounded windows, units, observation time and source references. A model can help explore causes, but physical limits and production safety envelopes are enforced outside its reasoning. A valve's permitted range, minimum replica count or maintenance restriction should remain checked even if the model's explanation is persuasive.

Use simulation or dry-run where meaningful, then bind real execution to resource scope and preconditions. High-impact actions may require distinct approvers or a privileged role. The executor uses short-lived authority for one operation, and records applied, rejected or unknown outcome. Verification checks independent signals after the action. A command accepted by a controller is not proof that the physical state changed safely or that users recovered.

For AegisOps, restart, scale, feature-flag change and rollback all belong in the production-change map. Assign risk by action and blast radius rather than by one generic tool label. A pre-approved runbook exception applies only to the precise action class and conditions permitted by policy. Unknown or destructive actions are blocked and escalated. Confidence helps prioritize investigation; it does not expand the allowed operating envelope.

Multimodal agents

Images, audio, scans and diagrams add evidence channels, not instruction authority. A screenshot may contain a fake instruction; a voice message may impersonate someone; a photo can be edited. Record source, capture time and quality alongside extracted fields. Keep confidence meaningful: a model's confident text is not a calibrated probability. Validation should check business rules and reconcile uncertain fields against approved records where possible.

Extract to structure early when that makes the task easier to verify. For an invoice scan, identify supplier, invoice number, currency and amount, then compare them with the procurement record. Retain the original under access and retention policy when audit requires it. Resizing, cropping and caching can reduce cost, but must not discard a field needed to decide eligibility. Track extraction versions so a changed model does not silently alter the same source record.

Build evaluations across image quality, document type, language, accents and manipulated inputs. Include failure cases that require clarification rather than a guessed value. Privacy review should account for incidental people, account details and background audio, not merely the field the user asked to extract. The specialist team may carry a camera and microphone, but its permissions still govern what it records, sends, retains and acts upon.

What changes and what stays universal

Research verifies claims against evidence. Coding verifies artifacts through isolated executable checks and review. Data verifies query meaning and result sets. Browser work verifies resulting application state. Voice verifies critical values and authority while meeting turn-taking requirements. Operations verifies independent post-action signals. Multimodal work verifies extraction and provenance. Each product should name its own false-completion condition, because a generic “the agent answered” metric cannot reveal these distinctions.

The agent harness supplies the universal controlled lifecycle: an owned goal, permitted capabilities, bounded context, state, budgets, authorization, recorded effects and observable completion. Reuse those mechanisms behind interfaces, then supply environment-specific adapters and acceptance checks. Specialization may require harness extensions, such as streaming media or a sandbox, but those extensions should have clear contracts. Do not copy an entire runtime for every new job when only its tools and verifier differ.

The cost model changes too. Research may spend on repeated retrieval; coding on sandbox time and long outputs; voice on streaming latency and session duration; operations on multiple evidence sources. Account for the whole task, including verification and failed attempts. A cheap answer that repeatedly fails its acceptance test is not necessarily cheaper work. Compare cost per successful outcome, and report safe escalations separately from unverified claims of completion.
Interview drills

To compare two specialized agents, explain their environment, action surface, evidence and dominant failure. Then identify the harness contract they share. A coding agent can run tests but must not control the protected judge; a browser agent can click but must verify the resulting record. This makes the answer specific without treating every specialization as a new architectural universe.

For a voice or operations design, separate responsiveness from authority. State the latency or recovery target, the external evidence that decides success and the policy that authorizes effects. Explain an interruption or unknown outcome. For a research design, show an unsupported question and the exact partial response it should produce. The strongest demonstration is often the boundary where the agent correctly stops instead of improvising.
Key takeaways

Specialists differ most in what they can observe, what they may change and how they prove completion. Reuse ownership and control, but choose verification suited to the environment. Read-only work still needs confidentiality and injection defenses; test execution remains untrusted execution; cancellation does not undo a committed effect. A field-service team is effective because shared dispatch and specialist evidence work together, not because every worker carries every tool.

Chapter 35. Architecture Selection Patterns & Senior Design Review

Knowing many patterns creates a new problem: a system can accumulate them faster than it earns their benefits. A router adds a decision, a specialist adds coordination, a memory adds retention, and a durable workflow adds operating responsibilities. The senior task is choosing the smallest arrangement that meets the actual requirements, then showing the evidence behind each addition. Complexity is justified by a need and a measured result, not by the vocabulary used in its diagram.

This chapter turns the earlier material into a selection and review method. We will use ShopAssist's billing-dispute flow as a worked design: answer policy questions, investigate duplicate captures, propose a refund and execute only under the required authority. Some steps are fixed; others depend on evidence. The design review examines both paths and asks what fails when the model, a dependency or a human decision is wrong.

ANALOGY / Choosing a treatment with a careful clinician A clinician does not prescribe every available treatment. They identify the problem, choose a treatment whose benefits fit it, consider side effects, and check whether the patient improves. Architecture selection similarly needs indications, limits and evidence. A sophisticated pattern can be the wrong prescription for a simple task. Where it stops: software design is not clinical diagnosis, and no architecture flowchart decides the answer automatically. Organizational authority, operating capacity and observed workload behavior must still be examined directly.

Pattern reference
Control patterns

A deterministic workflow is appropriate when required steps are known. It can still include model extraction or drafting inside nodes. For a refund, order lookup, eligibility validation, approval and accounting are usually mandatory. Their sequence should not depend on the model remembering it. A workflow becomes restrictive only when it tries to predetermine genuinely exploratory investigation, such as which evidence source will clarify an ambiguous dispute.

A router chooses among finite handlers. Use it for distinct intents with clear fallback behavior, such as order status versus returns policy. Measure misrouting on overlapping requests and allow clarification. A bounded ReAct loop lets the model choose the next tool from each observation; it fits open investigation, but needs cost, time and capability limits. Plan-and-execute makes a proposed sequence inspectable, with replanning when new evidence invalidates assumptions.

Reflection or evaluator-optimizer work is useful when the critic supplies a clear rubric, external evidence or a check the original generator did not perform. Repeatedly rereading the same draft with the same knowledge may add cost without reliability. Graph orchestration makes mandatory states, parallel work and pauses explicit. Use its control where it helps, without turning a trivial extraction into a distributed graph merely because a framework provides one.
Collaboration patterns

A supervisor coordinates scoped workers while retaining the task's goal, state and budget. This fits AegisOps when telemetry, knowledge and change investigation genuinely benefit from separate capabilities. A handoff transfers control between domains; it needs an explicit ownership transition. If accountability must remain with the original owner, expose the specialist as a bounded subtask instead. Returning findings and owning the incident are different responsibilities.

Remote agents belong at real organizational or runtime boundaries. A2A can carry tasks, status and artifacts, while the caller still constrains delegated authority. Parallel workers help independent questions meet latency targets; they hurt when quotas are tight or the tasks require each other's results. Hierarchy can reflect large ownership structures, but each level adds delay and ambiguity. Ensembles can reveal useful disagreement, provided they do not merely repeat correlated mistakes at greater expense.
Knowledge and memory patterns

Begin with baseline retrieval for a direct question over a governed corpus. Add agentic retrieval when the task requires choosing sources, resolving subquestions or checking sufficiency. Graph retrieval helps questions whose meaning depends on relationships, provided reliable entity and edge data exist. A diagram showing a knowledge graph does not compensate for missing or inconsistent entity definitions. Evaluate retrieval separately from the final answer so failures can be diagnosed.

Governed SQL tools suit quantitative questions with agreed definitions and entitlement rules. Their output should preserve the query, units, population and time interval. Memory supports continuity and personalization when the retained information has a lawful, useful purpose and a deletion path. It should not duplicate volatile system-of-record facts as authoritative truth. ShopAssist can remember a preferred language while still refetching a payment's current refund balance before acting.
Safety and recovery patterns

Risk-based approval applies to consequential actions under the organization's policy. A pre-approved runbook is a precise exception with bounded conditions, not a general license to skip review. A reader/actor separation reduces the combination of untrusted content and sensitive tools, while both sides still need validation and scope. Sandboxing contains generated code or UI actions; it requires an explicit filesystem, network, resource and secret policy.

Retries, replanning, compensation and escalation address different failures. A definite transient read failure may be retried. An unknown mutation outcome must be reconciled. A changed environment can require a new plan and approval. Compensation semantically reverses an applied effect when authorized and possible; it is not an automatic undo button. Evaluated model fallback or a degraded read-only mode can preserve useful service without substituting a different unapproved action.

Decision matrix: choosing the architecture

Ask first whether the next steps are known. If they are, begin with a workflow and use models only inside the steps that benefit from them. If the path depends on observations, use a bounded agent for the exploratory part. Then ask whether one domain, capability set and permission scope can handle the task. Do not split an agent merely because its prompt contains several headings.

Distinct intents may justify a router and handlers. Independent investigations may justify parallel workers. Different permissions, ownership or model requirements may justify specialists. Long waits or mandatory state transitions may justify a durable workflow around the exploratory loop. These questions are not a mechanical scoring system. A regulated approval boundary may outweigh a small latency gain; a team unable to operate extra infrastructure may favor a supported managed path.

Overlay authority, knowledge and recovery on the chosen control. Untrusted documents plus sensitive tools require scope and injection defenses. Executable code requires isolation. Quantitative answers require definitions and database enforcement. Cross-session continuity requires owned state and governed memory. A request lasting longer than the connection requires asynchronous status and durable progress. Each overlay should address a named failure rather than serve as decorative completeness.

For ShopAssist, start with a single bounded investigator reading order, payment and policy evidence. It returns a structured eligibility proposal. A deterministic service validates accounting and approval requirements, then dispatches the effect. No second agent is needed merely to call issue_refund. If the organization later separates policy research from private order access, that real permission boundary may justify an additional reader. The decision changes because the boundary changed, not because multi-agent designs became fashionable.
The architecture review
Walk one risky request

Begin with the user and intended outcome. A customer says two captures occurred for order ORD-104233. Authentication establishes the principal, while the order service checks ownership. The investigator reads current captures and applicable policy, producing evidence IDs. The validator determines whether the extra capture is eligible and fixes payment, amount, currency and logical effect identity. Only then is an approval request meaningful.

The support lead sees the exact proposal, evidence, expected impact, expiry and recovery options. The approval service checks the lead's role and records authority bound to that proposal. The executor revalidates current refund accounting and consumes or reserves approval atomically with local intent. It sends the persisted key to the payment provider. A timeout after provider processing becomes outcome unknown; continuation reconciles before another effect. This walk exposes more architecture than a diagram listing nine generic services.
Review through fixed lenses

The autonomy lens asks why an agent is needed and what each action class may do. The control lens asks who chooses the next step, what limits apply and what ends the run. The tool lens asks which capabilities mutate, which credential reaches them and how duplication is prevented. The state lens asks what survives a crash and how old records remain interpretable after a release. Each answer should point to evidence.

Context, knowledge and memory lenses examine what the model sees, how evidence is scoped, what is retained and what can be forgotten. Security and identity lenses examine injection, exfiltration, delegation and tenant separation. Governance examines data flows, audit and behavioral change control. Reliability asks about timeouts, dependency failures, uncertain effects, compensation and dead-letter recovery. Do not merge these into one vague “safety” checkbox; their failures require different controls.

Quality asks for labeled cases, critical slices, calibrated judges and outcome checks. Operations asks for SLOs, dashboards, ownership, runbooks and emergency controls. Cost and scale ask for admission limits, quotas, capacity and cost per successful task. Simplicity asks which component can be removed. A review should leave a small list of evidence gaps and decisions, each with an owner and due condition, rather than an unprioritized catalogue of possible improvements.

Ask what can be removed

Try removing a reflection loop that has no measured benefit, a second agent sharing the same tools and permissions, or a memory duplicating current application records. Replace a known-intent model router with rules where the data supports that choice. A smaller design is not automatically better: removing durable approval storage to simplify the diagram would violate the lifecycle requirement. Simplification preserves the necessary contract while reducing unnecessary machinery.

Use controlled comparisons to test disputed complexity. Hold model version, tasks, prompts, grading and environment constant while changing the mechanism. Use slice analysis to report success, safe escalation, false completion, cost, latency and operational burden by case type. The clinician analogy helps here: keep the needed treatment, remove the ineffective addition, and measure the outcome. Architectural taste alone is insufficient when the decision affects users and operators.

Production-readiness gates and launch checklist

Launch gates require an owner, pass condition and inspectable evidence. The design gate confirms requirements and autonomy boundaries. The security gate verifies scoped authority and adversarial behavior. The quality gate evaluates critical slices and uncertainty. The reliability gate demonstrates crash continuation, dependency failure and effect reconciliation. The operations gate verifies alerting, on-call access and recovery. Governance confirms data and change-control obligations. The rollout gate controls exposure and rollback through a canary release.

Zero successful forbidden actions is a required test result, not proof that no attack can ever succeed. State the corpus, threat assumptions and residual risks. Confidence intervals should use independent cases as their observational unit; repeated runs measure variability but do not turn one case into many independent tasks. A small suite can block known regressions while still requiring shadow observation and careful rollout. Avoid dressing finite evidence as universal safety certification.

For the ShopAssist launch, preserve read-only answers if refund execution is disabled. Test the kill switch at the executor, not only in the prompt. Rehearse provider failure, an approval that expires, a late response and a run that exhausts its budget. Operators must be able to locate the customer's status and hand off without inventing an outcome. A useful degraded mode tells the customer what is known and who owns the remaining work.

Increasing autonomy is another release decision. A high approval rate alone is not enough: reviewers may be rubber-stamping poor proposals. Examine error and reversal rates, acceptance accuracy, critical scenario coverage, blast radius and recoverability. Define the exact action segment eligible for changed policy, then stage the change with monitoring and a return to the prior mode. The model's confidence is evidence to analyze, not authority to remove the approval gate.
Senior system-design interview drills

A clear design answer follows the request through its boundaries. First clarify the users, goal, scale, latency, data and risky actions. State which parts are fixed and where adaptive choice helps. Draw the smallest coherent control plane. Walk one read path and one effect path, including approval and a crash. Then discuss evaluation, operations, cost and the simplifications considered. This order connects requirements to implementation instead of producing a diagram before understanding the problem.

For a telecom billing-dispute agent, begin with bill ownership and the allowed adjustments. Separate explanation from account mutation. Retrieve the governing tariff version and current account facts, then show how a disputed charge becomes a bound proposal. Describe what happens when evidence conflicts, when the billing service processes an adjustment but its response is lost, and when no eligible remedy exists. An explicit refusal or safe handoff is a valid outcome when the system cannot establish authority.

When asked to design an enterprise platform, state which shared services earn centralization: an LLM gateway for model accounting, policy, tool identity, approvals, run ownership and observability. Distinguish services that must be separate from modules that can share a process. Explain tenancy and fair admission under a workload spike. Choose one durable execution strategy and define its business-effect contract. A platform should support different agents without making every agent pay for the largest deployment architecture.

When asked what you would cut for an MVP, name a component and the contract preserved by the cut. Merge investigators with identical scopes, defer optional remote agents, or start with one evidence corpus. Keep eligibility, approval binding, effect reconciliation and basic operating controls. The question tests judgment: removing necessary safeguards is not simplicity, and adding every possible specialization is not future-proofing.
Key takeaways

Choose control for the work, then add knowledge, collaboration and recovery where explicit requirements need them. Review designs by walking real requests and demanding evidence for each promise. Treat launch and autonomy expansion as owned decisions with finite test evidence, operational rehearsal and staged exposure. Ask what can be removed without breaking the contract. The strongest design is the one whose complexity can be explained through the outcomes it actually improves.

Chapter 36. The AegisOps Blueprint

AegisOps is an incident commander for software services. It gathers observations, develops competing explanations, proposes remediation and coordinates approved action. Its goal is verified recovery or an honest safe escalation, with evidence that a human can inspect. This is an ambitious capstone because it joins the book's mechanisms in one coherent task. The blueprint describes a production-oriented design; completing a simulated portfolio does not certify a live production deployment.

We will follow a bad release that increases latency and errors in order-api. AegisOps must establish which version changed, whether the symptoms are actually connected to it, and whether rollback is permitted. The incident provides a concrete thread through identity, evidence, durable execution, approval, cost and verification. Alternative causes and unavailable dependencies are part of the design, not extensions added after the happy path works.

ANALOGY / The emergency-room team A patient arrives with symptoms, not a proven diagnosis. A coordinating physician asks specialists for evidence, considers alternatives, obtains appropriate consent, treats and observes recovery. AegisOps follows that coordination pattern for software incidents: triage, evidence, hypothesis, approved action and observation. Where it stops: an AI incident commander is not a clinician, and medical consent rules do not define software authority. Our permissions, action classes and verification criteria are explicit engineering policy enforced outside model judgment.

The business scenario

The enterprise operates services on Kubernetes with deployments managed through reviewed change systems. Alerts, logs, traces and change records arrive from different owners. A new order-api release is followed by elevated p95 latency and 5xx responses. Human responders must connect time windows, versions and dependency behavior before deciding what to do. AegisOps shortens that evidence-gathering work while keeping high-impact production changes under deterministic authority.

The supported journey begins with an owned alert, proceeds through scoped investigation, and ends in verified resolution or escalation. Communication and learning follow recorded facts. Every transition has a reason, and every effect has a recoverable record. If AegisOps is unavailable, the organization's ordinary alerting still reaches people. The agent is an assistant to incident response, not a single point of failure replacing the team's ability to respond.
Who AegisOps serves: personas and user stories

Asha, the on-call SRE, wants a useful evidence summary quickly and fears an unexplained restart. Marco, the incident manager, wants one timeline and fears contradictory updates. Priya, the service owner, wants the precise target and rollback plan and fears acting on the wrong revision. Lena, the security lead, wants scoped authority and fears an instruction in a log becoming a command. These needs turn the architecture into testable work.

The acceptance contract requires a triage summary containing severity, blast radius and cited signals; an approval card containing exact arguments, evidence, impact, rollback, verification and expiry; a precondition mismatch that blocks mutation; factual communication derived from state; denial of injected authority; short-lived resource-bound execution credentials; a reviewable postmortem; and recorded per-incident usage. Each story should appear in a phase test or game day. Features with no story need a specific justification.
Why this needs an agent

Investigation is adaptive: a trace finding can change which metric, runbook or deployment detail should be checked next. An agent helps generate and test hypotheses under bounded tools. It can prioritize independent investigations and explain uncertain evidence. The model should not determine accounting-like safety rules, authorizer roles, approval expiry or the permitted Kubernetes namespace. Those are stable rules better expressed as tested code.

An incident does not require nine agents by definition. The blueprint separates roles to teach the boundaries and support differing scopes; a smaller implementation can combine roles when the same permissions and context suffice. Keep a specialist only where it earns isolation, context, expertise or parallelism benefits. The capstone's teaching coverage must not become a requirement that every real deployment reproduce its number of agents.
What the final demo must prove

Trigger a synthetic bad-deployment incident and show durable identity, triage and selected investigation. Gather metrics, logs, traces, changes and relevant runbooks through typed tools. Produce multiple plausible causes and tests that weaken alternatives. Present a bound rollback proposal, require the specified approval, execute with current preconditions and a stable effect key, then observe a complete recovery window. Show how the same system responds when one of those steps cannot establish its contract.

The final package also demonstrates a process restart, duplicate alert, injected log, stale approval and a successful command followed by unhealthy service metrics. It includes a timeline, evidence-to-action links and cost accounting. A single successful rollback is insufficient: the system must repeatedly preserve authority and tell the truth when it cannot resolve the incident. That is the behavior evaluated in Chapter 38.
Non-functional requirements and SLOs

Use explicit illustrative targets to guide the capstone: triage p50 within three minutes and p95 within six; ranked hypotheses p50 within eight; no mutation without required authority; all report claims supported; complete approval cards; and no verified resolution without the specified observation evidence. Track model cost per SEV2 incident separately from infrastructure, with an illustrative median ceiling of two dollars and p95 of six. Replace these targets with local product requirements before live operation.

Ingestion and workflow availability have their own target, such as 99.9%, with humans still receiving alerts under degraded mode. Audit completeness and secret-free prompts are independent properties. An available agent can still propose poor actions, so uptime is not the headline outcome. Define sampling and denominators for each metric. Missing verification data is a failure to establish recovery, not a convenient absence of failing samples.
System context and containers

The context view places AegisOps among responders, alerting, observability, knowledge, change management, Kubernetes, ITSM, chat, identity, models and partner agents. Distinguish read relationships from external writes and production changes. Restart, scale, feature-flag change and rollback all affect production and belong in the action boundary. ITSM and chat writes also need scoped authority and data-loss checks, even when they cannot restart a workload.

The deployable execution parts are an entry API, durable workflow coordinator, workers, approval service and scoped tool gateways or executors. Shared dependencies include identity, model gateway, policy, PostgreSQL, caches, object storage and telemetry. Some can be modules before becoming separate services. The C4 model distinguishes context and container views; a container view should describe actual deployment units rather than count every conceptual box as a container. Label protocols and owners at the boundaries that matter.

Architecture

The entry API deduplicates transport events and correlates related alerts, then starts owned durable work. The incident workflow retains lifecycle state, waits and deadlines. The commander selects bounded investigations, while the harness enforces budgets, context and capability policy. The model gateway handles provider accounting. The evidence ledger stores source records independently of fluent explanations. The executor crosses the real change boundary; the verifier determines whether the goal was achieved.

This structure has two owners for different questions: the commander owns the incident plan, while deterministic services own authority and lifecycle invariants. A specialist cannot override the risk matrix through prose. A workflow replay does not repeat a recorded completed activity blindly, but a lost activity response can lead to retry. External effects therefore need downstream idempotency or safe reconciliation. The Temporal activity contract explains that distinction.
The agent team

Triage identifies affected service, severity and initial questions. Observability returns bounded metrics, logs and trace evidence. Knowledge retrieves versioned runbooks, ownership and past incidents. Change Intelligence examines releases, flags and infrastructure changes near the symptom onset. Security and Risk inspects signs of abuse and can narrow autonomy. Their outputs are structured findings with evidence, not independent instructions to other agents.

Remediation turns a supported hypothesis into a proposal with preconditions and verification; only the gated executor applies it. Communications produces state-derived updates with hypotheses labeled. Postmortem and Evaluator organize the timeline, lessons and quality evidence. The commander coordinates these roles and retains global budget ownership. Some roles need no model at all for a known task, and roles can share an implementation when that preserves their scope and accountability.
Tool registry - minimum production tool set

Read tools include metric queries, bounded log search, trace retrieval, workload status, recent deployments, flag state, runbook search, past incidents and ownership lookup. Each accepts validated identifiers and limited windows, returns evidence and exposes typed failure. Scope comes from verified context; the model cannot choose another tenant through a free-form query. An authenticated source may supply reliable numeric observations while its text still has no instruction authority.

External-write tools create or update incident records and send templated updates. Production-change tools restart, scale, roll back and change feature flags. Each contract names risk, allowed resources, maximum blast radius, required preconditions, effect identity, uncertainty response and compensation. The verify_slo capability reads measurements and returns a deterministic criteria result. Its evidence references let later reviewers distinguish the change response from actual recovery.
Composite skills

Package diagnose_http_latency as a bounded sequence of metrics, traces, dependency checks and change correlation. Package diagnose_error_spike around error slices, log signatures and known incidents. assess_bad_deployment compares versions and before/after evidence. These reusable procedures reduce repeated orchestration while retaining the exact evidence contract. A skill is useful because its steps and limits are tested, not because its name sounds like expertise.

safe_restart checks eligibility and replica safety, then uses the gated execution path and verification. safe_rollback includes revision preconditions, approval, rollout observation, recovery checks and a reviewed compensation route. verify_recovery, incident_comms and generate_postmortem each have distinct outputs. A procedural skill update changes behavior and therefore follows code review and evaluation. Do not let a postmortem model write a new production procedure into memory automatically.
MCP and A2A boundaries

Group MCP servers by ownership and effect class: observability, knowledge, external records and production changes. Pin server identity and tool schemas; a read server that introduces a mutating capability fails discovery and execution policy. Discovery does not authorize use. MCP connects capabilities, while authorization remains layered in the caller, gateway and downstream service. Its current protocol details should follow the official specification.

Use A2A for a capability owned by another team, such as database reliability or security operations. The handoff includes task and correlation IDs, caller identity, allowed scope, deadline, evidence references and expected artifact shape. Validate the returned artifact and retain its provenance. A remote agent's confidence does not grant local mutation rights. Reattach to a known remote task after restart instead of creating duplicate delegated work.
Canonical incident state

Store tenant, service, environment, trigger, detection time, severity and lifecycle status. Citation support comes from an evidence ledger whose entries retain immutable IDs, source/query locators, observation time and extracted facts. Hypotheses contain supporting and contradicting evidence, a possible falsification test and calibrated status labels. Proposed actions contain exact arguments, risk, preconditions, evidence, scope and recovery plan. Distinguish observed facts, inferences and authority rather than compressing all three into a trusted Boolean.

Memory design

Working memory is the current incident's durable state. Episodic memory stores reviewed previous incidents and successful or failed remediation sequences. Semantic knowledge includes curated runbooks, architecture and service records. Procedural memory is versioned skill code and configuration. Preferences can record low-risk team choices, such as update format. Each type needs provenance, retention and permitted use; none overrides current authority or system-of-record facts.

The write gate validates, classifies, redacts, deduplicates and obtains required review before persistence. A lesson such as “rollback solved this symptom” must retain the incident conditions and counterevidence, not become a universal command. Deletion covers serving records and derived indexes, with separately stated backup expiry and restore suppression. Recording lessons is useful only when the future investigator can see their scope and age.

Approval and risk matrix

Risk 0 covers scoped evidence reads; risk 1 covers permitted templated external updates; risk 2 covers low-impact reversible non-production actions within bounds. Risk 3 covers production restart, bounded scaling and flag changes, requiring ordinary approval unless an explicit runbook permits the precise case. Risk 4 covers rollback and other broad or sensitive production changes, requiring privileged approval from two distinct authorized people. Risk 5 covers unknown, destructive or irreversible unsupported actions and is blocked for escalation.

The runbook exception applies to risk 3 only in this blueprint. It never admits risk 4 or 5 merely because a procedure exists. The service validates approvers, proposal identity, hash, expiry and consumption. Precondition re-validation checks current resource revision and business conditions at the mutation boundary. All capabilities need scoped credentials; production changes additionally need authority tied to the approved action. Short lifetime and audience binding reduce exposure without replacing resource checks.
Threat model

Threat modelling includes prompt injection: logs, tickets, runbooks and remote artifacts can contain hostile instructions. Label them as data and constrain effect policy independently. Pin capability schemas and test schema drift against tool changes; deny unfamiliar tools rather than allowing a namespace prefix. Limit outgoing scopes, tenant data and blast radius. Bind approvals and prevent immediate replay before expiry. Enforce cumulative budgets against loops and costs. Use data-loss checks for communication and delegation, and a reviewed write gate for memory.

Map each threat to a negative test and residual risk. An injection suite proves behavior on its cases, not complete immunity. The model may still propose poor actions within its allowed space; evidence sufficiency, human review and independent verification address that remaining risk. Cross-tenant access should fail before data reaches context. Unknown outcomes should stop new effects until reconciliation. Threat modeling is most useful when it names the exact point that denies the adversarial request.
The core state machine

Detailed lifecycle states include detected, triaged, investigating, hypothesis ready, plan ready, waiting approval, executing, verifying, resolved, escalated and failed safe. The state machine enforces required steps while models work inside investigation and planning. Rejection and expiry do not become execution. An unknown effect outcome enters reconciliation. Failed verification leads to bounded replanning or escalation with the failed action recorded as evidence.

Technology stack

One implementation uses Python, FastAPI and Pydantic, with LangGraph behind owned interfaces and Temporal coordinating durable waits. Kafka carries alerts; PostgreSQL stores domain records and audit; Redis provides non-authoritative caches; object storage holds raw payloads; pgvector or a dedicated search system retrieves knowledge. OIDC, workload identity and policy-as-code govern access. OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana support operations. These are choices to justify, not mandatory brands.

Kubernetes and a reviewed deployment system host the services, with short-lived tool authority supplied outside model context. Git, Argo CD, flags, ITSM, paging and chat are adapters with their own owners. Use smaller model tiers for classification and bounded extraction, stronger tiers for hypothesis work when evaluations justify them, and an independently calibrated evaluator when needed. All model access goes through the LLM gateway for accounting and policy.

Estimate cost per incident from input and output tokens at each task tier. For illustration, small input/output cost is $0.25/$1.25 per million tokens, mid $3/$15 and strong $5/$25. A worked SEV2 run allocates triage 6k/0.6k tokens, investigation 140k/6k, hypotheses 60k/4k, planning 30k/2k, verification and communication 20k/2k, postmortem 40k/4k and sampled evaluation 30k/1k.

A companion scaffold is a learning start, not evidence that every integration is production-ready. Publish the exact release/tag and test assumptions. Failure modes

Property-based testing can vary approval identities, proposal revisions, expiry and crash timing while checking the same invariants: blocked actions never execute, altered proposals never inherit approval, and repeated transport attempts preserve one logical effect. Retain the generated counterexample as a deterministic regression set case. This complements model evaluations because it challenges the authority and recovery machinery without relying on fluent output.

A confident wrong diagnosis needs stronger competing evidence and verification, not broader authority. Specialist sprawl needs selection and budget measurements. Stale approval needs current preconditions enforced at mutation. An alert storm needs transport dedupe, correlation and admission control. Speculative communication needs state-derived claims. Silent model degradation needs versioned evaluation and rollout comparison. These controls make different failures distinguishable and repairable.
Interview drills

Explain why confidence above 0.9 cannot authorize rollback: rollback is risk 4 and requires the stated privileged approval. Explain how a log instruction can influence a hypothesis without crossing the action gate. Trace one proposal from evidence to bound approval, scoped token, effect result and independent recovery check. For MCP versus A2A, identify whether the remote owner provides a tool contract or owns an autonomous task.
Key takeaways

AegisOps earns adaptive reasoning in investigation and planning while keeping authority, lifecycle and completion criteria deterministic. One commander coordinates narrow roles; owned evidence and immutable proposals connect every decision to its basis. Risk policy bounds action, effect contracts support recovery, and a full observation window establishes resolution. The emergency-room analogy explains coordination, but the actual system becomes trustworthy through these inspectable engineering mechanisms.

Chapter 37. Building AegisOps Phase by Phase

The blueprint is intentionally broad. Building it all at once would leave too many uncertain boundaries: model behavior, tools, persistence, identity and effects could fail together. Instead, each phase adds one capability and proves the contracts on which the next phase depends. The early milestones investigate with evidence. Real mutation arrives only after durable execution, scope and approval are established. Chapter 38 adds sustained verification, operating evidence and rehearsal.

Treat the phase order as dependency order, not a guaranteed calendar. A simulated portfolio with fake services is much smaller than enterprise integration with reviewed credentials and production change processes. Record the team, scope and assumptions behind an estimate. An experienced engineer can make steady progress by keeping the first scenario narrow: a bad order-api release followed by latency and 5xx errors. Each phase must leave that scenario runnable and testable.

ANALOGY / Building a workshop before handing over its keys A workshop first needs an agreed purpose, sound structure, visible instruments, tested procedures and controlled access. Only after those are checked should a powerful machine be enabled. AegisOps is built in the same order: define the task, establish observation, prove reasoning, then grant narrow authority. Where it stops: read tools are not risk-free windows. They can expose sensitive data and carry hostile text, so confidentiality and input boundaries begin before any production mutation.
