APPENDIX E
Case Studies - Four Production Failures

These four cases are fictional composites for learning. Organizations, figures and timelines are invented; the failure mechanisms reflect the engineering contracts discussed in the book. They are not reports of the author's customers or verified incidents. Read each case by asking what the runtime knew, what authority it held, what evidence was missing and which change would have prevented the consequence. The model is one participant in the system, not its only possible cause of failure.

ANALOGY / Reading an accident investigation A published investigation reconstructs the sequence and asks how the system permitted it, rather than stopping at blame. Pilots and engineers study such reports to rehearse situations they hope never to face. These fictional cases serve that purpose for agents. Where it stops: they are teaching composites, not official accident findings or measured evidence about the frequency of real deployments' failures.
Case 1 - The refund that ran twice
Context and event

A retailer allows a support agent to refund up to INR 5000 under a reviewed policy. The provider normally responds within seconds. The harness uses an eight-second timeout and retries failed tool calls twice. During a slowdown, the provider applies a refund but its response arrives after the harness has given up. The runtime calls the same business action again without a stable provider idempotency key, and the provider applies another refund.

Over forty minutes, 214 customers receive unintended second refunds averaging INR 1850, totaling INR 395900. The assistant's confirmation text is fluent and usually accurate about at least one refund. Its tool-success metric looks healthy after retries. Finance's reconciliation finds duplicate effects rather than relying on the agent's summary. This case illustrates that model-quality and tool-response dashboards can stay green while financial correctness fails at the transport boundary.
Timeline and root causes

At 14:02, provider latency rises. At 14:05, the first duplicate effect occurs without an alert. At 14:31, finance identifies unexpected duplicate records. At 14:42, the owner disables new refund execution while support continues to explain status and hand off. By 15:30, the team begins reconciliation against provider records. Recovery requires establishing which effects actually occurred; issuing compensations before that evidence would create more uncertainty.

Figure E.1. The response was lost, not the refund. The missing control is repeat-safe effect identity, not better confirmation wording. A timeout communicates uncertainty about the result. Diagram labels in reading order: First request; Provider processes intended refund; Caller timeout; Runtime does not know the applied outcome; New unbound request; No stable effect key reaches provider; Second refund; Provider treats the retry as new work; Reconciliation; Finance finds duplicate effect records

The tool lacked provider idempotency despite support for it. The harness classified a timeout as definite failure and applied a generic retry policy to a financial write. It recorded no recoverable intent and made no outcome query. Monitoring counted eventual responses rather than expected logical effects. A preceding “not refunded” read would still race without atomic payment accounting. These failures belong in service and runtime contracts, not in a prompt telling the agent to be careful.
Repair and lesson

Persist the logical effect identity before dispatch, reuse it under the provider's documented retention rules, and reconcile after unknown outcome. Enforce cumulative refundable balance atomically in the payment service. Differentiate repeated delivery from a distinct legitimate partial refund. Reconciliation should alert on duplicate effect identities or exceeded accounting bounds, not simply more than one refund per order, which can be permitted. Test the provider applying an effect then losing its response across an actual worker restart.

The owner restores execution only after the effect and retry contracts pass. Audit links authority, intent, provider reference and reconciliation. For a provider without safe deduplication or status resolution, unresolved uncertainty goes to human handling rather than another financial write. The central lesson is narrow: repeat-safe retries require a service contract that establishes the prior result; a local unique row or confident response cannot substitute for it. Chapters 6, 7, 18 and 23.
Case 2 - The helpful email
Context and event

An inbox agent reads supplier invoices and can reply or forward messages with the shared mailbox's broad permissions. An attacker sends an email styled as an audit notice, including a hidden instruction to forward recent invoices and bank details to an external lookalike recipient and omit the action from the summary. The content enters the model alongside private records and a capable outbound tool. The runtime performs no recipient or data-loss check before execution.

The agent forwards twenty invoices and its daily summary does not mention them. The summary is produced from the same manipulated context, so it cannot serve as an independent audit. The system combined untrusted content, confidential data and outbound authority without a governing effect boundary. The visible user task was invoice extraction, but its credential scope exposed the mailbox's broader capabilities. A better wording instruction alone would not establish a durable recipient policy.
Root causes

The reader and actor shared a context and permissions. The forward tool accepted arbitrary recipients and attachments, with no approved external-send flow. The service credential represented the mailbox's broad standing rights rather than the task's narrow actor. No trusted runtime event recorded source message, destination and attachment decision. The threat model checked direct malicious requests but omitted instructions hidden in ordinary retrieved business content.

Figure E.2. Invoice data must not become send authority. Structured extraction reduces exposure but is not itself a complete permission boundary. The recipient and attachments are checked where sending occurs. Diagram labels in reading order: Supplier email; Untrusted content may include hidden instructions; Extracted invoice; Validated business fields with source identity; Recipient and data policy; Outbound decision; Allowlisted recipient, data check and required approval; Scoped draft or send; Executor uses only permitted mailbox operation
Repair and lesson

Restrict the reader to permitted extraction with no outbound tools. The actor receives validated fields and source references, while any retained text remains data. Limit the agent to scoped reading and drafting unless an explicit send policy grants more. External recipients are allowlisted, sensitive attachments are checked and required approval is bound to the exact outgoing message. Record audit independently of the model's summary, redacting content under retention policy.

Expand the attack cases with hidden text, multilingual instructions, lookalike destinations and attempts to suppress disclosure. Measure denied attempts and successful effects separately. A reader/actor split can reduce the attack surface, but a free-text schema still carries manipulation risk; deterministic scope and outbound policy remain essential. The lesson is that extraction does not authorize dissemination. Permission follows the actual recipient, data and effect, even when the instruction arrives in a familiar invoice format. Chapters 19-22.
Case 3 - The quiet cost explosion
Context and event

A business analytics agent handles thirty thousand conversations daily at approximately four cents per run, or $1200 per day. A Friday release changes SQL observations from a short bounded result to full result sets. Most final answers still look correct. For a common quarter-comparison task, large tool results enter history and are repeatedly resent, while ambiguous errors cause near-identical queries. No cost budget or loop guard establishes a stopping decision.

In forty-eight hours, sixty thousand runs average thirty-seven cents each: $22200 instead of about $2400. The illustrative difference is $19800. Customers do not complain because answer wording remains useful. Latency and error dashboards do not reveal the entire financial consequence. The release evaluation checked answer quality but did not compare tokens, cost or repeated observations by task slice, allowing a roughly ninefold cost regression to pass.
Root causes

Unbounded observations inflated every later model call. History retained raw results rather than references and useful summaries. Near-identical requests supplied no new evidence, but step limits alone still permitted expensive loops. The gateway recorded invoices without per-run budget enforcement or an hourly cost-per-success signal. A tool contract change had been treated as plumbing instead of a behavioral and economic release. No owner reviewed its context consequences on the heavy slice.

Figure E.3. A larger observation compounds later spend. The final two controls describe the repaired design; no chart invents measured improvement. Tool output size can alter cost without changing visible answer quality. Diagram labels in reading order: Full SQL result; Large response enters context without a bound; Retained history; Every later call carries prior raw results; Repeated query; Error causes variants without useful new evidence; Budget decision; Cap cost and stop nonproductive work; Measured release; Compare cost and quality by task slice
Repair and lesson

Cap context observations under an explicit policy, retaining source records outside context and returning summaries plus evidence locators. Measure whether compaction preserves needed facts. Add repeated-call fingerprints and a no-new-evidence rule, with cumulative step, token and cost budgets. A budget stop produces a truthful incomplete or escalation outcome. The service should not quietly return a cheaper guessed answer merely to satisfy its cost target.

Compare candidate and baseline cost per useful outcome, p95 tokens, latency and quality on the heavy query slice. Set locally justified alerts and regression ceilings rather than treating an example percentage as universal. Reconcile the usage ledger with actual provider billing rules. The lesson is that cost is part of outcome quality and operating reliability: it must be measured at the work unit and considered when tool, prompt or context behavior changes. Chapters 8, 23, 26 and 28.
Case 4 - The eval that lied
Context and event

A legal-operations team gates answers using an LLM judge of support by governing contract clauses. It calibrates the initial grader against human labels once, obtaining an illustrative kappa of 0.78. Months later, a release changes retrieval and replaces the judge with a cheaper model. Reported faithful answers rise from 91% to 96%. The team interprets the higher score as improvement without checking whether the measuring instrument changed.

Three weeks later, a reviewer finds answers citing clauses from the wrong contract version. Human relabeling of 150 answers gives 84% faithfulness under the intended definition. The new judge accepted near-matching text and ignored the governing-version requirement. These fictional numbers illustrate confounded measurement, not a measured reliability property of any named model. The team changed both behavior and grading, so the old and new scores were not a fair comparison.
Root causes

The judge and rubric were not treated as versioned measurement components. The changed grader lacked fresh calibration, and routine human samples had stopped. The rubric asked whether a clause existed rather than whether the source version governed the case. The release process allowed an attractive headline score to replace independent evidence. A valid-looking citation ID could pass even when the retrieval record established a different contract's authority.

Figure E.4. Hold the ruler steady when behavior changes. The repaired measurement isolates behavior changes from grader changes. A higher score is useful only when its meaning is comparable. Diagram labels in reading order: Confounded release; Retrieval changes; Uncalibrated judge changes; Headline score rises; Governing version defect hidden; Comparable measurement; Frozen labeled cases; Pinned calibrated judge; Deterministic version checks; Human samples track drift
Repair and lesson

Check governing clause and version deterministically before the judge sees the answer. Pin rubric, grader model and dataset; calibrate a grader change on fresh human labels, including version-conflict examples. Define a comparable measurement transition if the organization needs both old and new graders. Changing the judge is allowed, but it must have independent evidence and cannot silently redefine the release criterion while grading a changed agent.

Retain weekly human review with agreed disagreement analysis and drift alerts. Report the observational unit, rubric and confidence limits, not only a convenient aggregate score. Improve the criteria when reviewers find new gaps and retain the old measurement context for historical interpretation. The lesson is that evaluations are instruments with operating responsibilities. Prefer code for properties it can establish, and calibrate probabilistic judgments rather than treating a model's score as ground truth. Chapters 24 and 25.
What the four cases have in common

The refund failed at repeat-safe effect handling. The email failed at data and outbound authority. The cost case failed at observation bounds, budget and release measurement. The judge case failed at measurement ownership and source applicability. All involve the system around model behavior as well as the model itself. Repairing that system requires records, interfaces and operating decisions a reviewer can inspect and a test can challenge.

Use the cases as rehearsal prompts. Ask which source established the fact, which component owned authority, what survived the failure and what the system should report while the outcome is uncertain. Then implement the negative case against your own contracts. Keep the scenario's limits explicit: no fictional teaching case proves your live deployment safe. It helps you identify a mechanism that must be established through your own evidence.
APPENDIX F
Exercise solution guidance
Chapter 1
1.1. Account for a repaired decision
Keep accounting in the generation boundary and validation in the repair wrapper. Assert total usage independently of the returned final object.
1.2. Classify provider failures
Give the adapter a classified result/error contract, one retry allowance and a deadline. Give the controller explicit refusal and truncation branches.
1.3. Measure a real request
Time the request and first event separately. Compare output length only after controlling request content and provider settings; discuss observed variation.
Chapter 2
2.1. Draw the controlled route
Trace one concrete request. Replace the model with a hostile script and check whether the same boundaries still reject forbidden work.
2.2. Set autonomy per action
Use consequence and reversibility, not the agent's overall name. Record measurable criteria and a rapid configuration path for stopping future execution.
2.3. Test a false finish and a limit
Supply an independent verifier and fake executor counters. Add a waiting result to demonstrate that approval pauses without running the mutation.
Chapter 3
3.1. Compare two control shapes
Use scripted cases first for control-flow checks, then a fixed evaluation set for model behavior. Keep model/version/settings identical where possible.
3.2. Replan without repeating a write
Feed completed effects and unexpected observations to the planner. Validate references and compare the new proposal with the approved effect before execution.
3.3. Make a critic verify citations
Add real but irrelevant citation IDs to the cases. Measure support detection rather than counting how many comments the critic produces.
Chapter 4
4.1. Compose owned packs
Use a deterministic composer, record content hashes and add render tests for missing variables and incompatible output contracts.
4.2. Test difficult behavior
Assert effect counters and resource ownership at the executor. Use model evaluations to measure proposal quality, then investigate failing trajectories.
4.3. Demonstrate rollback
Make immutable release selection a configuration operation. Keep deployment history and run versions instead of replacing stored text in place.
Chapter 5
5.1. Define a released agent
Separate configurable agent behavior from generic controller logic. Identify any new verifier or capability extension explicitly.
5.2. Explain a run through events
Record decisions at their boundaries and retain source references. Verify that an investigator can explain the run without guessing from the final reply.
5.3. Stop a tool batch
Check cancellation before every execution and return explicit skipped/cancelled results for remaining call IDs according to the provider conversation contract.
Chapter 6
6.1. Improve a capability contract
Compare tool-choice behavior on fixed cases, then run contract tests independently of the model. Treat each missing field as a concrete ambiguity.
6.2. Handle a partial batch
Build an explicit dependency plan, use bounded invocation and collect expected per-call errors without hiding programming defects.
6.3. Test stable intent and uncertain outcome
Persist the accepted intent first, use an atomic downstream deduplication contract and reconcile the recorded pending operation on restart.
Chapter 7
7.1. Define the handover record
Trace each failure boundary and ask what would be lost if the process disappeared there. Add exact fields only where continuation needs them.
7.2. Rebuild an earlier position
Retain snapshot event offsets, apply legal transition checks in the reducer and test mixed approval outcomes explicitly.
7.3. Crash after external success
Separate intent persistence, external commit and outcome persistence in the test. State the downstream deduplication contract that makes recovery safe.
Chapter 8
8.1. Trace context cost and provenance
Use paired metadata/text records and a final serialization-aware count. Inspect one intentionally reordered and pruned request.
8.2. Compact without losing commitments
Extract commitments into typed state first, regenerate summaries from original records and keep current observations needed for the next action.
8.3. Refresh a stale payment fact
Define a maximum age for payment status, retain source version/time and reconcile against the authoritative service before mutation.
Chapter 9
9.1. Classify remembered information
Start with concrete items rather than a storage technology. Place each under the owner that can verify and govern its meaning.
9.2. Reject poisoned and lower-trust writes
Validate source evidence and apply transactional source-aware supersession. Keep an explicit conflict record when rejecting replacement.
9.3. Prove subject forgetting
Use a deletion workflow with read suppression and verified propagation. Audit identifiers/status without copying the deleted sensitive value back into logs.
Chapter 10
10.1. Package one repeated procedure
Keep business calculations in code, expose interpretation as a typed candidate and send every effect through the controlled tool boundary.
10.2. Measure progressive disclosure
Use the same task set and model release. Give summaries distinct purposes, then inspect the exact context manifest for each invocation.
10.3. Retire a skill safely
Publish the new immutable assembly, opt in test users, announce a compatibility window and prevent live approved work from silently changing effect semantics.
Chapter 11
11.1. Observe a durable wait
Retain the run identifier and both database files. Build a new Harness instance, inspect pending and supply the exact binding through the trusted demo reviewer interface.
11.2. Add current-scope revocation
Use a mutable authority fixture independent of stored run scopes. Approve the original bound proposal and inspect the executor's fresh policy result.
11.3. Port the contract to a framework
Reuse the same domain fake and acceptance cases. Add adapters around framework persistence/interrupts instead of assuming its transcript or turn limit fulfills every contract.
Chapter 12
12.1. Build a retrieval golden set
Retain source/version identifiers and evaluate retrieval before scoring generated answers. Include exact codes and policy exceptions.
12.2. Re-chunk and expand evidence
Preserve parsed headings/tables, update locators on expansion and compare retrieval/selection outcomes on the same queries.
12.3. Find a real but irrelevant citation
Represent factual claims explicitly and render accepted results from them. Record support-check method and uncertainty rather than claiming perfect entailment.
Chapter 13
13.1. Build a multi-source research path
Use source-specific tools, retain exact query/time/version records and check coverage and contradictions before final synthesis.
13.2. Stop repeated evidence
Key the ledger by stable source identity and apply relevance before accepting new evidence. Use the added-ID set as the progress signal.
13.3. Test a governed SQL boundary

Prefer reviewed parameterized operations when possible. For generated SQL, pin parser/database versions, reject unsupported forms and test the AST policy alongside actual database permissions/timeouts.
Chapter 14
14.1. Inspect the synthetic server
Use an isolated environment and the documented CLI. Test resource access separately from tool schema validation, then freeze the tested dependency release.
14.2. Reject contract drift
Hash a canonical representation, retain approved release metadata and apply the check before exposing the tool to the model.
14.3. Design an enterprise registry entry
Trace one permitted read and one denied change through host, gateway, server and backend. Specify compatible versions/extensions rather than assuming universal feature support.
Chapter 15
15.1. Specify a remote diagnosis capability
Validate the card using the pinned SDK/schema. Keep operational contact and approval policy in the registry; do not confuse advertised capability with permission.
15.2. Recover the same delegated task
Persist a logical operation before submission, implement atomic fake dedupe and lookup, then inject faults at each boundary. Keep a separate task deadline and RPC timeout.
15.3. Follow one cross-team investigation
Propagate trace context through the adapter and correlate status events. Validate and label returned artifacts before adding them to the commander's evidence.
Chapter 16
16.1. Bound every route back to investigation
Enumerate incoming edges to investigation before writing guards. Drive each route with scripted verdicts and count actual effects rather than trusting the final message.
16.2. Merge a partial investigation
Return immutable updates, merge through a declared reducer and store branch status separately from evidence. Inject failure and cancellation into each branch.
16.3. Resume an approval on another worker

Persist proposal identity and outcome records; use a fake downstream operation store to model atomic dedupe. In a durable engine, place all external calls in activities and test replay separately from activity retry.
Chapter 17
17.1. Compare a team with a simpler baseline
Use fake payment systems for comparable effects and repeat live-model cases where behaviour varies. Inspect critical slices rather than choosing from a headline average.
17.2. Stop a handoff loop
Enforce routing criteria outside the model, fingerprint the relevant task state and retain a single fallback owner. Test a legitimate new-evidence handoff separately.
17.3. Trace and merge one team investigation
Use child delegation spans and immutable evidence IDs. Merge at the owner through explicit rules; compare duplicate searches with a shared authorised evidence fetch.
Chapter 18
18.1. Prove approval cannot drift
Use immutable proposal records, canonical hashing and an explicit decision outcome check. Model the downstream version check and dedupe atomically in the fake, then inject faults between every step.
18.2. Design an approval card people can use
Keep the change and evidence prominent, include gaps and alternatives, and compare decisions against a reviewed answer key. Use observed confusion to revise the card.
18.3. Operate an approval queue
Model each outcome as an event and test restarts and late arrivals. Keep the human queue owner and the agent's remaining permissions explicit.
Chapter 19
19.1. Threat-model one agent
Use the pinned OWASP lists as prompts, then trace actual data paths. Include rendering, caches and memory rather than stopping at the tool registry.
19.2. Block an injected exfiltration request
Use a fake sender with a delivery ledger, not just a refusal-string assertion. Apply recipient and data-flow rules outside the model and include Markdown URL output.
19.3. Build a reader-actor boundary
Treat typed findings as evidence, preserve provenance and use trusted policy/resource inputs in the actor. Add both semantic and syntactic negative cases.
Chapter 20
20.1. Map the identity path
Follow a single request end to end. Record the token profile and resource-binding support actually available instead of assuming all OAuth providers behave alike.
20.2. Test layered permission decisions
Use trusted fake resource and approval stores, then vary one policy input at a time. Include aggregate refunded total and concurrent version changes.
20.3. Probe hidden tenant boundaries
Run identical requests under different tenants and entitlements. Inspect intermediate data, not just final response text, and include cache invalidation after permission changes.
Chapter 21
21.1. Demonstrate resource containment
Test provider controls rather than only code filters. Verify child processes and abandoned instances disappear after timeouts and worker crashes.
21.2. Remove credentials from analysis code
Fetch a projected dataset before execution. For live calls, define allowed operations and response fields, then enforce them outside the generated program.
21.3. Review browser and artifact release
Treat DOM, screenshots and downloads as untrusted/sensitive data. Parse actual formats and test output entitlement rather than relying on extensions or a single malware scan.
Chapter 22
22.1. Enforce a data-flow matrix
Carry trusted class, tenant, purpose and lineage metadata. Test forbidden destinations and expired exceptions rather than only allowed examples.
22.2. Reconstruct and protect one action
Use minimal content and protected references. Verify a chain against an independent anchor or append-only archive, and test missing linked events.
22.3. Review an autonomy increase
Use the current policy and model release, examine critical slices and distinguish actual deletion guarantees from delayed backup expiry or legal holds.
Chapter 23
23.1. Bound retry amplification
Classify faults and count attempts at the dependency. Separate normal requests from retries and test budget exhaustion across several workers.
23.2. Recover a saga after a crash
Persist intent before effects, reconcile by stable operation identity and record compensation completion. Inject crashes before and after every journal/effect boundary.
23.3. Define useful degraded outcomes
Write the degraded contract before implementing fallback. Check external state and handover content rather than asserting only that an answer was produced.
Chapter 24
24.1. Exercise every approval path
Keep the approval validator real and inspect a fake downstream ledger. Include crashes at effect/checkpoint boundaries rather than only before a call.
24.2. Generate difficult trajectories
Scope duplicate-effect assertions by operation identity, not by a global refund count. Shrink failed examples and save them as deterministic regressions.
24.3. Replay without repeating real effects
Compare event structure and observed fixture outcomes. Treat a new model/prompt run as an evaluation and explain which replay guarantees no longer apply.
Chapter 25
25.1. Build a case-level evaluation report
Aggregate each case's repeats and compare paired versions. Use Wilson only where the binary independence assumptions fit; use case/family resampling for grouped repeated scores.
25.2. Calibrate a judge against consequences
Adjudicate human disagreement, inspect unsupported claims the judge passed and refine the rubric/evidence. Do not choose one universal kappa cutoff as a replacement for error analysis.
25.3. Declare a release gate before running it
Compute the best possible lower bound at each planned slice size. Separate zero observed forbidden effects from a statistical assertion about the true future violation rate.
Chapter 26
26.1. Instrument one complete run
Configure an SDK/exporter in the application and instrument existing validated boundaries. Test both success and error paths and keep effect audit independent of trace export.
26.2. Build a useful operational dashboard
Use trace links/exemplars and a separate ledger for detailed cost attribution. Include explicit missing-data states rather than showing an empty measurement as healthy.
26.3. Find a stale-policy loop from evidence
Retain permitted context references and state diffs, then trace the first contradiction. Correct the relevant layer rather than changing several prompts and models at once.
Chapter 27
27.1. Define actionable service objectives
Specify denominators and data delay first. Derive error-budget burn only for objectives with a positive allowance and keep hard safety violations separate.
27.2. Make a measured canary decision
Use paired offline cases and a suitable live experimental method. Report counts and windows, not merely ramp percentages or overlapping marginal intervals.
27.3. Rehearse the brakes and recovery
Use an effect ledger and current policy checks on every executor. Follow the runbook from containment through verified recovery rather than stopping at the flag change.
Chapter 28
28.1. Explain one task's cost
Normalise provider billing categories before applying a formula. Compare the ledger with available invoice/usage records and investigate unexplained differences.
28.2. Evaluate a qualified cascade
Use the same cases and controlled systems, inspect critical slices and do not treat schema validity or self-confidence as proof of factual correctness.
28.3. Test caches and concurrent budgets
Use complete versioned keys and current authorisation at serve time. Model permits, estimated spend and actual settlement separately in the fake accounting service.
Chapter 29
29.1. Document the platform's ownership contracts
Start with logical responsibilities, then justify deployment separation through scale, duration and isolation. Trace one run and its failure recovery rather than listing technologies.
29.2. Reject a stale worker
Advance an epoch atomically on takeover, check it at consumers and preserve operation identities. Test visibility expiry, lost renewal and worker crashes separately.
29.3. Rehearse an honest regional restore
Inject a completed-but-unrecorded effect and prove the restore reconciles it. Do not count database health alone as recovery success.
Chapter 30
30.1. Build a policy-aware gateway attempt
Use explicit adapter error categories and a durable fake accounting ledger. Inject timeout after generation and compare local reservations with reconciled provider usage.
30.2. Measure a self-hosted task route
Load-test the intended prompt/output mix and traffic, not only peak throughput. Retain managed routing when the self-hosted candidate does not meet the task floor.
30.3. Find the serving operating region
Identify the actual limiting regime and repeat after quantisation or scheduling changes. Do not assume the knee is always KV saturation or that more GPUs always improve cost.
Chapter 31
31.1. Run one refund flow in two engines

Keep domain services framework-free. Persist the effect ID before dispatch, make the fake provider honor it, and translate each engine's pause into the same owned approval record. Run deterministic cases before comparing live-model quality.
31.2. Prove the permission boundary

Use an exact allowlist and pinned schema registry in both discovery and execution. Do not allow by namespace prefix. The negative test must observe the downstream invocation count, not only the assistant's response.
31.3. Write an evidence-based decision record
Describe the decision trigger, options, measured evidence, consequences and revisit conditions. Keep unresolved limitations explicit rather than filling them with invented benchmark numbers.
Chapter 32
32.1. Restart a real approval process

Keep definitions shared, put counters in persistent test instrumentation and use a fresh database per case. Persist an effect intent before calling a provider fake that deduplicates by key. Also kill after provider success but before checkpoint completion.
32.2. Compose an investigation without duplicate evidence
Return additions or merge immutable evidence by ID. Give each worker scoped input and a deadline, then validate the joined partial result rather than assuming all branches succeeded.
32.3. Govern memory and approval together

Apply authorization before store access, a write gate before persistence and an explicit delete path. Exercise every policy branch with plain-function tests before connecting the graph's interrupt adapter.
Chapter 33
33.1. Map your actual building blocks
Begin with behavioral contracts, then record service choices. Verify the difficult cases, such as late approval and quota exhaustion, rather than marking a block complete because a product exists.
33.2. Recover a lost workflow start

Persist an ingestion and dispatch intent under a stable digest of source and event ID. Retry idempotent engine start, record acknowledgement and test every crash boundary with counters in durable fake storage.
33.3. Write and test a migration plan
Move read-only work first, compare outputs and operational behavior, then define the separate cutover/reconciliation requirements for effects. Do not claim portability from container startup alone.
Chapter 34
34.1. Specialize one controlled harness
Choose one environment and define what success means before adding tools. Reuse the runtime boundaries, introduce only required extensions and test the verifier independently of a live model.
34.2. Write two different verification strategies

Use unsupported citations for the research negative case and a weakened assertion or malicious test command for coding. Show which trusted layer detects each defect and which evidence a human can inspect.
34.3. Budget a voice turn and an interrupted effect

Measure first audio separately from complete task time. Cancel presentation safely, retain the effect identity, reconcile the payment and read back its actual result before accepting another consequential request.
Chapter 35
35.1. Review AegisOps and propose three cuts

Consider merging specialists with identical scopes, replacing a known-alert router with rules and delaying optional remote boundaries. Keep the approved-effect and verified-recovery path intact. Use evidence rather than diagram size to justify the cuts.
35.2. Record three pattern decisions
State the concrete trigger, not a general preference for a framework. Separate observed results from proposed measurements and retain the cost and operating consequences alongside quality.
35.3. Run a forty-five-minute design review

Spend the opening on requirements, then the core diagram and risky sequence. Reserve time for critical evaluation slices, operating recovery and a justified simplification. Score the quality of the evidence rather than the number of boxes.
Chapter 36
36.1. Add a bounded Capacity role

Use saturation, pending workloads and queue/latency evidence as selection signals, not a universal CPU threshold. Return findings to the commander and route any change through the existing proposal contract.
36.2. Bind a feature-flag proposal
Keep the proposal immutable, derive tenant scope from verified identity, and validate distinct approvers where required. Consume or reserve authority durably and record typed denial reasons.
36.3. Reprice and test the incident budget
Calculate input and output separately, apply only the provider's actual cached-input policy and record usage by incident. Compare quality before using routing or early stopping to claim a saving.
Chapter 37
37.1. Complete the evidence milestone

Enforce limits in the adapter, preserve scope and source IDs, and seed independent evidence for the alternative cause. Require the hypothesis test to record its support and contradiction rather than assert on final wording.
37.2. Expire and replay an approval
Keep approval authority in an owned durable record and signal only its identity. Validate every field on continuation, reserve or consume atomically with intent, and inspect the fake change ledger.
37.3. Prove restart and unknown-outcome recovery

Persist instrumentation outside the worker, use a provider fake with deduplication and a lost-response mode, and test reconciliation under the documented service contract. Follow confirmed effects into the verification stage without claiming recovery prematurely.
Chapter 38
38.1. Reject false recovery

Pass explicit action completion time and expected windows to a pure verifier. Reject invalid numeric data in the adapter, enforce required dependency checks, and use a durable coordinator for polling. Retain evidence IDs for every accepted bucket.
38.2. Turn a game-day deviation into a gate
Assert on effects and verification records rather than final wording. Version the fixtures and accepted outcomes, label critical slices, and avoid leaking held-out answers into prompts.
38.3. Complete one extension with operating evidence

Reuse the core proposal and effect contracts. Add only the new boundary needed by the extension, update its threat model and release gates, and keep hard safety criteria separate from the weighted portfolio score.
Chapter 39
39.1. Design a fourth focused track

Choose one narrow request such as a permitted account unlock. Keep evidence gathering separate from authority, define the downstream effect/reconciliation contract and draw the critical failure sequence before adding agent collaboration.
39.2. Measure honest insufficiency

Include absent dimensions, unretained periods and undefined metrics. Verify every partial claim against ledger entries and report correct refusal, false refusal and confident wrong answers separately.
39.3. Guard a resumable maintenance task

Compare to a trusted base outside the editable environment and scope publication through the PR writer. Permit lockfile changes only in the reviewed upgrade mode, preserve attempted approaches as evidence and test a lost PR response before retrying publication.
APPENDIX G
Self-check answers
Chapter 1
1.1. A model proposes issue_refund. Has money moved?
No. It has expressed an intent. The runtime must validate, authorize and execute an accepted request before an external effect occurs.
1.2. What does schema-constrained output leave unresolved?
Business meaning, resource ownership, current preconditions, permission and whether the cited evidence supports the decision.
1.3. Why count a response rejected during repair?
The generation already consumed latency and may have incurred token cost. Omitting it understates usage and can defeat budgets.
1.4. Can a common message type discard all provider continuation fields?
Only if the chosen provider contract permits it. Some reasoning APIs require opaque items across tool turns, so adapters must preserve required information.
Chapter 2
2.1. Can a fixed workflow contain an agentic node?
Yes. A workflow can control the overall process while delegating one bounded investigation to a model-directed loop.
2.2. Why is a tool-free final response not enough to mark a refund task complete?
It is a model claim. The controller needs the payment-system record and the other acceptance evidence defined for the task.
2.3. Where should a captured-amount limit be enforced?
At the refund service or tool boundary against current authoritative records, with prompt guidance providing an additional behavioral aid.
2.4. Does a stop request erase an in-flight mutation?
No. Stop scheduling new work, then cancel where supported or reconcile the active operation's actual outcome.
Chapter 3
3.1. Why is reflection not simply a higher-autonomy pattern than ReAct?
Reflection describes review and revision, while ReAct describes ongoing action selection. A fixed workflow can contain reflection, and a ReAct agent can omit it.
3.2. What should a critic contribute?
A concrete check, external evidence or explicit rubric that can reveal an error, plus an acceptance status that downstream code can use.
3.3. Why can a plan require new approval after replanning?
Changed steps may change the actual effect, resource or amount. Approval applies to a bound proposal, not an unrestricted future plan.
3.4. Does parallel processing guarantee a cheaper answer?
No. It can reduce wall time while repeating instructions and adding reducer work. Measure total tokens, cost and partial-failure behavior.
Chapter 4
4.1. Does placing a customer subject line inside a system template make it trusted?
No. Trust depends on its source and validation, not its containing role. Put free customer text in the request/data portion.
4.2. Why reject two versions of the same pack during composition?
Their text can conflict while a dictionary manifest silently records only one version, making behavior and provenance disagree.
4.3. What does escaping an untrusted passage actually protect?
The wrapper's delimiter/attribute structure. It does not remove hostile meaning or enforce permission on subsequent actions.
4.4. Why distinguish invalid model proposals from executed policy violations in tests?
The proposal may be a behavioral error while the runtime boundary correctly rejects it. The two require different remediation.
Chapter 5
5.1. What does an agent definition change without necessarily changing the harness?
Instructions, permitted capabilities, model policy, limits and supported acceptance configuration within the runtime's existing contracts.
5.2. Why must cancellation be checked before each tool operation?
One model response may contain several operations. A single check before the response would allow later work to continue after a stop request.
5.3. Which owner handles replanning after a failed step?
The controller. Provider retries belong to the adapter and safe tool retries to the executor; replanning changes control flow.
5.4. Does a framework-neutral API make every approval signal safe?
No. The signal still needs authenticated authority, exact proposal binding, expiry checks and fresh authorization before execution.
Chapter 6
6.1. Does hiding a tool from the offered list remove the need for execution checks?
No. A model or caller may still name it. The executor must reject unknown or unauthorized requests independently.
6.2. Why exclude narrative evidence from a refund effect key?
Its wording can change while the business effect stays identical, producing a new key that defeats duplicate recognition.
6.3. Why can check-before-act still duplicate a write?
Concurrent workers can both observe absence, or an earlier completed effect may not yet be visible. Atomicity or a safe reconciliation contract is needed.
6.4. What does compensation mean for a sent email?
A new mitigating operation, such as a correction. It does not erase the original delivery and may require its own review.
Chapter 7
7.1. Why is a context summary not the execution source of truth?
It is selected and potentially lossy. Exact accepted intents, approvals, usage and outcomes belong in retained state and referenced records.
7.2. What should a reducer do with a rejected approval?
Record rejection under the legal transition rules and prevent the rejected effect from executing; it must not unconditionally resume the mutation.
7.3. Does optimistic concurrency alone prevent duplicate external effects?
No. It rejects stale state writes, but a worker may already have submitted an effect. External deduplication, fencing or reconciliation is also needed.
7.4. Why reject a future schema version?
Older code cannot assume it understands the newer record's meaning. Silent parsing can discard or misinterpret fields needed for safe continuation.
Chapter 8
8.1. Why must the manifest be created from selected paired records?
Ranking and pruning can change order and membership. Pairing retains the correct source for each piece actually sent.
8.2. What must a complete context budget count beyond visible user text?
Instructions, messages, tool/output schemas, serialization overhead and reserved output/provider reasoning capacity under the endpoint's contract.
8.3. Why keep a proposed refund distinct from a completed refund in state summaries?
Compression can otherwise turn intention into a false operational fact, causing unsupported promises or incorrect recovery.
8.4. Does a fresh retrieval timestamp prove a policy is current?
No. The retrieved document may be superseded. Effective date, version and source authority must also be checked.
Chapter 9
9.1. Is a vector database sufficient to implement governed memory?
No. It supplies retrieval, while memory also needs purpose, identity binding, write rules, provenance, correction, validity, retention and deletion.
9.2. Can high model confidence replace a verified customer fact?
Not by itself. Supersession depends on the fact's authority and evidence policy, with conflicts handled explicitly.
9.3. What is the difference between decay and deletion?
Decay changes retrieval priority; deletion removes or suppresses records and derived copies under the applicable retention policy.
9.4. Should remembering that a user calls themselves an admin grant scope?
No. Authorization comes from authenticated identity and policy, not a memory statement.
Chapter 10
10.1. Does loading a skill's instructions automatically execute its procedure?
No. Instruction loading supplies know-how; an executable skill invocation needs its own runtime, authority and outcome contract.
10.2. Why retain exact resolved dependency versions when ranges are declared?
Ranges express compatibility during resolution. Exact versions/hashes explain what a released package and a past run actually used.
10.3. Can a signed skill grant itself a financial scope?
No. Signature proves source identity, not permission. The host and effect service enforce authority independently.
10.4. Why does a script not necessarily have zero token overhead?
Even when its contents execute outside context, descriptions, invocation paths, arguments and results can consume tokens.
Chapter 11
11.1. Which mechanism makes the demonstrated crash recovery avoid a second refund?
The fake payment service atomically stores effect-key deduplication with its balance change, while the runtime persists the accepted identity and reconciles it on restart.
11.2. Does resume reset the run's deadline or consumed usage?
No. They remain in durable state. The resumed operation checks the original absolute deadline and remaining allowance.
11.3. Why is the crash test stronger than replaying a completed ledger entry?
It exits after the service commits and before the runtime saves the result, exercising the uncertain window that ordinary successful replay does not cover.
11.4. What must be added before using this loop with arbitrary network tools?

A bounded async or process-isolated invocation contract, provider/service deadlines, appropriate cancellation and uncertain-outcome handling, plus the required identity and distributed ownership controls.
Chapter 12
12.1. What does a citation-ID membership check prove?
Only that the cited identifier exists in the selected evidence set. It does not establish semantic support or complete coverage of the displayed answer.
12.2. Why can parent expansion require a different locator?
The model may use facts outside the matched child. The citation must identify the actual expanded section/version that supplied those facts.
12.3. How do recall@k and hit rate@k differ?
Recall is the fraction of all labeled relevant items found; hit rate is whether any relevant item was found. Both need explicit treatment of unanswerable cases.
12.4. Does baseline RAG have to omit quality checks?
No. Fixed pipelines can rerank, enforce freshness, verify citations and evaluate support. Agentic RAG changes who controls retrieval decisions.
Chapter 13
13.1. What changes when RAG becomes agentic?
The model adaptively controls whether, where and how to retrieve and when to stop. Fixed pipelines can already have sophisticated quality checks.
13.2. Why count stable evidence identities rather than appended list length?
Repeated passages can grow a list without adding information. Unique relevant accepted records provide the intended progress signal.
13.3. May corrective retrieval broaden tenant or entitlement filters?
No. It may adjust authorized relevance/search choices, but access restrictions remain enforced regardless of weak results.
13.4. Does a SELECT root plus LIMIT make generated SQL safe?
No. Nested writes, functions, relations, row access and query cost still matter. Database-role/RLS/time/resource controls provide containment.
Chapter 14
14.1. How does MCP differ from model function calling?
Function calling produces model intent. MCP exchanges capability discovery/invocation between an application client and a server after the host's checks.
14.2. Why pin descriptions as well as input schemas?
Changed wording can poison tool selection or instructions even if the argument fields remain identical.
14.3. What distinguishes modern negotiation from legacy initialization?
The 2026-07-28 modern contract carries version/capabilities per request, while older revisions use an initialize/initialized handshake and their transport/session rules.
14.4. Does a timeout prove an MCP mutation never happened?
No. The client may stop waiting after the server/backend committed. Retained intent and authoritative reconciliation are required.
Chapter 15
15.1. Does a stable A2A message ID guarantee that a retry creates no new task?
No. Send Message idempotence is optional. The remote adapter needs an agreed, tested server-side deduplication and recovery contract.
15.2. What should happen when a worker requests a missing cluster identifier?
Obtain the identifier from authorised state or a human and continue the existing task. Do not silently invent it or restart unrelated work.
15.3. What does a verified Agent Card signature establish?
The card's origin and integrity under the trusted signing key. It does not establish skill quality, current health or truth of returned artifacts.
15.4. Who owns the incident after the commander delegates database diagnosis?
The commander retains the overall goal and stopping decision. The database worker owns only its scoped delegated task.
Chapter 16
16.1. Why does an approval node not by itself guarantee that approval cannot be bypassed?
A prior node could already hold and execute the protected tool. Capabilities and executor policy must enforce the same boundary as the graph.
16.2. What must a deadline join record when one investigator does not return?
The missing branch and its reason, alongside available results. The downstream conclusion must retain the partial-evidence limitation.
16.3. Does a checkpoint after every node prevent duplicate external effects?
No. A crash can occur after the effect but before the checkpoint. Use stable operation identity and downstream deduplication or reconcile an uncertain outcome.
16.4. Where should a model call run in a replay-based durable workflow?
In an activity or equivalent recorded I/O boundary, not directly in deterministic workflow code.
Chapter 17
17.1. What justifies a second worker?
A measurable benefit such as different tools or authority, independent parallel work, context partitioning or an externally owned capability, large enough to exceed coordination cost.
17.2. Why can three agreeing agents still be wrong?
They may share the same model, evidence or false premise. Agreement is not independent verification; check evidence and observed outcomes.
17.3. May a research worker's report approve the refund it recommends?
No. It is evidence or a proposal. An independent policy and approval record must authorise the exact financial operation.
17.4. Who should stop a supervisor-worker investigation?
The supervisor or owning workflow, using goal, progress and budget criteria. A worker can finish its own task but does not own the overall run.
Chapter 18
18.1. Why compare the decision digest with a recomputed proposal digest?
Two matching stored hash fields can remain unchanged while mutable arguments change. Recomputing from the immutable action and context verifies the operation actually being authorised.
18.2. Can matching arguments turn a rejected decision into permission?
No. Check that the decision outcome is approved before any execution path, then validate identity, binding, expiry and entitlement.
18.3. Why is a fresh read followed by a write not always enough?
Another actor can change the resource between them. Use a downstream atomic version or precondition check when freshness is required.
18.4. Where should a reviewer's correction go?
Into a labelled feedback record and a reviewed improvement process. It should not automatically become a permanent memory or permission rule.
Chapter 19
19.1. Why can an innocent user trigger indirect injection?
The agent reads attacker-controlled material while carrying out the user's legitimate request. The attacker does not need to speak directly to the agent.
19.2. Does a typed reader report establish that its requested recipient is authorised?
No. Shape validation cannot establish entitlement. The actor must independently check destination, purpose, provenance and resource policy.
19.3. Where should credentials live?
In the protected executor and identity system, outside model context, memory and ordinary tool outputs. Use narrow, short-lived credentials.
19.4. Why track unsafe attempts when policy blocks every tested effect?
Attempts show model vulnerability and may reveal changing attacks. The effect boundary's zero observed violations is necessary but does not make future monitoring unnecessary.
Chapter 20
20.1. What is wrong with the union of user and agent permissions?
It grants actions allowed to either principal even when the other is not entitled. A user-directed operation must satisfy both ceilings and the task/resource policy.
20.2. Does RFC 8693 always issue a short-lived dual-identity token?
No. The authorisation server's configured policy and token profile determine delegation claims, scope, audience and lifetime.
20.3. Why check both resource and arguments after allowing a tool?
Permission to use a refunds tool says nothing about access to this payment or whether this amount and recipient are allowed.
20.4. Where should a tenant leak be prevented?
At every boundary, including retrieval before context assembly, memory, tools, caches, telemetry and exports. A refusal after unauthorised retrieval is too late.
Chapter 21
21.1. Why is truncating stdout after execution insufficient?
The collector may exhaust memory while capturing it. Enforce a streaming byte cap during execution and separately bound artifacts and scratch storage.
21.2. Does a microVM remove the need to review host configuration?
No. Runtime/jailer settings, mounts, device exposure, patching and network policy remain part of the isolation boundary.
21.3. How should generated code obtain private input data?
Through an authorised harness fetch or a narrow policy-checked proxy, without receiving the broad credential used by the harness.
21.4. Why add a reaper when the tool has a finally block?
A killed worker may never run finally. Provider lifetime enforcement or an independent reaper must remove abandoned environments.
Chapter 22
22.1. Does approval of a self-hosted model authorise every restricted-data task?
No. Placement is one condition. Entitlement, purpose, transformations and any reviewed exception must also permit the flow.
22.2. Why is reversible tokenisation not automatically anonymisation?
The protected vault or other information can reconnect the token to a person. Re-identifiable records still need appropriate privacy controls.
22.3. Why does a hash chain need protected anchoring?
A writer able to replace the entire chain can recompute all hashes. An external trusted digest or protected append-only store makes wholesale rewriting detectable.
22.4. Which changes need governance review?
Behaviour-changing code, prompts, policies, tools, models and autonomy settings, with the relevant owners and evidence for the resulting risk.
Chapter 23
23.1. What does a refund timeout establish?
Only that the caller did not receive the expected response in time. The effect may have happened. Reconcile or retry the same logical operation under its downstream deduplication contract.
23.2. Why is a local action ledger insufficient for one external effect?
A crash can occur after the external commit but before the local success record. The downstream operation identity or authoritative reconciliation must cover that gap.
23.3. What should a saga report after a failed compensation?
Compensation-pending or manual-recovery-required with the unresolved effect. It must not automatically label the result failed-safe.
23.4. Why reserve part of a run budget?
So the system can checkpoint, verify known effects and hand over safely when exploratory work reaches its limit.
Chapter 24
24.1. Why can an agent approval invariant be tested without a live model?
A scripted model can request the forbidden action while the real validator and fake effect store demonstrate that execution is denied.
24.2. What is wrong with checking only approval_requested?
A request may be rejected, expired or bound to a different proposal. Executed protected effects need a valid approved decision for the exact operation.
24.3. Why reset a fake environment for every property-test example?
Generated examples otherwise inherit mutable state and can fail or pass for the wrong reason. Test-framework fixture scope may not reset it per generated example.
24.4. When does replay become an evaluation?
When a changed prompt, model or environment produces new decisions rather than consuming the recorded responses under the original controlled context.
Chapter 25
25.1. Why are 180 trials from 60 cases not 180 distinct cases?
Repeated runs measure variation on the same task. Generalisation uncertainty must preserve case or family clustering rather than treating every repeat as an independent scenario.
25.2. What does kappa add to raw judge agreement?
It adjusts observed agreement for the raters' marginal label frequencies. It does not replace inspection of critical false accepts or provide a universal trust threshold.
25.3. Can 45 perfect independent binary cases meet a 95% lower-bound gate using the displayed Wilson method?
No. Their lower bound is about 92%. Under that exact two-sided rule, at least 73 perfect independent observations are required; other assurance goals may need more.
25.4. What should a release comparison estimate directly?
The paired candidate-minus-baseline change on the same cases, with appropriate clustering and uncertainty, alongside absolute safety and quality gates.
Chapter 26

They create unbounded time-series cardinality. Keep detailed IDs on controlled traces/logs and use bounded dimensions plus exemplars or links.
26.2. Does a context manifest guarantee exact reconstruction?
No. It identifies selected sources, but replay also needs accessible immutable/versioned content or permitted snapshots and other control-relevant inputs.
26.3. Where can sensitive content bypass a prompt-field redaction rule?
Exception messages, stacks, nested attributes, logs and alternate exporters. Apply source allowlists and test error paths, with Collector filtering as an additional layer.

Recorded decisions, context and actions. It does not establish privileged access to the model's internal reasoning or prove the recorded rationale caused the decision.

They reflect different populations and constraints. A long human wait can be acceptable under its policy while active processing has a much shorter objective.
27.2. What does a canary traffic percentage tell you?

27.3. Should a pinned in-flight run ignore a new mutation kill switch?

27.4. What remains after rolling back a faulty prompt?
Previously executed and outcome-unknown effects still need reconciliation or compensation, with named owners and verified outcomes.

Retries, failures, tools and evaluation contribute to the cost of achieving the goal. A cheap call can produce an expensive or unsuccessful trajectory.
28.2. May a low remaining budget downgrade a high-risk task below its quality floor?
No. Eligibility and quality constraints remain. Use a qualified route that fits or an approved stop/degraded outcome.
28.3. What makes a semantic cache different from prefix reuse?
It substitutes a result for a merely similar request, which can be semantically wrong. Prefix reuse processes an identical supported prefix, while still needing privacy controls.
28.4. Why atomically reserve tenant allowance?
Concurrent requests can otherwise all pass the same balance check. Reservations account for in-flight work and are settled to actual or reconciled usage.

The durable stores or workflow history own run state and continuation. Workers load and advance bounded steps under explicit ownership.
29.2. Why can two workers overlap after a lease expires?
The old worker may be paused rather than dead and can resume after takeover. Owner-aware leases and fencing at state/effect boundaries must reject stale authority.
29.3. What should autoscaling consider besides worker CPU?
Queue depth/age, progress, tenant fairness and shared provider/tool capacity. More workers cannot create unavailable downstream quota.
29.4. What makes a restored mutation retry safe?
Stable operation identity plus available downstream dedupe/reconciliation records for the retry horizon, current policy and resource checks. A checkpoint alone is insufficient.

Features, tool-call formats, errors, streaming and billing semantics can differ. The adapter validates and normalises the contract the harness actually requires.
30.2. Should every failed provider attempt refund its entire reservation?
No. A confirmed unprocessed rejection differs from a timeout with unknown consumed usage. Release concurrency separately and settle or reconcile spend/token allowance.
30.3. What does continuous batching change?
The active batch admits new requests and removes completed ones during generation. An individual completed request leaves; the scheduler continues under capacity and latency constraints.
30.4. When is narrow model training justified?
When a stable high-volume task, reviewed data, held-out quality evidence and operating capacity justify it after comparison with simpler prompt/routing/retrieval changes.

A session can preserve conversation history without storing pending execution, remaining budgets, approved effect identities or reconciliation state. Check the exact persistence contract.

Persist the new server-owned snapshot and return a pending-approval status with exact call identities. It must not present an incomplete run as a final answer.

Use the same models, prompts, tools, policies and evaluation cases, repeat probabilistic trials, and report outcomes together with persistence, safety and operational evidence.

The graph has no merge rule for the conflicting writes and raises an update error. Add an appropriate reducer; do not assume one update wins.
32.2. Why does a separate execution node still need idempotency?
It may be retried after the external effect completed but before its completion was recorded. Node separation fixes interrupt-related replay, not the external crash window.

No. The deterministic policy blocks and escalates that action class before execution. Approval is not a mechanism for overriding the blocked class.

A checkpoint preserves one thread's execution state. A store retains governed application records across threads, with its own scope, provenance, retention and deletion rules.

Delivery, ordering, acknowledgement and redelivery semantics can differ. The adapter must preserve the application's ownership and recovery contract, not only method names.

Workflow dispatch can still fail before the engine accepts the start. A durable dispatch intent or an idempotent start-and-recovery mechanism must close that gap.

No. It may operate execution infrastructure, but the application still validates the principal, payment, approval, current accounting and external-effect contract.

The source event's ingestion identity must remain stable. Correlation windows group related incidents and must not turn a repeated delivery into new work.

It can expose confidential questions or records through retrieval and outbound requests, and retrieved content can manipulate proposals. Scope, egress and evidence checks remain necessary.
34.2. Where should hidden tests execute candidate code?
In an isolated disposable environment without harness secrets or host privileges. Keeping test definitions hidden does not make the candidate code trusted.
34.3. Can voice interruption cancel a completed refund?
No. Stop generation or safe pending work, then reconcile any in-flight mutation and report the actual outcome. Cancellation is not compensation.
34.4. What is the primary evidence of operational recovery?
Independent post-action signals satisfying explicit criteria over the required observation window, with adequate coverage. A command's success response alone is insufficient.

Only where adaptive investigation adds value. Mandatory eligibility, authority, approval and effect handling remain deterministic even when model calls appear inside the workflow.
35.2. What makes a second agent worth adding?
A measurable benefit from specialization, permissions, ownership, context separation or independent parallel work that exceeds its coordination and operating cost.
35.3. Does zero successful attacks in an adversarial suite prove universal safety?
No. It establishes behavior on the stated corpus and assumptions. Residual risks, shadow observation, staged rollout and operational controls remain necessary.

The required outcome and the contracts that establish authority, evidence, recovery and operation. Removing a required approval or reconciliation boundary is a defect, not simplification.

Adaptive investigation, hypothesis development and proposal drafting can use it. Authority, risk gates, budgets, effect identity and verification conditions must remain enforced independently.

Restart, scale, feature-flag change and rollback all affect production. External chat and ITSM writes also require scope and data policy even though they are a different effect class.

Not in this blueprint. The exception is restricted to explicitly allowed risk 3 cases; risk 4 needs privileged distinct approvers and risk 5 is blocked.

It deduplicates local intent records. One external effect additionally requires downstream deduplication, atomic business conditions or outcome reconciliation under an explicit contract.

Tools need verified bounds independent of model arguments. A valid service-name string or tenant label alone cannot prevent access to another service or environment.

It raises asyncio.TimeoutError. The workflow catches it and follows its expiry/escalation policy; it should not interpret the normal return as an approval Boolean.

The resource can change between that read and the mutation. Pass the expected revision to an executor that checks and mutates atomically, or returns a conflict.

Its consumed or reserved action authority and logical effect identity, validated against the owned proposal. A matching hash and unexpired timestamp alone do not make it single-use.

No. The stated criterion needs a complete covered window after confirmed action completion. Before that it is pending; missing coverage is insufficient evidence.

As an explicitly recorded escalation or residual-risk disposition, not verified recovery. Otherwise the requirement that every RESOLVED incident passed SLO verification is false.
38.3. Why still run game days after one hundred scenarios pass?
The finite suite checks modeled cases; realistic dependencies, permissions and timing can violate assumptions the fakes omitted. Rehearsal findings become new regression cases.
38.4. What does the mutation kill switch leave to do?
It prevents new effects at execution while diagnosis continues. Already submitted effects still need reconciliation and truthful status; a switch cannot undo them.
Chapter 39
39.1. What proves a refund survived a crash safely?

The provider/effect ledger and authority records show one intended effect after crash, continuation and replay attempts under an explicit idempotency/reconciliation contract. Repeated confirmation text is insufficient.
39.2. What may the analyst infer from a missing seller-type dimension?
That the approved data cannot support that breakdown. It cannot infer marketplace exclusion or invent a first-party number without evidence establishing those facts.

Use separate reviewed task modes: ordinary repair protects lockfiles; an upgrade mode explicitly permits required manifest and lockfile changes while retaining independent verification and protected CI.

No. Hard authority, effect, scope and execution criteria must pass independently. The rubric helps compare evidence and find improvement areas; it does not certify live production safety.

No. That tests a no-effect failure. The displayed post-commit fault tests whether recovery handles an effect that happened without a local acknowledgement. Both positions matter and require different fixture evidence.

No. Its point estimate is 95%, but the Wilson lower bound is about 91.04%, below the predeclared 95% floor. Gate decisions use the specified bound, not the point estimate.

No. It conceals false acceptance of 9 of 30 unfaithful answers. Inspect those errors and critical slices against a task-specific rule. Kappa is about 0.632 for these marginals, but that summary also cannot replace consequence-based review.

No. The swapped presentation chooses S, so this pair provides no stable winner. Use balanced orders, repeated or appropriately controlled judgments, and rubric-based adjudication. The two rows flag an evaluation weakness without proving a population bias rate or which reply is actually better.

26. Observability for Agent Systems
26A. May an operator create a replacement refund while only the middle frame is available?

No. The original outcome is unknown. Reconcile OP-61 through its authoritative status or supported deduplication contract before choosing recovery. The missing span does not authorize a new financial effect.

26B. Should an exception message containing a customer email bypass this policy because it is diagnostic?

No. Error paths follow the same classification rules. Record a safe error category and an authorized reference when needed; raw exception text can disclose content even when prompt fields are filtered.

26C. Does adding the four durations mean the customer waited 28 seconds?

No. The sum counts nested work repeatedly. The customer-visible run spans 12 seconds; the investigation already contains its two children. Use actual start/end relationships to calculate elapsed time and distinguish parent duration from time spent outside child operations.

27. AgentOps & Production Operations
27A. Does verified enforcement at 10:03 mean the refund incident is fully recovered?

No. It establishes the checked executor restriction. RF-441 still exists, and the incident owner must scope other applied or unknown operations and follow authorized reconciliation or compensation procedures. Publication alone also did not establish the enforcement time.

27B. Can the candidate promote because both routine estimates are 95%?

No. Matching point estimates do not establish non-regression. Use the predeclared comparative analysis, its required counts and critical-slice conditions. These marginal Wilson intervals expose uncertainty but do not replace a two-sample or planned sequential decision rule. Any observed forbidden effect follows its separate containment rule.

27C. At 2.5% failed requests, what is burn rate, and does it authorize five forbidden refunds?

The burn rate is 2.5 / 0.5 = 5 times the target allowance rate. It does not authorize any forbidden refund. Availability budgets describe an operating objective; an observed unauthorized effect triggers its own containment rule. Alert decisions also need the declared windows, traffic and response policy.
Return to visual 27C.
28. Cost, Latency & Model Routing Engineering
28A. If attempt B times out with unknown usage, should all 30 cents return immediately?

No. Preserve the uncertain usage reservation under the accounting policy and reconcile with authoritative usage where possible. A timeout does not prove no processing occurred. Release the concurrency permit separately when the attempt ends; that does not erase financial liability.
Return to visual 28A.
28B. Would raising the similarity threshold to 0.99 prove the next cache hit is safe?

No. A similarity score cannot prove semantic equivalence. Evaluate false hits and enforce the relevant condition, policy version, freshness and entitlement checks. If the request cannot satisfy the cache contract, retrieve current evidence instead. Neither answer reuse nor similarity grants permission to issue a refund.
Return to visual 28B.
28C. If stock takes 7 seconds instead, when does the answer finish under the same assumptions?

At 8 seconds: max(7, 5) + 1. The stock branch becomes the critical path. Parallelism overlaps independent work; it does not remove the need to perform or pay for both reads. Quota contention, retries or extra joining overhead would require a different timing model.

29. Production Agent Platform Architecture
29A. Can B infer that no rollback happened because its checkpoint says outcome unknown?

No. Unknown records the missing knowledge, not absence of an effect. B must reconcile RB-82 through the deployment service while preserving the logical operation identity. It may resume protected work only under current ownership, authority and resource checks. The downstream dedupe retention contract must still cover any retry.
Return to visual 29A.
29B. What breaks if only the state store checks the epoch?

A stale worker could still start a new external operation even though its state write is rejected. The protected effect boundary needs an ownership contract too. Effects accepted before takeover can remain uncertain and require their operation ledger; later fencing does not undo them.
Return to visual 29B.
29C. If the relay publishes H-93 and crashes before marking it sent, what must the consumer tolerate?

A repeat delivery of H-93. The relay may publish again because its local record is still pending. The consumer needs a durable idempotent handling contract for that event. 30A. If region A has no quota, may the gateway choose the available region B?

No. Capacity pressure does not override data placement. None of the other listed routes is currently eligible. Use the declared bounded degraded outcome or human escalation. Even a qualified model response remains a proposal and does not authorize a production mutation.
Return to visual 30A.
30B. Would four 4,096-token requests need exactly 512 MiB of total device memory?

Sharing, paging, precision and parallelism can change the actual cache layout. Measure the chosen engine before setting admission limits.

No. This scheduler can admit prepared C at boundary 2 when B finishes. C then completes at boundary 5 under the toy one-step-per-iteration assumption. 31. Framework Mapping: LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Spring AI & Others
31A. Can copying conversation messages alone safely resume this approved refund?

No. Messages can omit the pending call, bound approval, remaining allowance and unknown effect status. 33. Cloud & Enterprise Integration Tracks
33A. If the managed runtime reports success, which record proves the rollback actually applied?

36A. At 10:10, may the commander announce verified recovery because RB-82 applied at 10:09?

No. Re-asking could change the command sequence and reinterpret prior progress. Replay uses the recorded D-7 result. Example scope: Original matched-request cases and diagnostic choices. The source supplies the troubleshooting principle, not a causal verdict or remediation authorization.

Temporal Technologies. Open primary source.
Workflow replay requires deterministic command sequencing. External API calls, database queries and model invocations belong in activities so recorded outcomes can support deterministic continuation.
Example scope: Original INC-93 records; assumes compatible workflow code and durable recorded activity completion. External-effect safety remains an independent application contract.

Lianmin Zheng and coauthors. Open primary source.
Model judges can exhibit position bias: presentation order can influence their preferences. Judge behavior therefore needs evaluation alongside the behavior being scored.
Example scope: Original AegisOps answers and constructed position-sensitive judge outputs. No paper result, model accuracy or frequency of bias is reproduced.

Wilson intervals estimate uncertainty for a binary proportion using the observed count and sample size. The lower endpoint differs from the observed success rate.
Example scope: Original 120-case hypothetical outcomes and curriculum gate. Counts are constructed; this chart is neither a production result nor a safety certificate.

THE COMPLETE EDITION
Corrections and edition updates
Report a correction

Send corrections to juned.alam.dev@gmail.com. Use the subject Agentic AI Engineering - correction. Include the edition/version from the copyright page, the chapter and section heading, the printed page number, and a short description of the problem. A source, calculation or small reproducible example helps distinguish a technical error from a different design choice.

For code problems, include the lab name, Python version, installed dependency versions, command, expected result and observed result. Remove credentials, customer data and private records before sharing a reproduction. The examples use fictional records and local fixtures; a report should not require access to a reader's production system.
How corrections are recorded

Reports are reviewed before they become confirmed errata. A confirmed entry records the affected edition, stable chapter/section, issue, correction and first corrected version. Page numbers can move after typesetting, so chapter and section identifiers remain the preferred reference. Unresolved questions remain distinguishable from verified errors.

When a corrected file is issued, its version and preparation date change and the companion changelog records the differences. Examples and their dependency notes are updated together when a correction changes executable behavior. This process does not imply a fixed response time or a guarantee that every future framework release will be supported.
Edition status and learning scope

Version 1.0-rc.1, prepared 17 October 2026, is a publication review candidate. Independent human technical review, professional copyediting and target-reader testing are pending. The preparation date is not a claim that the book has been publicly released.

AI tools were used to generate and revise manuscript text, assist with examples and technical checks, and create cover illustrations. Automated checks and AI-assisted review do not establish independent human approval. Technical diagrams are editable illustrations developed for the book; the case studies and named teaching systems are fictional.
Working with the companion

The attached Agentic_AI_Engineering_companion.zip contains the example guides, dependency lists, tests and the chapter sources used by snippet tests. Keep the extracted chapters/ and examples/ folders together. Read START_HERE.txt before choosing a lab and consult its guide for the boundary between executed checks, simulated services and unexecuted integration work.

The diagrams, analogy limits, exercises and self-checks are part of this complete book. Technical references remain in the chapters and appendices so readers can inspect the mechanisms and version-specific claims behind the explanation.
